subject: pocket-rewriter pair 1: the 0.8B's rewrite drops transparency, and the image obeys
body:
g5, the transparent glass bottle, rendered at exactly the gallery's setting
(Q4_K, 512 square, 20 steps, vendor sigmas, cfg 1.0, seed 42, --mmap) with only
the prompt swapped for the 0.8B's rewrite. ~134 s a step against 87 for the raw
prompt: the rewrite is ~10x longer, and the denoiser pays for every text token.

Raw alpha, before flattening:
  raw prompt     alpha 0 0.11%  1-31 1.19%  mid 0.48%  224-254 10.75%  255 87.47%
  0.8B rewrite   alpha 0 0.00%  1-31 0.00%  mid 0.00%  224-254  5.02%  255 94.98%

Fully opaque -- worse than the raw prompt's fringe. The rewrite explains it: the
0.8B's g5 rewrite contains no transparency instruction at all ("transparent",
"alpha", "RGBA", "cutout" all absent) and substitutes "the white background... a
soft gray drop shadow". The image is a better product photograph and does exactly
what the rewrite asked, which is not what the user asked.

The 9B teacher's rewrite of the same prompt keeps the words but asks for "a
gray-and-white checkerboard transparency preview background" -- a picture of
transparency, not transparency. Its image renders later in the queue; the
prediction (a painted checkerboard, opaque) is being registered before it exists.

One sampled rewrite per arm; a different draw could differ.

subject: pocket-rewriter: the measured text stage, all four arms on seven prompts
body:
The rewrites the image pairs will be built from, measured on four CPU cores:

  arm                  valid JSON  answer words  thinking words  wall (median)  peak RSS
  0.8B Q8_0 llama.cpp     7/7         342             0            14.1 s        1.7 GiB
  0.8B fp32 transformers  7/7         342             0            61.1 s        4.8 GiB
  2B   Q8_0 llama.cpp     7/7         316             0            26.8 s        4.1 GiB
  9B   Q4_K_M teacher     7/7         348            483           386.9 s       10.1 GiB

The teacher reads a 2,481-token system prompt before every request and thinks
for a median 483 words; the students do neither and answer at the same length,
about 27x faster than the teacher.

Two readings a first pass got wrong and corrected before commit: the reference
arm stores its output under a different key, so it is 7/7 valid, not 0/7; and
the teacher does not corrupt quoted text -- every character survives -- it
splits two strings apart ("面馆" then "NOODLE BAR"; "EDGE AI" over "SUMMIT"),
where both pocket models kept each string whole.

Decoding is sampled (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, seed 42), so each rewrite is
one draw: the two runtimes' rewrites of the same prompt share only 4-10% of
their words while matching on every structural measure. The image pairs compare
one draw each, and the article is being told to say so.

subject: Qwen-Image-2.1 CPU gallery, 5 of N: transparent glass -- the background is opaque
body:
Prompt, verbatim: "This is an RGBA image with transparency. A clear glass bottle
of green olive oil with a cork stopper. The image has alpha channel and the
background is transparent."

Q4_K, 512 square, 20 steps, cfg 1.0, seed 42, four CPU cores.

The published file here is flattened onto white, and flattening HIDES the result:
an opaque white background and a transparent one look identical on white. The
raw RGBA output measured before flattening:

  alpha 255      87.47%   the whole background, painted white
  alpha 0         0.11%
  alpha 1-31      1.19%   a thin halo along the bottle's silhouette, plus one
                          stray blob -- every pixel under 32 lies within the
                          bottle's bounding box
  midrange        0.48%
  mean alpha    251.0

So this is not the matte behaviour the article already documents (a transparent
background with hard edges); there is no transparent background at all, and the
clear glass of the neck is opaque too. "99.19% of pixels within 7 levels of an
extreme" is true and means nothing here but "almost everything is opaque".

The cause is not yet known and is not asserted: the transparent teapot the
article already measures came out of ComfyUI with 25-34% of pixels at alpha 0, so
the model can do it. Candidates are the prompt format the transparency path
expects, how stable-diffusion.cpp decodes the RGBA VAE's fourth channel, or Q4_K
at 20 steps. The agent running the experiment has the measurements and is
checking which before the gallery section describes it.

subject: Name the subject in every title: 39 articles and one blog post retitled
body:
A title is what shows in search results, in link previews, in the feed and on
every RelatedArticles card across the site, and in most of those places it is
the only thing a reader sees. Forty of them did not say what the article was
about. "Order is not noise", "The single writer is a Go map", "The lesson is not
in the skill", "Which half of the scaffolding gets eaten" -- good hooks, and not
one of them names a model, a project or a lab.

Each now leads with its subject and keeps the hook it had, which is the
`Subject: hook` shape most of the corpus already used:

  Order is not noise
    -> Jev is not deterministic, and option order is not noise
  The single writer is a Go map
    -> Google's ax agent runtime: the single writer is a Go map
  The test is whether one option can read another
    -> Where to use Jev: the test is whether one option can read another
  Which half of the scaffolding gets eaten
    -> Thinking in Blender: which half of the 3D scaffolding gets eaten
  96 of 100, on a 50/50 inbox
    -> Jev + Kimi K3 fraud detection: 96 of 100, on a 50/50 inbox

Some already named a product but not the model the article is actually about,
and those now say it: "MoVA: ..." is K2-Horizon-MoVA-36B, "Cinference's 450
tokens a second" is Qwen3.8-27B, "VRAM is a policy" is about WanGP and YuE2.
"GAE: ..." now says TencentARC's, because GAE on its own is the far better
known Generalized Advantage Estimation. Four that had the subject trailing at
the end now lead with it.

One title changed for accuracy rather than naming: "AgentJev gets both halves"
claimed more than the body supports, since the article itself says the
cross-candidate channel is untested for carrying a reference. It is now
"AgentJev-0.6B: exact order invariance, and options that still interact",
which is what was measured.

Slugs are untouched, so no URL changes and no redirects. Sixteen in-prose links
cited an old title verbatim as their anchor text; those now cite the new one.
No title is duplicated, and none is longer than titles the corpus already had.

subject: qwen-image-2-1: the CPU section, and a correction to its own result
body:
Completes ba7f4bf, which took the artifacts. This is the lede pointing at the
section, and a correction the author made after looking at the pixels a second
time.

The correction is the part worth reading. The cfg 4.0 run was first written up
as making "both requested lines readable". It does not: the first line's words
are fused into "4 CPUcores" and the frame is badly underexposed. Caption, alt
text and the body sentence now say "discernible" and name the fusion. I checked
the image myself before taking the change -- it is a downgrade of the agent's
own headline, made against its interest, and it is right.

The finding stands either way: at 2.88 bits and 8 steps, guidance buys text
fidelity and resolution does not. 256 to 512 square cost 4.4x the time and made
the chalk LESS legible; turning guidance up cost 2.3x and brought the text part
way back. That is what you would expect if the bits Q2_K discarded were
carrying fine conditioning rather than layout.

Three things in the measurements that were not in the article before:

  the VAE's compute buffer is 9.4x the denoiser's at 256 square -- 613.19 MB
  against 65.24 MB. The autoencoder is 4.7% of the parameters and most of the
  activation memory at small resolutions, so any budget derived from parameter
  counts gets this backwards.

  text encoding is under 5% of an 8-step 256 square run and under 1% at 512,
  which retroactively justifies where community optimisation effort has gone.

  nothing in the prompt asked for transparency and the output still came back
  RGBA, mean alpha 254.97, 99.93% of pixels within 5 levels of opaque. Third
  quantisation, non-transparency prompt, same matte result as the two 1024px
  samples already in the piece.

What is NOT measured is in falsifiers rather than prose: no 1024/40-step run
(the ~10 hour figure is an extrapolation from two resolutions, with a stated
6-15 h band), and no quality control -- there was no disk for a second denoiser,
so Q2_K and the 8-step budget are confounded and the piece says so.

check:spacing run against CpuLedger and the seven other new pages: clean.
Weights and build tree deleted; 13 GB free.

subject: Qwen-Image-2.1 generated on four CPU cores, with no GPU: the artifacts
body:
Three images and the measurement record from actually running it here. The
published low-VRAM figures -- 3.05 GiB measured, 2 GB claimed -- both assume a
GPU; this machine has none (/dev/dri absent, no CUDA, no Vulkan), 4 Xeon cores
and 15 GB of RAM.

The documented Q4_K_M route is 14.63 GB of weights against 11 GB of free disk,
so it does not fit. The route that does:

  runner     leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp @ 2bb7294, ggml CPU backend
  denoiser   Q2_K, 2.56 GB, 2.88 bits/param  (not Q4_K_M)
  encoder    Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct Q4_K_M, 5.03 GB
  vae        bf16, 0.68 GB
  total      8.27 GB downloaded, 7.23 GB resident across the three buffers

The result worth keeping is the one nobody would have predicted: the chalkboard
text is legible at 256 square and smudged at 512, on the same prompt, the same
seed and the same 8 steps. Text rendering is this model's headline capability,
and more pixels made it worse.

data/cpu-run.json carries what makes this checkable rather than anecdotal: every
repo revision and filename, per-stage wall clock (text encode, sampling, VAE
decode), resident buffer sizes per component, download bytes and seconds, the
CPU's ISA flags, the sampler, the scheduler and seed 42. It also states the
claim under test in its own field, so the numbers cannot drift loose from what
they were measuring.

Images verified before committing rather than trusted from their filenames:
14,027 / 9,099 / 31,100 unique colours, full dynamic range, and looked at.

The article section that will present these is still being written; the ledger
component remains unreferenced until it lands.

subject: modular-llm-inference-handbook: the finished article
body:
Five of the handbook's rules are correct formulas attached to the wrong
variable, and all five live in the calculators a reader copies rather than in
the prose, which is mostly careful.

  acceptance length  Leviathan's tau is printed eighteen lines below a bullet
                     defining alpha as accepted/proposed -- what serving stacks
                     log -- but the formula wants the per-position conditional
                     rate. Fed the logged metric it is 55.3% low at gamma=7 and
                     NON-MONOTONIC: it says widening the draft window shortens
                     rounds, while every measured row rises. `MAL = 1 + AR*gamma`
                     fits 7/7 rows of the MI300X sweep exactly, and 6/6 of
                     cinference's MTP-3 pairs. 13 data points, 13 exact fits.
                     Inverting it per row recovers the intended variable: the
                     drafter barely degrades (0.890 -> 0.839), the logged metric
                     collapses 41%.
  KV-cache shape     all three places use num_attention_heads;
                     num_key_value_heads appears nowhere in 70,000 words. The
                     prose gets Llama-3-8B right and links the calculator as its
                     working; the calculator returns 4x that. Across its own six
                     exemplar models: 3x, 4x, 5x, 8x, 16x, and 56.9x on
                     DeepSeek-V3, where MLA is the wrong shape entirely.
  hybrid models      Qwen3-Next-80B: 192 GiB claimed against 6 GiB real, exactly
                     8x GQA times 4x hybrid. Also kills the flat "KV grows
                     linearly with sequence length" -- 61% of a 2,048-token
                     request is fixed recurrent state.
  memory overhead    multiplicative on weight bytes, so quantizing bf16 to 4-bit
                     quarters the KV allowance while the cache does not move and
                     real headroom rises 2.9x. The handbook states the correct
                     version once and contradicts it 90 lines later on the same
                     page.
  TP constraint      past tp_size = num_kv_heads the cache replicates rather
                     than shards; vLLM's own max(1, kv_heads // tp) says so.

The vendor-bias angle is not the story, which is itself a checkable finding.
Framework mentions at HEAD: vLLM 117, SGLang 104, MAX 70. Git archaeology shows
why -- every PR came from bentoml/ branches until #190, modular/ from #192, so
this was BentoML's handbook, and MAX's mention density went 4.38 -> 9.93 per

                   kev said the repeat-request control was one nobody had run,
                   and the sibling had published it the same day. They reconcile

**Nine numbers that did not survive re-derivation.**

  qwen38-pd-serving  549 generated tok/s/GPU should be 556. 9216/1024 is exactly
                     9, so the article's own "a ninth of the headline" is exact
                     at 556 and wrong at 549. Five sites, plus the dependent
                     10.3 -> 10.4 tok/s/user.
  mini-agi           cited 318M, 357.7M and 243M characters for one sample. The

  carveout           an 8x cut in frame encodes described as a cut in VRAM, in
                     an article whose own falsifier worries that it raises VRAM.
  agent-jev-06b      "Six decades" is 5.3 comparing medians, 5.9 comparing worst
                     cases. Both stated.

subject: Add check:links:external, a link audit the build never had
body:
`validate:links` only ever asserted that no article is an orphan -- it says
nothing about whether a link goes anywhere. Nothing in the toolchain checked
that `](/articles/some-slug)` resolves to a file that exists, and an internal
link to a deleted or renamed article is a 404 in published prose that every
existing check is happy with.

This covers both classes. Internal: every site-absolute link into
articles/blog/notes/projects/snippets/papers must resolve to real content,
anchors must name a heading that exists, and `[[wikilinks]]` in notes must
target a real note. External: every http(s) URL in the corpus, HEAD with a
GET fallback, concurrency capped and grouped by host so one domain is not
hammered.

It classifies rather than just passing or failing, because this environment
lies about some hosts: `api.github.com` returns 403 here and `x.com` returns
402 through the proxy, and neither is a broken link. Only 404 and 410 count
as failures; blocked-by-environment and timeout are reported separately.

Kept OUT of `pnpm validate` on purpose -- it makes network calls, which is
the same reasoning that keeps `check:spacing` out. It sits beside that one as
an explicitly-run check. `--internal-only` skips the network entirely, and
that path is cheap enough to run often: 882 internal references, all
resolving.

Tooling only. The link fixes this turns up land separately.

subject: laya-vs-jev: the scoreboard compares two different exams
body:
A T-Rex arena that races Laya running locally on MLX against Jev over
TypeSafe's hosted API. My first read was that this measures the network
rather than the models, which it does — but the repository says so first
and better, in a section headed "Keeping it fair to a slow model" that
ships two mitigations and then concedes "What stays unfair is physics."
So the piece is about what an honest head-to-head actually measures, and
the answer is the harness.

The finding is that the two players are not asked the same question. The
prompt is built from the player's own measured latency: Pilot.timing()
feeds Planner.plan, which sets the safe set, the recommended action and
the distance printed in the state line, because the obstacle moves during
that player's round trip. Over the repo's own 122-snapshot benchmark
sample the two receive an identical question 13.9% of the time; the
distance differs 95.1% of the time, by a median of 136 px. All three
actions are safe for Laya on 71.3% of snapshots and for Jev on 19.7%.

That reframes the hero screenshot, which carries two numbers the prose
never gives: BEST MOVE PICKED, Laya 71% against Jev 89%. The higher score
belongs to the more forced exam — Jev is told fewer actions survive, so
there is less room to pick wrongly. Both finish on 1,175 with zero deaths
and the board declares Jev the winner, which is not the direction the
framing invites you to expect.

Also found, and verified here before accepting: build_question's dict
comprehension tests `a == best` before `plan.safe[a]`, so the recommended
option is prefixed "Safe." unconditionally. When the player's timing
leaves nothing safe the model is handed `run: Safe. Lands on the large
cactus. Best.` — on all 30 such snapshots at Jev's timing and 14 at
Laya's. It lands on the slow player twice as often. The `robust` flag
that would fix it is already on the Plan; the formatter never reads it.

Four corrections to the brief I wrote, all the agent's:
- Results are published, in prose tables and the screenshot, just not in
  any machine-readable form. "No committed results" was half right.
- LayaBackend runs in a spawned child process, not in-process, so one
  player's latency cannot leak into the other through the GIL.
- The jump window is 13-26 frames measured from the physics, median 18,
  not the doc's 18-28. 88.5% of obstacles have a window narrower than one
  serial round trip, which is the quantified case for concurrency.
- The planner benchmark makes 366 calls over 122 snapshots, not 366.

Per-decision agreement is not recoverable from anything the harness
emits, so the article proposes the offline run instead: Planner and
build_question are deterministic and model-free, so fix one timing tuple,
generate the question set once and ask both models identical strings.

Redistributing the screenshot needs Apache-2.0's licence and NOTICE, and
it contains Chromium sprites, so the BSD-3 notice ships too — the pattern
the SAM piece established yesterday. Cross-reference added to laya-mlx,
whose "zero mentions of Jev across 285 tracked files" stays true of those
two repos but no longer of the family.

subject: Three articles: jev-linkmap against our own link graph, laya-mlx, Qwen-Image-2.1
body:
All three started from a social post and ended somewhere the post did not
go. In each case the repository or the licence file says something the
announcement leaves out.

**jev-linkmap** rebuilds a site's internal link map with a decision model,
which is the feature `lib/related.ts` added to this site two commits ago
by a dumber method. Published as a comparison, with our own numbers and
our own failure mode named: tag overlap cannot tell whether a link belongs
on *these words*, so it appends the same block to every page, and the
recency tie-break lets one page take 41 inbound links while the tail
starves. Their method places links inside prose the page already had, and
on the thing a reader notices that is the better product.

Three figures I gave the author were wrong and are corrected in the piece:
- 679/8,460 is not a yes rate. 2,383 verdicts clear the rubric's own gate
  (28.2%); the drop to 679 is `max_links_per_page: 3`, a constant in a
  JSON file, which discards 1,704 model yes answers across 221 pages.
- The editor that cut 392 of 679 links is not a human. `linkmap-
  verified.json` records `"editor": "claude-opus-5"`.
- All-in cost is $17.91, not $15.27 — the $2.07 editor pass is in the
  README and not in the post. Per kept link that is $0.0624 against a
  quoted $0.000952, and the shipped artifact is 3.7x cheaper than a full
  Opus pass, not 240x.

The finding is better than any of that. With the eval queue frozen, moving
the thresholds from 0.70/0.50 to 0.65/0.40 with no rubric text changed
buys 19 of the 20 recall points at higher precision than the $15.51 of
tuning reaches. And the referee reads the rubric System 2 wrote, so the
loop rewrites the exam and the examiner together — judged against the one
referee pass made under a rubric no model authored, the tuned rubric
agrees on anchors 51.4% where the untuned one agreed 70.8%. The README
says "the referee is a strong reader, not ground truth"; the announcement
drops that sentence.

**laya-mlx** ports Laya to Apple silicon. Neither repository mentions Jev
anywhere in 285 tracked files, so "50x faster than Jev" is the poster's
framing; the repos' own same-machine figure is 1.39x. 60 decisions/second
is in the repo as the row that fails its deadline on 100% of ticks. The
fixed-option-count constraint that jev-in-the-browser found in an ONNX
export appears here too and harder: K is a literal in all six published
bundles, and the Snake bundle is exported at K=4 because Snake has four
directions.

I removed a fabricated quotation from this one before committing. The
draft attributed a sentence to the README that appears in neither repo;
replaced with the real one, which is less flattering — "the current ANE
adapter's three sequential calls do not establish a consistent full-game
speedup over compiled MLX."

**Qwen-Image-2.1** is not Apache-2.0. The LICENSE is the Qwen Research
License Agreement dated 2026-09-20: "FOR NON-COMMERCIAL PURPOSES ONLY",
with Non-Commercial defined as "research or evaluation purposes only".
Verified against the file, not the card. It is the first Qwen image model
that is not Apache-2.0. Also: the denoiser is 7,115,124,736 parameters
summed from the shard headers, which is 27.8% of the 25.6B pipeline the
recommended path actually loads, and the one benchmark chart is Qwen's
model on Qwen's prompts judged by Qwen's fine-tune, on the Chinese-prompt
run, which the chart does not say.

subject: A narrated film for mixture-of-experts
body:
58 seconds, eleven beats. A dense feed-forward slab lights up whole for
every token that crosses it, then separates into a stack of eight; a
router scores them and two light, with the other six untouched. The beat
that makes the film worth having is the second token: it arrives and
takes a different pair, so the reader sees that the model is dense over a
batch and sparse only per token — which is the thing prose keeps failing
to land. A blueprint interlude holds the memory-versus-compute split, and
a traffic histogram shows load imbalance as one expert taking most of the
arrows while others idle.

Delivered as one coherent change rather than piecemeal. I held the video
out of the previous two commits on purpose: the encode was complete and
valid on disk, but the caption track and the <Video> embed were not
written yet, and `validate:assets` would not have caught it — it checks
that referenced assets exist, not that existing assets are referenced. A
narrated film without captions is the accessibility regression CLAUDE.md
names, so shipping it in that state would have been worse than waiting.

1.06 MB webm, 1.10 MB mp4, 17 caption cues, `narrated` so it gets
controls rather than a silent autoplay. Verified by pulling frames from
the delivered mp4 rather than from the report.

That is six narrated films and thirteen ambient loops; the build confirms
every one of the nineteen still gets the right player. Function trace
holds at 54.9 MB against Vercel's 250 MB with public/ now at 236 MB, so
none of these assets are being traced into the article route.

Unverified, same as the Kalman film: nothing here can listen, so the
narration's pronunciation has not been checked.

subject: A narrated film for the Kalman filter
body:
66 seconds, eleven beats, on the article that had no figure and the most
drawable mechanism in the corpus. The anchor is the belief ellipse and it
is in every shot: drawn around a dot with its axes marked, pushed along
the motion model and growing as it goes, met by a tall narrow measurement
ellipse, and then replaced by their product — which is visibly inside
both once the three are slid onto one centre.

That containment is the point of the film and it lands twice, which is
what makes it worth making: once as nested ellipses on paper, and once in
a chalk-on-navy slice where the product curve's peak clears a dashed rule
drawn above both inputs. A gain rail then shows the two extremes, trust
the sensor and the estimate jumps onto every reading, trust the model and
it sails straight past, before a real filter run closes it with a
sawtoothing uncertainty band.

The caption separates what is drawn from what is exact, rather than
blanket-disclaiming a frame where the geometry is load-bearing. The
scatter, the lever and the ellipse sizes measure nothing. The update
ellipse is the real normalised product of the two on screen, so the
nesting is the covariance inequality rather than a composition choice,
and the closing band's width is the actual square root of P.

Contact sheets caught what code could not, over three passes: geometry
sized for a 1:1 frame and unreadable at 240px in 16:9, three near-blank
gain shots, `aster` drawing a filled core that put a black blob over the
payoff, a blank first frame that would loop badly, a camera pinned so it
hid the one thing the drift shot is about, an estimate trail lagging a
fix behind, and measurement dots that read black at thumbnail size.

Narration written first and the timeline fitted to it, as the skill
requires: every beat clears the Kokoro headroom, mix at -17.4 LUFS.
1.01 MB webm, 1.01 MB mp4, captioned, `narrated` so it gets controls.

Unverified: nobody in this pipeline can listen to it, so the
pronunciation of "Kalman" has not been checked. Worth one playback.

subject: Retract Monolith 1.0, and finish the figure sweep
body:
The figure work turned up something bigger than a missing figure. The
Hugging Face repo for Monolith 1.0 now holds a single 436-byte README and
nothing else: the experiment is over, the ~3TB of weights are gone, and
the lab says the model it published "is an inflated version of the
original Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct model". I checked that directly rather than
taking it second-hand — the API reports fileCount 1, largestFile 436,
usedStorage 0, lastModified 2026-07-18. The article is dated 2026-07-17,
so the retraction landed the day after it went out.

Kept, not deleted, with a retraction callout at the very top and a
rewritten description. The mechanisms it explains — top-2 MoE routing,
two-stage YaRN, self-speculative decoding — are real techniques and stand
on their own; what does not stand is that any of it describes a model that
shipped. The <ModelCard> panel already reports the empty repo, which is
now evidence rather than metadata.

Second problem in the same article: the four benchmark charts showed
comparator values that appear nowhere in Basalt's published table. Their
provenance was not recorded and I could not reconstruct it. Since the
prose introduces them as Basalt's own comparison, I replaced every
comparator with the figure from basaltlabs.org/monolith and said so in the
lead-in, so the chart is now internally consistent with the source it
claims. This makes the claim look worse, not better — 99.4 against a
best-comparator 44.4 on HLE rather than 61.2.

Figures: four agents worked 21 articles; 11 of them had nothing worth
taking and stay figureless. tgrep's repo contains no image files at all,
Desert Ant's "charts" are HTML bar divs, btl-4 and hauhaucs-qwen-fastmtp
publish no images, glm-5-3-flash-mlx has a wordmark and eleven badges.
Refusals are listed in each article's source note where it made a claim
about them.

Two sources publish their diagrams as in-page animations or inline SVG
with no image file to download — Arcee's nac write-up and both Thinking
Machines announcement posts. Captured at final state rather than
redrawn, since the pixels are then the source's own rendering; each
article says so in the first caption.

Other corrections found along the way:
- kda-half-life said the K3 report does not state the gate's functional
  form. It does, at Eq. 5, and Figure 3a plots it — which is now the
  figure sitting under that sentence.
- btl-3 called a 70.0% score "a fifth of those cases still slip". It is
  30%, and the chart added above it has a 30% bar on that category.
- ternary15m, prime-agent and glm-5-3-flash-uncensored each had a source
  note claiming their sources ship no figures. All three now do.

subject: Add the film, the diagrams and the code the batch was missing
body:
A narrated 69-second film on any-model-can-be-jev, answering the question
that keeps coming back: what actually goes into a decision model and what
comes out. An ordinary model writes one word per forward pass, each fed
back; inside, the last position is a column of numbers and the written
word was simply the largest. The same model is then told to write
nothing — it runs once, the port closes, and the caller supplies the
options. The column is read only at the rows those options name, and
those numbers normalised are the whole output. Then the fork: one shared
page is one pass but position is an input, so swapping two options moves
the answer; a page each makes order inexpressible but leaves a question
spanning two options with no page where both appear, so there is nothing
to find and the bars come up empty.

Built with the vendored hand-drawn-canvas-animation skill. The contact
sheet caught four defects invisible in the code: a zoom that collapsed
the opening shot, geometry too small to read at contact size, two
transition devices back to back, and a ledger shot that did not read.
Voiced with Kokoro-82M and retimed to the measured audio rather than the
reverse — every beat fits with at least 0.25 s of headroom. Captioned,
`narrated` on <Video> so it gets controls instead of a silent autoplay.
1.07 MB mp4, 948 KB webm; only the output is committed.

Diagrams and real quoted code across the eight thinnest articles of the
batch. jev-scores-zero was the thinnest at 1,782 words with no code and
no figure; it now has the binomial argument drawn (P(X=0 | n=100, p=1/3)
= 2.46e-18, computed in the component rather than asserted), the three
scoring architectures as the token windows they actually build, and five
fences from openjev and Laya. tabfm had no code at all and now has seven
fences. Every snippet names its repo, path and commit; the one invented
example is labelled as invented.

Three corrections found by checking rather than by patching around:

- cua-s1-forms claimed none of them published calibration. False on the
  day it shipped: cua-s1-forms carries an ECE in its checkpoint sidecar,
  and Bespoke published a 13-dataset study one day later finding Jev has
  the lower ECE on 11 of 13 subsets — against their own interest. The
  section is narrowed to what is actually still missing.
- three-tiers said Stanley's policy blocks hold 64 constants, 41
  thresholds and 23 caps. Recounted from the repo at 85f39e7: 8 blocks,
  41 probability literals and 28 other entries, two of which alias a
  shared threshold and one of which is a minimum, not a cap. Now 69 /
  41 / 25.
- jev-scores-zero said Jev "wins almost all" of the fifteen rows. It
  loses two. Also re-attributed a quote to the file it is actually in.

subject: Take the orphan rate to zero, and check it stays there
body:
RelatedArticles ranked by tag overlap per page, which left 20 articles
with no inbound link from anywhere: ranking is per-page, coverage is a
property of the whole graph, and the recency tie-break piles the same
recent hubs onto many lists (the busiest took 40 inbound links) while the
tail got none.

Moved the computation to lib/related.ts, where it runs once over the
corpus and memoizes. Prose links count toward coverage, so an article
cited in a sentence needs no help. A second pass then places each
remaining orphan on the page it matches best, with explicit tie-breaks
(higher score, then shorter list, then slug) so the same corpus always
produces the same plan and the rendered HTML does not churn between
builds.

122 orphans before any of this, 20 after tag overlap alone, 0 now.
In-degree min 1 / median 5 / max 40 over 254 articles.

scripts/check-links.mts asserts it, wired in as `pnpm validate:links`.
It can only fail when an article shares no tag with anything else in the
corpus, and it says so — the fix is a tag, not a shrug.

remark-math treats `$` like a code-span delimiter, so any two literal
dollar signs on a page pair up. "It costs $0.0041 per solved task against

subject: Add the WebMCP benchmark piece and "What a decision model cannot do"
body:
**webmcp-windtunnel** — "The 245x factors: 15x of interface, 16x of price". The
brief asked for the multipliers to be decomposed rather than repeated, and the
board supports it: 112x and 245x are ratios of median model cost, and both
factor cleanly into an interface term and a price term. Separating them moves
the interesting number from 245 to **15** — the interface is doing the work
worth writing about, and the rest is per-token pricing.

**what-decision-models-cannot-do** — and this is the one I am most pleased with,
because the agent set out to prove a thesis and reported that it does not hold.
The hypothesis I gave it was that one architectural choice produces all five
reported limits. It produces **two**. Two more are the opposite prices of a
decision the shape leaves open, and the fifth is something else again. An agent

subject: SEO: emit machine-readable citations, and use TechArticle
body:
Researched current practice rather than guessing, then checked the site against
it. Most of the 2026 checklist was already done here — JSON-LD throughout, a
Person entity with sameAs, @id entity references, BreadcrumbList, dateModified,
an author graph, llms.txt, .md twins and permissive AI-crawler directives. Two
real gaps, and one thing I got wrong.

**citation.** Every article on this site is built on primary sources and cites
them inline, but that was only ever prose. The schema now carries them as data:
citationsFromBody() pulls arXiv abstract pages, DOIs, GitHub repositories and
Hugging Face repos out of the body, deduplicated, capped at 20 and order-stable
so the emitted JSON-LD does not churn between builds. Measured across the
corpus: 213 of 252 articles emit at least one, 617 citations total, mean 2.9 per
cited article. This is the single most relevant signal for this site
specifically — an answer engine deciding whether a page is grounded reads the
citation graph, not the paragraphs.

**TechArticle instead of Article.** These are technical explainers and the more
specific type is the one search and answer engines match on.

**What I got wrong:** I added a knowsAbout block to the Person entity as an
E-E-A-T signal and it was already there, better scoped than mine — the existing
list is concrete where mine was generic. Removed my duplicate rather than
replacing theirs. Worth recording because it is the second time this session
that auditing before assuming would have saved a step.

Not fixed, because it cannot be fixed from a repository: backlinks. Nothing in
here creates one. The measured position remains 1 social draft file against 252
articles, and that gap is a decision, not a defect.

subject: Add TabFM, the score-endpoint piece, Jev-as-substrate, and semantic grep
body:
Four more back, and the pattern across them is that the interesting finding is
almost never the headline.

**TabFM** — "the tabular foundation model where 98.8% of the weights never see
a cell". 1,639,444,522 parameters, of which 1,619,925,002 are an ordinary
24-block transformer reading one 2048-d vector per row. The part that actually
reads a table cell is **36,032 parameters**. The zero-shot claim holds and
synthetic-only pretraining genuinely forecloses the contamination risk that
dogs every other tabular claim — but the "single forward pass" is thirty-two of
them.

**any-model-can-be-jev** — the strongest correction in the batch. SGLang has
shipped `/v1/score` since **June 2025**, returning a probability per named
candidate token on an ordinary generative checkpoint, one forward pass, no
decoding. It was built for rerankers **fifteen months before the System One
category existed**. That is the entire mechanism, and it reframes the week: the
readout is a serving flag, not a model property.

**jev-as-substrate** — "every pixel is a Choice". jev-paint asks one 16-way
Choice per pixel; a 32x32 painting is 1,024 questions in 8 requests for about
half a US cent. The agent then read the code and found the confidence-to-brush
-width mapping gates strokes off below 1.92 effective colours — **so the widest
brush is the one it never draws**. That is the kind of thing only reading the
source finds.

**search-by-meaning** — 309 lines of zero-dependency Node. The argument against
vector search is right and worth restating: cosine distance has no complement,
so "about a refund but not a request" is not expressible as similarity, while
1 - P(proposition) is.

Validate green: 251 articles, 284 MDX files.

subject: Fix the H1, add related articles, and ship two more pieces
body:
## SEO fixes, from an audit Satyajit ran

**H1.** The homepage H1 was the bare name — 14 characters, and a weak document
title: it tells a search engine, or a reader arriving from a link, nothing about
the subject. It now carries the name and what the site is about, 54 characters,
with the qualifier styled down so the visual hierarchy is unchanged.

**Internal links.** The audit flagged repeated and over-long anchor texts. The
measured problem underneath was worse: of 243 articles, **116 had no inbound
internal link at all (48%)** and 87 had no outbound one (36%), with 51 fully
isolated. Orphans get crawled less and rank worse, and it lands hardest on the
newest work, which has had least time to be linked by hand — cua-s1-forms and
three-tiers both had zero inbound links despite being the strongest recent
pieces.

components/site/related-articles.tsx computes related pieces from tag overlap at
build time, Jaccard-scored so a five-tag article cannot out-rank a tight pair
just by having more tags to collide on, tie-broken by recency. Mounted on every
article page. The anchor text is the target article's own title: descriptive,
and unique per target, which is precisely what the audit meant. Not "read more".

This cannot fix backlinks. Nothing in this repo can — those come from other
people citing the work.

## Two more articles

**generative-ui-by-decision** — the agent installed json-render and ran
`experimental_composeSpec` against its real catalog through a stub evaluator
that recorded every payload. Composing a screen is not one call per slot: the
round-trip count is **constant at 2** for a new tree regardless of element
count, membership then placement. So "rendered in milliseconds" survives, but
the denominator is two round trips, not one per component. It also found that
**28.4% of a select call is one 271-byte instruction string repeated verbatim
across 30 questions**, and that the request body is dead linear at 668.6 bytes
per candidate, hitting the documented context ceiling at ~196 candidates.

The finding that keeps recurring across this whole batch: confidence is
produced, range-checked, surfaced in the trace, and **read by nothing**. No
threshold, no fallback, no handoff anywhere in the repo.

**three-tiers** takes a late wording edit from its agent.

## Corrections carried in from agent reports

Three things I told an agent were true and were not, now corrected in the
article rather than repeated: "up to 193x faster and 444x cheaper in our tests"
is TypeSafe's own homepage figure, not a benchmark result from the post I
attributed it to; `dimensionalOS/dimos` has no Jev integration at all, zero
occurrences at the commit checked; and jev-recruiter publishes no recruiting
numbers, its README saying explicitly that inherited measurements "describe the
upstream agent, not recruiting performance".

Validate green: 250 articles, 283 MDX files. Typecheck clean.

subject: Add four articles: Splash, ORPO, LiveTranslate, SAM 3.1
body:
Four back from the batch, and every one of them leads with the denominator or
the caveat rather than the headline. That was the brief and it held.

**Splash** — "144 tok/s needs 502 GB/s, and Apple sells two M5 Max chips". The
agent did the bandwidth arithmetic rather than repeating the number: one decode
step reads 16.73 GB, computable from the repo's own tensor shapes and its
4.5-bit pack, and Inco publish the acceptance length separately, so both figures
can be checked against a memory bus. The written benchmark's 74 tok/s on an
M5 Pro needs 84% of that chip's peak bandwidth; the 144 going around needs
502 GB/s, which only one of the two M5 Max variants Apple sells can supply. The
claim is not wrong, it is underspecified — and which chip you have decides it.

**ORPO** — the maths survives and the compute story does not. The odds ratio is
chosen for its gradient behaviour and that argument holds up. But the frozen
reference model is 13.49 GiB against 107.91 GiB of trainable state at
Mistral-7B, so dropping it cuts 25% of per-step FLOPs, not half. The agent also
found the result the paper never emphasised: GSM8K is the one benchmark where
ORPO is the only preference objective that improves.

**LiveTranslate** — the better result is the one nobody quotes. Average lagging
2.8s to 2.3s is the headline; the same figure also publishes xCOMET-XXL 83.0 to
85.7 on the same 70 directions, which matters more, because in simultaneous
interpretation latency and quality normally trade and here they did not. What
does not survive: the 2.8s baseline is Qwen's own previous model rather than a
competitor, and the eval is 19 languages, not the 60 the announcement implies.

**SAM 3.1** — three different speedup numbers, all true. The model card says ~7x
at 128 objects, the blog says throughput doubles, the paper says 5.2x. The
difference between them is the whole story: the number is a slope, not a
speedup. Meta published the entire curve, including the point where multiplexing
is 7% slower, which is worth crediting.

All four carry 10 to 12 falsifiers, real figures from their sources served
locally, and receipts. Validate green: 248 articles, 281 MDX files.

subject: Add "The middle tier is not in the middle"
body:
First article back from the batch, and it disagrees with the post it was asked
to examine, which is the right outcome for an essay that was supposed to test a
claim rather than relay it.

The claim: agents now split three ways — deterministic code, a decision model, a
reasoning model — and the decision tier sits "in between". The split is real;
the agent read three codebases built that way. The spectrum reading is not. On
the six properties that actually distinguish the tiers, three are not monotonic
and two bottom out in the middle. The decision tier is the only one that cannot
see across its own options, and the only one that cannot tell you why it chose.
So it is not medium-reasoning; it is a different kind of thing that happens to
sit between the other two on cost.

The constructive half is better than the critique: Stanley's router and an xArm7
harness independently show the same workaround, and the workaround turns out to
be the architecture — deterministic code builds the relation, then hands it down
as an independent question. That is the same shape three other projects reached
this week without coordinating.

It also lands the measured version of TypeSafe's homepage headline. Against the
one matched, replayable head-to-head in this ecosystem: cost per call 336x
measured against 444.6x claimed, which broadly survives; latency per call 4.57x
measured against 193.6x claimed, which does not. The caveats cut against the
finding rather than for it — one seed-0 trial, and both sides are remote HTTP
endpoints, so the network inflates Jev's absolute latency and makes 4.57x a
floor rather than a ceiling.

The detail worth keeping: Jev used 226 model calls and 113 control cycles
against the frontier model's 212 and 106. Per decision the expensive model was
better. The entire win is per-call price, not fewer decisions — a cleaner story
than the headline, and only visible by reading the logs.

One observation the agent found in the harness that is worth its own note: Jev
reports 98/96/93/86 percent on its four output heads, while both GPT columns
report 100 percent across the board — self-reported JSON confidence against a
native probability. That contrast is the whole argument for calibrated decisions
in one table.

10 falsifiers, three original components, receipts cross-checked against the
prose. Validates clean.

recorded in the file and they cut the honest way: this is one seed-0 trial, and
both sides are remote HTTP endpoints, which inflates Jev's absolute latency and
therefore makes 4.57x a conservative floor for Jev rather than a ceiling.

subject: Add @huggingface/transformers, and keep its 140 MB out of every function
body:
An agent building the in-browser decision-model demo installed
@huggingface/transformers, which pulls onnxruntime-web: 140 MB in node_modules,
almost all of it WASM.

That is a deploy hazard, not just weight. Vercel rejects any serverless function
over 250 MB uncompressed and /articles/[slug] already traces at ~53 MB because
it bundles every article, so if the output-file tracer decides that 140 MB is
reachable from a server route the build fails. This branch has already been
broken once by exactly that mechanism, so the guard goes in before the import
does rather than after the failed deploy.

next.config.ts now excludes onnxruntime-web and @huggingface/transformers from
outputFileTracingExcludes for all routes, under both node_modules and the pnpm
store path. These are browser runtimes by definition — nothing server-side can
legitimately need them — so excluding them is correct rather than a workaround.

The dependency is committed ahead of the code that uses it, which is backwards,
but leaving an installed package uncommitted while ten agents work in the same
tree is worse. If the demo turns out not to be viable — the model download plus
a 140 MB runtime may simply be indefensible as a page weight, which is a
legitimate finding — this comes back out along with the excludes.

subject: Cut the RLCD film into shots, per the rule it was still breaking
body:
The film followed style.md on palette, renderers, devices, guides and
misregistration after the last pass, but it still broke rule 10 — shots run 0.8
to 2.5 seconds — with beats of 3.5 to 7.0, and rule 12, one thing per shot. Both
were named as outstanding in that commit rather than hidden, and this fixes
them.

The fix is to stop treating a narration beat as a shot. A spoken line can carry
across a cut; the picture does not have to sit still for six seconds while it
finishes. A small shot() helper splits a beat into sub-shots and reports which
one tau falls in, so five scenes now cut inside a single line:

- uses, three shots: CHOICE, then SCORE, then NOUL, each alone and filling the
  frame instead of three columns of nine small boxes sharing it. This is the
  rule 12 fix as much as the rule 10 one.
- route, two: the requests land along the axis, then the threshold arrives and
  takes sides. The dots stay grey until there is a threshold to be above.
- tally, two: the hundred marks fill, then the bars answer them.
- proper, two: the curve draws itself, then the ball settles on 0.70.
- gapdocs, two: what is published, then what is not, each centred on its own
  shot rather than two columns read at once.

Average shot length goes from 5.4s to about 3.9s across eighteen shots. That is
a real improvement and it is still above the rule's ceiling; the remaining gap
is bounded by the narration, since a beat cannot be shorter than the line it
carries. Going further means writing shorter lines, not cutting faster.

One bug worth recording: sceneGapDocs read `sh` on its title line and declared
it two statements later, so every frame in that scene threw on the temporal
dead zone. Frame 0 rendered fine and the failure only appeared under --grid,
which walks the whole film — a good argument for looking at the contact sheet
before the full render, which is already the first bullet in CLAUDE.md.

Durations are unchanged, so the af_bella narration was re-muxed untouched.

subject: Add the Jev-scores-zero article, and correct the RLCD piece
body:
Paras Chopra's independent benchmark puts Jev at 0 of 100 on relational choice
— questions where one option's content decides another — on a suite where the
same model scores 100% on rule/evidence judgment and 98% on ARC-Challenge.

Zero is the informative number, and it is why this is an article rather than a
line in the digest. A model that finds a task hard scores badly and floors out
near chance. Getting none right across a hundred attempts is not difficulty; it
means the question being answered is not the question being asked.

That makes it the behavioural signature of something the RLCD piece could only
argue from two sentences of documentation: Jev's options never share a context.
If each option is encoded and scored alone, an option that refers to another
option is referring to something absent from its forward pass. The earlier claim
was labelled Reasoned and carried a falsifier; this is the outcome that
reasoning requires, and a strange one under any architecture where options see
each other. It also sharpens the parallelism claim — not just questions in
parallel, but options within a question, at the cost of a class of question
being unanswerable by construction.

On Laya, the article corrects a claim rather than repeating it. Laya is the most
complete open System One so far — 421M ModernBERT-large, Apache 2.0, the same
three primitives, and the only one publishing both a calibration error (0.081)
and an option-order stability figure. It is being described as predating Jev by
months. Three independent timestamps say otherwise: PyPI upload time
2026-09-18 04:38:51, the Hugging Face commits API 2026-09-18 05:05:55, and the
GitHub first commit the same day — three days after Jev launched on the 15th.
PyPI and HF set those server-side; GitHub's history was rewritten and one of its
own commit messages says so, which is why it is listed last.

What is real is the prior work, and it deserves crediting properly rather than
dismissing with the overclaim. arXiv 2510.01237, 23 September 2025, assesses
model uncertainty before generation and routes on it — a year ahead of Jev, and
genuinely the idea behind confidence-gated routing. It is described in the
author's write-up as "the exact framework for schema-based decisions guided by
reinforcement learning"; it is a hallucination-mitigation paper. Adjacent and
early is a better story than first, because it is checkable.

Two corrections to my own earlier work, made in place rather than quietly:

The RLCD article said the only Jev calibration number in existence was one
outsider's MMLU probe. TypeSafe still publishes none — that half stands — but
third parties have since measured ECE 0.246 and order-instability 0.13. The
claim should have been about who publishes, not about what exists, and the
original sentence is left visible above a dated note.

The cua-s1 article's order-sensitivity section now points at the 0/100, because
order-insensitivity and option-isolation are the same property and that result
is the price of it.

Credit where the benchmarks are honest: Laya's BENCHMARKS.md disarms its own
comparison ("Jev figures are third-party published, never measured here") and
reports its base checkpoints scoring near chance zero-shot. Chopra published row
eight when burying it as an outlier was available. Both are worth more than any
number in either release.

subject: Add a Manim explainer of the decision readout, narrated
body:
The hand-drawn film argues why calibration is worth optimising for. It is the
wrong instrument for the mechanism, which is arithmetic: a slice out of a logit
vector and a softmax over three numbers. So the cua-s1-forms article now opens
its two-families section with a second film built in Manim — the tool
3Blue1Brown is made with — at 51 seconds, narrated and captioned.

Five beats: the ordinary forward pass and its 151,936-wide logit vector; a
decision model stopping there and boxing three rows; the softmax done out loud,
subtract-max then exponentiate then divide; the same option list reversed with
27.8% of decisions changing; and the other family, whose head has output
dimension one and runs once per option.

Every number on screen is real rather than illustrative, which is the whole
reason to animate this rather than draw it. The three logits — 22.0, 26.375,
24.375 — are openjev's committed option_logits for the first row of
authored144, and the exp values, the Z of 1.147923 and the three probabilities
are that arithmetic carried out. The head shapes are read from
open-jev-deberta's safetensors header. The 27.8% is measured by joining
openjev's option_reversal rows back to the originals they came from.

Narration reuses the film-narration skill unchanged, which is the useful part:
Manim's timings are fixed by code rather than chosen to fit speech, so the
scene is instrumented to print self.renderer.time at each act boundary and the
beat durations are written to match. Every beat cleared the Kokoro threshold on
the first attempt.

Toolchain notes, since none of this was installed: Manim CE needs
libcairo2-dev and libpango1.0-dev, plus a LaTeX with dvisvgm for MathTex. The
site's own Hanken Grotesk is used for the prose, converted from the woff2 the
hand-drawn film already embeds, because pango cannot read woff2.

CLAUDE.md's film section was also stale in two ways and is corrected: it still
named Piper after the switch to Kokoro, it stated a single 0.5s headroom figure
where the requirement is per-engine, and it assumed every film is hand-drawn.

subject: Add a snippet: the two ways to read a decision out of a model
body:
The architecture explanation kept landing at the wrong level, so this is the
mechanism as runnable code instead of prose. Both functions take the same
arguments and return the same shape — one probability per caller-supplied
option, no text generated, option count not baked into any weight — and the
mechanisms underneath have almost nothing in common.

Family 1, vocabulary readout: the options are text in the prompt, the model
picks a letter, and the forward pass is the ordinary next-token one. You slice
the rows for "A", "B", "C" out of a 151,936-wide logit vector and renormalise.
That is openjev, Nimble, and any LoRA on an LLM.

Family 2, per-option scalar scorer: no letters and no vocabulary. The head's
output dimension is one and it runs once per option, so N is a loop bound. The
snippet carries open-jev-deberta's real tensor shapes — 0.weight [1024, 3072],
2.weight [1, 1024], 3,147,777 parameters — read from the safetensors header
rather than transcribed from a card.

Then the three consequences, in the order they will bite: order sensitivity
(27.8% of openjev's decisions flip on a reversed list, measured from its own
committed predictions), cardinality (16 options in family 1 because that is how
many single-token letters there are, against 255 for Jev), and cost (one forward
pass regardless of N, against N head evaluations over a shared encoding).

The first family's claim is checkable and checked: openjev commits both
option_logits and probabilities, and recomputing softmax over the logits
reproduces the committed distribution across all 144 rows to 9.7e-08, which is
the six-decimal rounding in the JSON. The returned probabilities are exactly a
softmax over the sliced rows and nothing more.

subject: Follow the animation skill's own style rules, and measure option-order bias
body:
Two things, and the first is a correction.

## The film was not built the way the skill says to build it

Satyajit asked whether I had actually used the skill. I had used its core.js and
skipped its procedure, which says to read references/style.md before drawing
anything. Reading it, the film broke six of the fourteen rules:

- **Rule 11, palette discipline.** The colours were typed out as hex literals in
  the film. They happened to be risoPop's values, which is not the point — they
  are now destructured from PAL.fills.
- **Rule 5, two renderers over one geometry.** There was no blueprint mode at
  all. The penalty-plot section is literally "look inside", so it now runs in
  blueprint: chalk on night, and the puppet keeps its geometry and loses its
  fills, which is what the rule asks for.
- **Rule 10, transition devices.** There were none. The blueprint now arrives on
  an ink blot wipe, the first device in the rule's own order of preference.
- **Rule 6, guides show.** Construction lines with ticks now sit under the
  penalty plot, so it reads as a drawing being made rather than a chart.
- **Rule 4, misregistration is an accent.** No scribble anywhere. Added on the
  torso only — one part per frame, never a background.

Still outstanding and worth naming rather than hiding: rule 10 also wants shots
of 0.8 to 2.5s and mine run 3.5 to 7.0, and rule 14 says the sign-off is the
only text a film needs while mine is captioned throughout. The second is a
deliberate override — Satyajit asked for captions and a grotesk, and the user
beats the style guide. The first is a real miss that needs cutting within
narration beats rather than one shot per beat, and is not done here.

Durations did not change, so the af_bella narration was re-muxed unchanged.

## 27.8% of openjev's decisions flip when you reverse the option order

The question that prompted this — how a model can take options that change per
request, and whether their order matters — has two different answers depending
on which family the model is in, and the article now says so with a measurement
rather than an argument.

openjev is the vocabulary-readout family, and its src/semif_phase1/direct.py is
the plainest statement of it anywhere: one forward pass, slice the rows for the
tokens "A", "B", "C" out of a 151,936-wide vocabulary, softmax those. The
options are text in the prompt; the model only ever picks a letter. There is
even a guard refusing to run unless each letter is "one exact round-trip token".

So order is a liability there, and openjev ships the experiment that shows it:
an option_reversal perturbation carrying the base_id it was derived from. Joining
each reversed row back to its original, the model changes its mind on 10 of 36 —
27.8% — and confidently in both directions, going from 'insufficient' at p=0.871
to 'contradicted' at p=0.987 on evidence that did not move.

The part worth keeping: accuracy hides this completely. The reversed set scores
80.6%, identical to the irrelevant-context set, because flips land on and off
gold in roughly equal measure. It is visible only because openjev publishes
per-row predictions and the provenance to pair them.

The scalar-scorer family does not fix this; it cannot express it. No letter, no
position, nothing for a prior to attach to — which is exactly what TypeSafe
claims for Jev when it says the model "doesn't see a level's number or its
neighbours", and why the ordering has to be imposed client-side afterwards.

drops, no horizontal overflow at 360 and 390px.

subject: Add the open System One article: cua-s1-forms, Nimble, jev-ultrafast
body:
The RLCD piece had to reconstruct Jev's architecture from two context limits
and one sentence about scoring levels separately, because TypeSafe publishes
fourteen words about it. A week later three projects have rebuilt the shape in
the open with weights, data and training code.

content/articles/cua-s1-forms.mdx:

- **cua-ai/cua-s1-forms** is the reconstruction, built. 706,048 parameters
  trained from scratch — byte-level embedding, a 2-layer encoder at width 128,
  and an attention head whose output dimension is one, evaluated once per
  option, with cross-entropy taken over the live option count. That is the
  per-option scalar scorer the last article argued Jev must be, under MIT. Its
  234,067-row synthetic dataset is the more transferable contribution: forms
  padded with forced look-alike confuser pairs so the model must read the whole
  label, and splits made disjoint by the exact sorted set of element
  descriptions rather than by form name.
- **bespokelabs/Bespoke-Nimble-9B** contributes a data recipe rather than an
  architecture. Contrastive curation builds examples in pairs that differ in one
  sentence, where that sentence flips the answer and the pipeline verifies the
  fact is unknowable without it. 2,676 training examples take Qwen3.5-9B from
  215/324 to 292/324 and clear an untuned 27B.
- **browser-use/jev-ultrafast** is the harness, and its contribution is a
  boundary: the runtime enumerates the controls that exist and the model returns
  an index into that list. No screenshots, no coordinates, and no generated
  selectors, which is containment rather than optimisation.

Three things the article says that the releases do not:

The 99.7% vs 83.6% figure measures a specialist at home against a generalist
measured cold — cua-s1 trained on 150k rows from the generator that produced the
eval, Jev having seen none of it. The trycua source release says as much itself.

Nimble's 106 ms against Jev's 246.7 ms compares local GPU compute with an HTTPS
round trip. The unremarked number in the same table is more interesting: the
untuned base is 58.1 ms on the same rows and hardware, so the adapter nearly
doubles latency, which is what an unmerged LoRA looks like. That one is a
falsifier, not an assertion.

And the through-line: not one of the three reports a calibration number, in a
category whose name is "calibrated decisions". Bespoke come closest with "the
calibration is implicit", which is their own untested hypothesis — their words
are "didn't do ablations" and the objective uses hard labels. The open
reproductions have closed the gap on architecture and training and reproduced
the silence on the thing the category is named after.

Credit where it is due, and it is the most credible thing in either release:
Bespoke published Jev at 302/324 against their own model's 292/324, on their own
benchmark, having built the eval themselves.

Two original SSR components, zero JS: OptionScorer draws the forward pass with N
as a loop bound rather than a weight, and ContrastivePair shows a curated pair
with its one edited sentence. Plus a receipts table across all four
implementations and four falsifiers.

with 12 SVGs and the receipts table. No space drops, no horizontal overflow at

subject: Add a film-narration skill, and name the third RLCD
body:
Two things, both from questions the film raised.

## brand-crew/skills/film-narration

Our own skill, not vendored. Packages the Piper pipeline used on the RLCD film
so the next narrated film is a command rather than an afternoon: narrate.py
takes a beat script, synthesises one clip per scene, places each at its scene
offset, normalises to -17 LUFS and emits both voice.wav and a WebVTT caption
track; mux.sh mixes the film's generated score underneath as a bed and produces
the mp4, webm and poster.

Two things the skill enforces because getting them wrong is quiet rather than
loud:

**The narration sets the pace, not the film.** Write the line, measure it, and
lengthen the scene to fit. narrate.py exits non-zero on a beat that overruns
rather than letting it clip.

**Piper is stochastic.** The same text resynthesised comes out a different
length — measured across one 13-beat script run twice, drift reached 0.42s on a
single five-second line, in both directions. A beat that fits with 0.2s to
spare today overruns tomorrow, which means the film stops being reproducible
from its own script. The threshold is 0.5s and the reason is written down.

That finding came from running the committed scripts against the real film
rather than trusting the ad-hoc versions that produced it, and it changed the
film: six scenes were too tight under that drift, so the film is 69.3s with
every beat now carrying at least half a second of silence before the next cut.
Re-rendered, re-narrated and re-muxed through the committed scripts end to end,
so the skill is known to reproduce what is committed rather than assumed to.

The skill also carries the rule that the component change implies: a narrated
film must pass `narrated` and must ship captions, because browsers only
autoplay muted and narration without captions is an accessibility regression.

## The third RLCD

Searching for how RLCD is trained is actively misleading, and the article now
says why. RLCD was already taken: Yang et al. 2023 (arXiv 2307.12950, Berkeley
and Meta, with a reference implementation at facebookresearch/RLCD) published
"RLCD: Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Distillation for Language Model
Alignment" — a real RLHF-family method with a paper, code and ablations. So the
string has three referents: that one, TypeSafe's "reinforcement learning for
calibrated decisions", and the community's "constrained decoding" guess that
nobody ever claimed. The only one of the three that is TypeSafe's is the only
one with no method attached, and it is easy to find Yang et al. and believe you
have found the answer.

Also checked the premise behind the article's central claim against the open
web rather than TypeSafe's properties alone. Independent write-ups reach the
same conclusion: the reward function, architecture, training procedure and
calibration methodology are all undisclosed.

is film-narration's own published SKILL.md. The skills index lists 17 and still
excludes the vendored one. Article, mp4, webm and vtt all serve with the right
content types, no space drops, no overflow at 360 and 390px.

subject: Rebuild the RLCD film as an explainer, and keep the vendored skill unpublished
body:
The film was a five-beat statement of the contract. It said what Jev is and
never said why any of it works, which is the question the article exists to
answer. Rebuilt at 62 seconds in thirteen beats, and the middle of it is now an
argument rather than an assertion.

The new material:

- **What you actually ask it.** The three request shapes from the docs —
  Choice up to 255 options, Score 2 to 10 ordered levels, Noul one probability.
- **What the number is for.** Requests scattered along a confidence axis and
  split by a threshold: above it ships on its own, below it a person looks.
  That is confidence-gated routing, TypeSafe's own headline pattern, and it is
  why the calibration argument matters commercially rather than academically.
- **Why a model would ever report a number that makes it look unsure.** This
  is the centrepiece and it is a real theorem, drawn. Hold the true belief at
  0.70 and plot the expected penalty against what the model reports. Under a
  linear penalty the curve is a straight line, so the minimum is at the edge
  and the ball rolls off it: always claim 1.00. Under Brier the curve has its
  minimum at exactly 0.70 and the ball settles there. That is the whole of what
  makes a scoring rule proper, and it is what "calibrated decisions" names.
  Both minima verified numerically before the caption asserted them: linear
  argmin 1.0000, Brier argmin 0.7000, derivative zero at q = p.
- **The gap.** The published output contract against four blank lines for the
  loss, the reward, the training data and a calibration number.

Geometry is now derived rather than eyeballed. handAt() computes where the
puppet's hand actually lands from its own body plan, and the card stack, the
pointing arrow and the highlight are laid off that, so the arrow starts at the
fingertips and runs level instead of floating near them. One BASE line, one
column centre, one PAD for every standoff.

The build caught something validate cannot. The site republishes every
brand-crew SKILL.md byte-for-byte at /.well-known/agent-skills/ with a sha256,
and the vendored skill's frontmatter is not valid YAML: its description is a
plain scalar containing a colon-space, which lenient parsers accept and
gray-matter throws on. Two things follow.

The frontmatter is rewrapped as a folded block scalar, carrying the identical
1,565 characters with no escaping and no change to the prose. Recorded as the
third local delta.

And lib/skills.ts now skips any skill directory containing a VENDORED.md. That
endpoint advertises the skills that author and maintain this site, with a
digest per file. Serving somebody else's SKILL.md from it would put their work
under our name and our digest, which MIT permits and honesty does not. The
skill still installs with the plugin and still works locally; it is just not
advertised as ours. Verified: the index lists 16 skills, the vendored one is
absent, and its URL 404s.

subject: Add the Jev/RLCD deep dive, with a character-led film
body:
The three existing Jev pieces cover the claims, the inference mechanism and
the downstream repos. None of them answer the question that keeps being
asked: how the model is built and trained, and what RLCD actually is.

content/articles/rlcd-calibrated-decisions.mdx, ~7,700 words:

- RLCD expands to "Reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions", not
  constrained decoding. Verbatim from the AI primer and corroborated by the
  launch post's comparison table.
- The complete published specification is three bullets plus a frequentist
  gloss. Grepping all 835,504 bytes of llms-full.txt, the launch post, the
  manifesto and evals.typesafe.ai returns zero hits for loss function,
  Brier, expected calibration, reliability diagram, proper scoring,
  cross-entropy, fine-tuning, checkpoint or distillation, and zero for ECE
  as a whole word. There is no published calibration number for Jev.
- Two undocumented formulas recovered from TypeSafe's own worked examples:
  score is the expectation of the level index under the returned
  distribution, exact on 6 of 6 published Score answers; confidence is the
  top probability rescaled, (p_max - 1/N) / (1 - 1/N), fitting 12 of 15
  pairs. All three misses are off the primitive reference pages, and the
  quickstart one matches normalised entropy instead, so the docs carry two
  inconsistent conventions for a field that gates routing.
- Checkpoint anatomy for four open reproductions, every shape read from the
  real safetensors header by HTTP range request.
- The first reliability diagram computed from openjev's committed logits:
  252 rows, frozen Qwen3.5-4B, no training. The miscalibration runs the
  wrong way for routing — honest where it is confident, overconfident in
  the middle, where a threshold has to work.

The film is rebuilt from scratch. The previous one was a flat wireframe
diagram that did not explain itself: boxes, thin lines and a tick. This one
is character-led and captioned in Hanken Grotesk, the site's own face, so
the argument reads without narration — an LLM writes, Jev instead points at
one of your options and says how sure, and the same hundred answers under an
honest number and a dishonest one produce two bars whose shortfall is the
thing RLCD is named after. The hundred marks illustrate what calibration
means operationally; the caption says plainly that they are not a
measurement of Jev, and points at openjev's real numbers further down.

All three films recompressed with ffmpeg, x264 crf 33 and VP9, audio

subject: Memoize the content loader: 142ms per call to 0, build 5m10s to 2m
body:
The content layer re-globbed, re-read, re-parsed and re-Zod-validated every
file of a kind on every single call. Measured: 142 ms for the 238 articles,
paid in full by getArticle(slug) to return one item.

That cost multiplied everywhere. A page render calls it several times over
(the page, generateMetadata, and the JSON-LD), and the build does that for
every article plus its OG image plus its .md variant. The dynamic routes --
/search, /api/search, /api/ask, /api/chat, /api/mcp -- paid it per request.

Content is read off disk and is immutable for the lifetime of a deployment,
so it is memoized per kind. unstable_cache is the documented tool for
non-fetch data but it wants an async function and adds serialization; load()
is synchronous and in-process, so a module-level memo matches the data's
actual lifetime and costs nothing.

Memoization is skipped when NODE_ENV is development, where the files change
under us and re-reading is the entire point. Verified both ways: in
production the second and subsequent calls are 0 ms, in development every
call still re-reads at ~150 ms.

Callers receive a shallow copy. Several of them `return load(...)` straight
through, and a single in-place sort by one caller would otherwise corrupt
the entry for every later reader.

Measured on a clean build: wall time 5m10s to 2m00s, all 238 articles still
prerendered, largest function trace unchanged at 52.1 MB. Verified against
pnpm start rather than dev -- article body, articles list, .md variant with
its receipts tables, /api/search, and a 404 for an unknown slug.

subject: Add lexing-on-the-gpu and confidence-gated-fraud-detection
body:
Two subjects where the headline number is real and the thing it is measured
against is the story.

Pareas lexes, parses and analyses on the GPU, and its thesis claims it beats
simdjson on large inputs. The comparison's baseline is simdjson single
threaded on the other benchmark machine, at 0.86 GB/s on the 442 MB file --
well below what simdjson is normally quoted at. More importantly the timing
excludes the PCIe upload: Appendix C reports Upload as a separate column and
leaves it out of Total, while a table three pages earlier in the same
appendix includes its transfer in Total. Two definitions of Total in one
appendix, and the simdjson comparison uses the one that drops the transfer.
Counting it, the win on the largest file falls from 3.03x to 1.86x and one
file flips to a simdjson win.

The repo has no test comparing its token stream to a reference, so the
article builds one around the project's own dead-code interpreter, driving
its real generated tables through the same merge operator the kernel uses.
Against CPython's json on fourteen inputs: an uppercase hex escape is
rejected though RFC 8259's ABNF is case-insensitive, a raw DEL in a string
is rejected though the RFC allows it, and invalid UTF-8 is accepted silently
-- which matters because simdjson validates UTF-8, so the two programs in
that bar chart are not doing equal work.

It also quantifies the thesis's own unquantified warning. Rebuilding the
table generator and editing the grammars: one string rule is 97.6% of the
JSON table, adding a single string rule to the compiler grammar takes it
from 7.4 MB to 126.5 MB, and adding a block comment exceeds 2.8 GB and dies
with bad_alloc. That last row is published as a lower bound and labelled as
one.

The fraud-detection piece is about a demo whose only artifact is a 12.8
second screen recording, so every number in it is read off the frames. The
full confusion matrix recovers: 45 of 49 fraud caught, zero false alarms,
precision 100%, recall 91.8%. The base rate is 50% -- the app's own footer
says so, and says that confidence is not accuracy and a balanced sample is
not production prevalence. The thread carries none of those caveats, and
that gap is the article.

Precision of 100% was measured against 50 negatives, so the exact one-sided
95% bound puts the false-positive rate at up to 5.8%; at a realistic 0.5%
prevalence that same bound puts precision at 7.4%. The published spend also
rules out the mechanism the demo advertises: the per-email cost pins the
input at about 705 billed tokens, which leaves roughly five output tokens
per escalated review. The expensive model emitted a label, not a chain of
thought. And at least three of the four residual errors were escalated,
reviewed and still returned wrong -- "review fixed 5, broke 0" counts flips,
not agreements in error.

subject: Fix the Vercel deploy: keep public/ out of serverless functions
body:
The deploy was failing with "The Vercel Function articles/a6b-k-expansion is
266.43mb uncompressed which exceeds the maximum uncompressed size limit of
250mb". Reproduced locally by summing each route's output-file-tracing
manifest: /articles/[slug] traced to 266.4 MB, matching Vercel's figure to
the decimal.

Two causes, one of them mine.

First, public/ was being traced into serverless functions, where it has no
business being -- Vercel serves it from the CDN. The <Receipts> component I
added reads its committed JSON with readFileSync(join(process.cwd(),
"public", src)), and lib/markdown.ts does the same for the agent-facing .md
variants. Because `src` is not a literal, the tracer cannot tell which file
is wanted and conservatively includes all of public/. That is 214 MB of
figures and video, and since <Receipts> is registered globally it reached
every MDX-rendering route: eight routes between 221 MB and 266 MB, seven of
them just under the limit and one over. It also compounded -- every figure
an article added inflated eight functions at once, which is why the first
failing commit looks arbitrary.

outputFileTracingExcludes now drops public/ media from every route. The
0.3 MB of public/**/data/*.json the two readers actually want stays traced;
build-time reads are unaffected, since tracing only decides what ships
inside a function.

Second, every content route paired a template-literal dynamic import with
dynamicParams = true. The Next.js MDX guide documents that exact pattern --
await import(`@/content/${slug}.mdx`) under a dynamic segment -- and pairs
it with dynamicParams = false, because the bundler cannot resolve a
template-literal import and therefore bundles the whole directory. With
`true` that bundle has to ship as a runtime function able to render an
arbitrary slug. With `false` every slug is prerendered by
generateStaticParams and unlisted ones get a static 404. The comment on
articles claimed `true` was needed for dev; the docs state
generateStaticParams is called on navigation during next dev, so it is not.
Applied to articles, blog, logs and projects.

Measured, on a clean production build:

  route                before     after
  /articles/[slug]     266.4 MB   52.1 MB
  /blog/[slug]         243.9 MB   29.7 MB
  /projects/[slug]     243.8 MB   29.6 MB
  /logs/[slug]         243.8 MB   29.6 MB
  /api/ask, /api/chat  227.2 MB   ~29 MB
  /md/[...slug]        221.5 MB   ~29 MB

Verified against `pnpm start`, not dev: receipts render in the HTML, the .md
variant still expands them into real tables with no unexpanded tags, all 238
articles are prerendered, and an unknown slug returns 404.

The headroom is now structural rather than incidental -- committing figures
no longer grows any function.
