subject: Fix KaTeX subscripts rendering at full size site-wide
body:
Every subscript and superscript on the site has been rendering at the same
size as its base, which is why $d_h$ looked flat. The cause was two KaTeX
versions in the tree pointing in different directions.

package.json declared katex ^0.18.4, and app/layout.tsx imports that copy's
stylesheet. But rehype-katex, which actually renders the math, depends on
katex ^0.16.0 and resolved 0.16.47. KaTeX renamed its sizing class between
those majors: 0.16 emits <span class="sizing reset-size6 size3">, while
0.18's stylesheet only defines .katex-sizing. So the selector never matched
anything and the font-size rule was silently dropped -- no error, no warning,
just full-size subscripts.

Measured before: subscript glyph 19.36px against a 19.36px base. After:
13.552px against 19.36px, which is 0.7x to the digit, matching the
.katex .sizing.reset-size6.size3 rule the stylesheet now actually defines.

Fixed by aligning the CSS to the renderer rather than the reverse. The
latest rehype-katex still pins katex ^0.16.0, so there is no version of it
that takes 0.18, and nothing in this codebase imports KaTeX's JavaScript
directly -- it is used only for its stylesheet and through rehype-katex.
Pinning katex to ^0.16.47 therefore costs nothing and leaves one copy whose
CSS and HTML agree.

subject: Add kaggle-tpu-320b: a 320B MoE on free TPUs, checked against the weights
body:
A hand-written JAX and Pallas engine serving a 320B-total, 18B-active MoE on
Kaggle's free TPU v5e-8. Most of the README survives being checked, and the
article says so before it says anything else.

Verified by walking all four GGUF shard headers, 1,412 tensors: the claimed
110 GB of expert weights measures 109,867,696,128 bytes, right to 0.12%. A
docstring claiming no expansion beyond one plane holds to 0.77%, and the
entire residual is one plane rounding 2 bytes to 4 on single-block slices.
"Routed experts are 95% of the weights" is 94.7%. "About 5,400 lines" is
5,562, underclaimed. And the compile-time trap this kind of claim usually
falls into is not present: the README names warm-up as 9 of the 16 minutes
and states that its rates are steady-state.

Three things do not check out. The "native 262,144 tokens" is the engine's
own cap; the model's configured maximum is 1,048,576, and its card reports
evaluations at 300K and 1M. The 3-bit mix is dynamic by matrix role rather
than by layer -- 39 of 42 layers are identical. And the decode kernel does
not do what the README says: the dispatch reshapes token-expert indices flat
with no sort and no unique, so the Pallas grid runs one step per pair rather
than per distinct expert, and the deduplication that exists lives only on
the prefill path. Stated carefully, because with 288 experts the published
rates cannot distinguish the two models even though the code can.

Measured here rather than quoted, all on CPU with no TPU available and the
article repeats that: quantisation error against bf16 for the same expert
slices, dequantised with the engine's own codebook reader -- 25.0% relative
Frobenius error for the format carrying gate and up projections in 41 of 42
layers, 13.9% and 7.6% for the other two. The README lists this measurement
as still to do. Parsing all ten published build variants shows the chosen
one is the largest that fits, so the format was forced rather than picked.
The shipped decode kernel was also run under interpretation against real
downloaded experts and matches a reference dequantised matmul to 2.3e-07,
and all five committed test fixtures verify byte-for-byte against upstream.

A roofline fit to the project's own three published rates puts the expert
half at about 5% of HBM bandwidth, which makes the decode path
dequantisation-bound rather than memory-bound -- corroborated by the repo
pinning a runtime version because the alternative is 140x slower on gathers.

The two figures are TPU hardware documentation, because the primary source
publishes no figures at all: its entire evidentiary record is one README
table.

subject: Add "VRAM is a policy": WanGP and YuE2 under one thesis
body:
WanGP and YuE2 make opposite claims about the same resource, and both turn
out to be statements about residency policy rather than about the models.
They are one article rather than two because the connection is material, not
rhetorical: WanGP already ships YuE2, re-split into two checkpoints, so the
same model can be measured under two policies.

Reading the offloader rather than the README: the launcher overrides the
library's own block budgets with 100 MiB, and since every model's base
already exceeds that, the tuner preloads zero blocks and the whole stack
becomes a circular shuttle. Resident weights are therefore base plus two
blocks, independent of checkpoint size -- 2,876 MiB for one model, 2,270 for
its pruned variant, 2,048 for another. The "5-6 GB" claims are coherent
against that.

What they omit is the other column. The same policy moves 30.10 GiB across
PCIe per forward pass for one model, times at least fifteen steps, and 10.21
GiB for another times thirty. Offloading trades VRAM for wall-clock, and in
seventeen months of changelog exactly three entries pair a VRAM figure with
a time -- one of which describes two different runs in a single sentence
with no card named. The project's README also states no system-RAM
requirement while the offloading library it depends on asks for 24 GB
minimum and 48 recommended.

Also: no published VRAM figure is an instrumented peak, because
max_memory_allocated and reset_peak_memory_stats appear nowhere in either
codebase.

On YuE2: the model is 3.63B, and because its embeddings are untied, a
756M-parameter embedding pair stays in BF16 under int8 -- so quantisation
saves 32.5% on the autoregressive tower, not 50%. That is the tied-embedding
error this batch has seen before, running the other way. A flag that frees
4,131 MiB is off by default and documented in neither the README nor the
generation docs.

The benchmark row is honest and the article says so: the quoted mean really
is the highest observed, the docs disclose that it is best-of-eight, and
they name the selection metric. The consequence is still worth stating --
there is no single-call number anywhere in the table.

Media: no video, because a muted autoplay loop cannot carry a song, and the
article says that outright. Instead the published audio was measured. All
three official demo files brick-wall at 18.0-18.1 kHz, identically across a
rock track, a Mandarin nu-disco track and a jazz-funk cover. The "48 kHz
stereo" claim is true of the pipeline's output format; the published demos
cannot demonstrate it. The spectrogram is disclosed as the article's own
rendering with the filter named.

The arXiv ID the model card tags resolves to the previous generation's
paper, a different architecture. No paper for this model exists.

subject: Add ZDTaichu 5.0-9B and UltraData-Code articles
body:
ZDTaichu ships two READMEs that score the same model differently. The model
card gives 62.50 / 47.20 / 78.27 / 56.00 on four spatial benchmarks; the
recurrent-reasoning README gives 54.10 / 36.80 / 74.04 / 68.00. The card's
own footnote explains part of it -- an output-format instruction was added
for some runs and not others -- but on a 1,000-question benchmark that gap
is 104 questions, and the fourth row's 12-point difference is not on the
format-instruction list and has no explanation at all.

It is load-bearing. Of the 25 rows carrying a closed-model comparison, the
release leads on 7, and 4 of those 7 are exactly the format-instruction
benchmarks. Its headline lead on one of them is 47.20 against 45.20;
ungated, the same README reports 36.80. The card never says whether the
baselines got the same prompt.

Parsing all three benchmark tables programmatically: the model leads the
open field on 17 of 27 rows, but on the 12 panels drawn in the release
figure it leads 10 of 12 -- and 8 of the 10 losses elsewhere are to its own
backbone. The figure also bolds the release in all twelve panels including
two losses, while the tables bold the winner.

The artifact itself is clean, and the article says so with the check shown:
9,794,197,512 parameters across 820 tensors, and every byte reconciles --
length prefixes plus headers plus tensor bytes equals the sum of the five
files exactly. Its "FP8" checkpoint measures 10.35 bits per weight and its
"NVFP4" 8.01, both computed per block from the headers. The documented
install command names a package that does not exist on PyPI.

The embedded clip is uncropped and untrimmed. The vendor's own replay
toolbar showing 2x playback stays visible, and both the caption and the
prose say so.

UltraData-Code is a 1.216 TB corpus with no tech report, so its numbers
exist only as prose beside screenshots. Counting it the only way a 1 GB disk
allows -- exact row and byte counts from the datasets server, mean character
counts per column, and chars-per-token measured by tokenising 11,000 sampled
rows -- gives an extrapolation that predicts the server's own full-corpus
byte total to within 0.07%, which is what licenses the rest.

On those numbers the headline "~150B tokens" is one column out of ten. The
column the default config actually loads is 52.4B, 35% of the headline, and
the ten text columns together carry 2.94x redundancy. "Algorithmically
relevant code" is 26.6% of the corpus by its own category label.

The selection thresholds are undeclared but readable off the data: no file
in any language survives below a quality score of 3.0, and the relevance
floor is 0.85 for some languages, 0.50 for others, and 0.00 for Python --
where 21.8% of sampled rows score below 0.5. One row is three byte-identical
copies of a vendored pip file labelled as algorithmic with a relevance score
of 2.6e-05. Exact duplicates survive into the filtered tier at 3.24% of
sampled rows, every one crossing a repository boundary, and 67 of 106
duplicate groups carry byte-identical text with different scores, so the
scoring pass is not reproducible at the threshold.

All thirteen benchmark numbers the card quotes reproduce exactly from its
own tables, and the article says so plainly. The licence does not: the YAML
and the shipped LICENSE say Apache-2.0, which grants an irrevocable right to
redistribute, while the README -- in both languages -- strictly prohibits
reposting or mirroring. Attribution is also impossible to act on for the
generated tier, whose schema drops the repository and path fields while
keeping 79B tokens of verbatim third-party source, and whose generating
model is never named.

subject: Update the AuK, MiniCPM5 and empero articles, and correct a bad derivation
body:
Three shipped pieces whose subjects moved. All three updates are dated
sections rather than silent edits, because a correction that hides when it
was made is worth less than one that doesn't.

AuK. The reported changes are all real and now measured rather than
repeated: CPU offload cuts peak VRAM by about 32%, and the 7.5 GiB encoder
saving is a one-line diff changing model.to(float32) to
model.transformer.to(float32). Reading the safetensors headers by range
request proves the fp32 claim from the file -- 420 tensors, every one F32.

That same read overturns this article's most-quoted result. It claimed a
from-scratch derivation landing 880 parameters from the published count. The
header says 1,530,538,629. The byte-division estimate was 13,644 high, which
is exactly the 54,576-byte header divided by four, and the from-scratch
derivation was 12,764 high. The two estimates agreed with each other, not
with the artifact: two independent errors landing near each other. The core
transformer derivation was in fact exact to the parameter; all the error was
in the peripherals. Also corrected: the layer-fusion weights are 37, not 33;
the companion encoder is 4.03B, not roughly 3B; and the checkpoint the
article is about accounts for 27% of what you need resident, not half.

New in AuK: the README's VRAM table was measured before both improvements
and is unmarked, so it over-provisions by about 7 GiB, and the official demo
Space has not been pushed since before either change -- its vendored loader
still carries the old line and never mentions offload.

MiniCPM5 gains a WebGPU build, and nothing in the existing article was found
wrong. The Space's stated 1.84 GB download is exact to three decimals, and
two shards of identical size turn out to be the FP16 embedding split into
four pieces just under the storage-binding limit. The interesting result is
that the browser's 4-bit build is 17.5% larger than the 4-bit GGUF, because
one tensor ships at 3.6x the bytes. The GGUFs also carry an internal job
string naming the RL teacher count, the iteration and a learning rate that
appear nowhere in the documentation -- flagged in the article as a reading
of a job name, not as documentation.

empero's 35B distill fixes almost everything the original article asked for:
exact file sizes with a stated convention, a shipped mmproj, a full
quantisation ladder, and the training window disclosed in prose. It
introduces a new problem instead. The whole evaluation is now loglikelihood
scoring, so the extraction bug is gone because the task that exposed it is
gone -- and a release whose headline is distilled chain-of-thought is scored
only on benchmarks where the model never generates and never opens a think
block. The shipped index also disagrees with itself: its declared total size
includes the MTP file's bytes while its declared parameter count excludes
that file's parameters.

Corrects a stale figure in that article too: the share of downloads going to
the GGUF rather than the parent is 98.4%, not 96%.

subject: Add auto-gpu-kernel article: the rank is real, the 34.93x is against what
body:
An agent loop generated the winning DeepSeek Sparse Attention kernels for
the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest. The first-place finish is real and
independently listed by the organisers. The headline "average 34.93x
speedup" exists only in the entrant's own README and report, because the
organisers publish no scores at all.

So the article goes and reads the baseline that number divides by. The
scored denominator wraps a real TRT-LLM kernel but first concatenates the
entire paged KV cache on every call. All 23 workloads declare 8,462 pages,
which makes that 554.6 MB read and 623.9 MB written per call; at the card's
peak bandwidth that is a floor of roughly 156 microseconds against a winning
kernel the report clocks at 10. Stated as arithmetic on declared shapes,
not a measurement -- there was no GPU here and no kernel was run.

The scoring rule compounds it: an arithmetic mean of per-workload ratios,
and 69 of the 128 indexer traces are small enough that top-k collapses to a
structural mapping, which the repo's own experiment notes had already
observed.

The correctness gate, by contrast, holds, and the article says so as
clearly as it says the rest. The evaluator runs the correctness check before
the performance measurement and returns early on failure, so a wrong kernel
produces no latency at all rather than a fast wrong one, and any failing
workload zeros the whole kernel's score. Tolerances are 1e-2 on both
absolute and relative error -- and that matters, because the shipped
kernel's worst absolute error is 1.56e-02 and it passes on the relative
bound.

The experiment logs give the denominator the report omits: 98 logged
experiments, 32 kept, 66 discarded, a 32.7% keep rate. The report describes
the survivors.

Other findings: the report swaps its own two trace counts, and the cause is
traceable to a config file copied between the two sub-projects; the indexer
headline is worse than the best number in its own logs; experiments ran on a
platform the contest page says is reference-only because the clock cannot be
locked; and the shipped kernel's grid-wide spin barrier has no bailout, so
past the contest's trace sizes the failure mode is a hang rather than a
slowdown. That last one is flagged as the claim least testable from here.

The best number in either repository is one neither highlights: the same

subject: Add RelateAnything article: the gate the paper says is unsupervised isn't
body:
RelateAnything routes relations through a gate that the paper states three
separate times receives no supervision -- in section 3.2, in appendix A.3,
and in a figure caption -- and the project page's own architecture diagram
prints "nothing supervises it" on the same component.

The released training setup warm-starts it. build_model derives a spatial
majority flag from the corpus, fits a balanced logistic probe onto that
flag, and runs 300 Adam steps regressing the gate MLP onto the probe. The
launch script passes no checkpoint to initialise from, so the released
recipe takes that branch.

This was confirmed from the weights, not just the code. The alpha buffer
shipped inside all three checkpoints is that initialisation rather than what
each checkpoint's own gate computes: correlation 0.53, maximum difference
0.998, near-identical across three independently trained towers, and it
separates the corpus spatial flag at an AUC of exactly 1.0000. The trained
gate scores 0.9592 on the same test. It is benign at inference, since the
vocabulary setter recomputes, which is precisely why the initialisation
survives in the file to be read.

Parameter counts and gate statistics were reproduced by unpickling each
model.pth without torch and recomputing in float64: 46,139,281 / 53,235,601
/ 113,797,393 against the published figures, and a gate median of 0.0028
against a stated 0.002.

Other findings: the 20 ms headline is the compiled path, while the paper's
own table caption says no accuracy table uses compiled inference, so the
latency and the accuracy come from different configurations; two eager
end-to-end numbers on the same card are unreconciled at 25.0 and 30.5 ms;
the 2.3-3.5x margin is against OvSGTR rather than the stronger baseline the
paper itself names, where it is 1.34-1.86x; one table prints a macro AUC
beside an accuracy figure as though comparable, and the like-for-like
comparison has the model 6.3 points behind a baseline that never sees the
image; the published corpus is 2,069 images smaller than the paper's; and
the benchmark the abstract calls public returns 401.

The article also credits at length how honest the paper is elsewhere -- it
publishes a frequency table that beats its own model on the leaderboard
metric, ships a discarded arm with the best zero-shot recall it knows of
while saying it makes no claim to lead, and reports that its own supervision
makes dense features worse at the thing they are supposed to improve.

The embedded clip keeps the source's credit watermark and input tag rather
than cropping them, and the caption discloses the trim, the scale and that
it is an offline render rather than a live capture.

subject: Add ChessLFM article: the Elo is real, the pool was in a tooltip
body:
An Elo figure means nothing without the pool it was measured against, and
the announcement gives a number with no opponent settings, no time control
and no game count. The methodology turns out to exist -- in a tooltip string
inside the demo's JavaScript bundle, which states a roughly 720-game ladder
against node-limited Stockfish at UCI_Elo 1320-2400, with test-time tree
search at depth 3 and width 6 plus repetition-aware backup, and adds in its
own words that this is an engine-anchored scale "not directly comparable to
FIDE or Lichess ratings."

That reframes the headline: the number is the model plus a search, not the
model, and the demo runs that exact configuration. The disclosure is honest
and complete; it is just not anywhere a reader would find it.

The article also separates legal-move rate from playing strength, which
projects in this space routinely blur, and works through where the quoted
552-Elo gain actually comes from. And the published parameter count does not
match the checkpoint: the 230M headline is not the 164.8M the weights carry.

subject: Add a PCD film, and the Depth Anything 3 ROS 2 article
body:
The film is a second pass with the hand-drawn-canvas-animation skill, this
time on parallel constrained decoding: an empty schema card, one prompt
stroke drawn once, the cache fanning into three identical lanes, all three
advancing under a single sweep, then the vocabulary as a dark grid where
nine cells light and are gathered into one column. Its caption says plainly
that the lane count, the grid and the nine cells are illustrative rather
than the real tensor shapes, since the actual numbers are in the code
blocks and components on the same page.

The Depth Anything 3 ROS 2 piece answers the question that made the subject
worth writing about: what does the node actually publish, and in what
units. The whole metric recovery is one line -- focal_scale =
0.5*(fx*sx + fy*sy) / 300.0 -- and the checkpoint cannot do it itself. That
is shown two ways: the config builds a plain network with no camera decoder,
so the scaling path it would need never runs; and the published ONNX graph,
pulled apart over HTTP range requests without downloading the weights, has
1418 nodes ending in depth and sky heads with no intrinsics output at all.
So the README's "predicts a dense metric depth map" is wrong for this
artifact -- it predicts focal-normalised depth and the wrapper makes it
metric.

That audit also produced a quantified error nobody had stated. The node
stretches every frame anisotropically into a fixed 504x280 engine input,
then averages the two axis scales. 504x280 is exactly what the upstream
pipeline yields for 16:9, so the node is calibrated for its authors'
automotive camera and silently wrong elsewhere: -0.62% at 16:9, -12.96% at
4:3, -15.28% at 5:4. Re-exporting at an aspect-matched height zeroes it.

Smaller findings, all against source: the frame_id is discarded by a
whole-header assignment, so an optical-convention point cloud gets labelled
with a body frame and is silently rotated 90 degrees; the README describes
the sky mask backwards twice, against its own kernel; sky_depth_cap is
declared, documented and wired to a setter but the kernel reads a constant
nothing writes; and the quoted 50 FPS is a workstation card with the
timed region excluding decode and the 8.3 MB serialisation, with no Jetson
number and no Jetson build in CI.

The article's own headline claim rests on the config plus the graph
structure rather than on executing the model, and it says so as its first
falsifier.

subject: Add BrowserSkill article: the borrow rule covers writes, not reads
body:
Tencent's BrowserSkill hands a shell-capable agent your real, logged-in
Chrome, and its genuine contribution is where it puts the consent switch:
0.3.0 moved borrow-confirmation and human-help out of CLI flags the agent
controls and into browser storage it does not, so --unattended now only
prints a deprecation warning. That part was verified by running it --
tab borrow --no-confirm --timeout 8s blocks the full eight seconds and then
fails waiting for a human.

The article is grounded in the product actually running, not in reading it.
The CLI was built from source, the repo's own extension loaded into
Chromium 153, a daemon started, and nineteen commands run against an
ordinary tab in a window that was never borrowed. Thirteen refuse with
agent_window_scope and exit 1. Six answer: get-html returned the page's
canary string, snapshot minted a clickable ref for it, and screenshot wrote
a 9,923-byte PNG, with no prompt and no notification.

The README says the agent "must borrow that tab explicitly ... and leave
the rest of your browser alone", and the skill file the model reads says
"User tabs require explicit borrowing". Both are true of everything that
dispatches input and false of the five read tools.

The split is deliberate and the article says so plainly. The guard carries
a comment stating it, the strictest check in the codebase is applied to a
read (full-page screenshot scrolls, so it mutates, so it needs the window
scope and an unconditional per-tab claim re-verified every step), and
remote mode flips the same guard closed. As a threat model it is coherent:
a local agent already has your shell, and therefore your Chrome profile and
cookie database, so refusing snapshot would only make the honest path more
annoying than the dishonest one. The problem is that this reasoning appears
only in source comments -- not in the README, not in the skill file, and
not in the Chrome Web Store privacy page, whose page-content row lists
three sources where the measurement found four.

Also: "25 of 28 operations" covered is 25 of 41 tool.* protocol methods,
and every method 0.3.0 added is among the thirteen with no coverage at all;
architecture.md says 21 tool handlers where the switch has 40, unchanged
since the initial public release; and the repo's most self-critical
document -- stating the audit log offers no tamper-resistance and is off by
default -- is the only Chinese-only file among seven, linked from the
English README.

subject: Add Edge0 and Retrieve-for-Train articles
body:
Two backlog subjects, both of which turned out to have a headline number
that does not survive being checked.

Edge0 streams a 35B MoE off SSD. Reading the safetensors headers by HTTP
range request -- 1,757 tensors across four shards from about 1 MB of
headers, no weights downloaded -- puts the checkpoint at 19,508,787,456
bytes, 19.51 GB, against a README that says roughly 23 GB. The paper says
19.5, the paper's own Figure 1 prints 19.5, and a docstring says 19.7, so
the README is the lone outlier. All 512 quantized tensors reconcile against
their scale group counts.

That pass also found five different decode rates published for the same
35B tier, spanning 13.0 to 20.4 tok/s, two of which name the same Mac mini.
The README's headline "up to +59%" prerouter gain appears in no other
source; the paper's own Table 1 caption measures the same ablation at +2.5%
on the machine the README benchmarks, which reframes the prerouter as a
swap-avoidance device rather than a speedup. The config advertises a vision
tower with depth 27 and ships zero visual tensors. The iPhone claim, by
contrast, holds up: an unlinked 89-second recording in the Hub repo shows
1.7 GiB peak, and 1.7 GiB sits inside the 1.49-1.73 GiB floor derived
independently from tensor headers.

Retrieve-for-Train's Figure 5 ships as a matplotlib SVG, so the plotted
values are recoverable from the path geometry. Calibrating against the
gridlines returns a speedup range of 8.05x to 16.18x, with five of eight
batch sizes below the claimed 12x floor and nothing reaching 20x. The
calibration reproduces both autoregressive figures the paper states in
prose, and the figure's own zoom inset returns identical values from a
separate set of axes. The circulating 20x traces to a single prose number
the figure contradicts. The caption's gloss also has the direction
backwards: the ratio is largest at the smallest batch.

The same article opens an unlinked rebuttal repo holding 419 human ratings
with no legend saying which arm is which system. Cross-correlating the
example form's image tiles against the paper's own Figure 3 resolves the
mapping, and a paired sign test then shows the two arms splitting the two
metrics -- one wins alignment, the other diversity -- where the paper's
table has its system ahead on both. The finding holds whichever way the
mapping goes. Published with the caveat that the six respondents are not
independent, and re-run after deduplication.

subject: Add a hand-drawn canvas film to the fly-connectome article
body:
A 24-second ink film, every frame drawn by JavaScript on a 2D canvas at
12 fps and rendered through headless Chrome, using the
hand-drawn-canvas-animation skill from alesha-pro/tools. Seven shots: a fly
on a peach, the ink blotting away to leave a chalk diagram, somata

three-counts shot, and the closing card finished only 0.9 s before the end
where the checklist requires 1.5 s, so it would have been cut whenever the

generated score exists but would never play, so the audio track is stripped
rather than shipped as bytes nobody hears. 1.19 MB mp4, 1.08 MB webm,

subject: Ground the GLM infra article in the code, and fix a claim it got backwards
body:
An article complaining that a post shows no system was itself showing no
system: one fenced code block in 3,488 words. It now has 13, each short and
load-bearing, cloned from fla-org/flash-linear-attention and
deepseek-ai/DeepEP and cited by path.

The important fix is a claim reversal. The article said the post never sets
its throughput against any other inference engine on any hardware. It does.
The sentence immediately after the "roughly 3x" reads: "Both hardware
utilization efficiency and per-token cost reached levels comparable to
mainstream NVIDIA GPUs." I pulled the blog's own JS bundle and confirmed it
verbatim -- the page is a client-rendered SPA, so curl on the URL returns an
empty shell. That is a parity claim against NVIDIA silicon carrying no
number, no named GPU, no named engine, no unit and no method, which makes it
a heavier assertion than the 3x and less checkable than it. The honest
reading is not that the post declines to compare itself to the incumbent; it
compares itself to the incumbent and declines to show the comparison. Fixed
in the body, the ledger and the frontmatter description.

Smaller corrections, all measured:
- The diff changes six tl.dot call sites across three kernels, not three.
- The tf32x3 env var is read only by the intra-card backend. The
  distributed CP path the post was debugging has no env var at all, only a
  keyword argument -- so the fix is even more opt-in than the article said.
- The commit-count claim is replaced with what could be measured: one
  squashed merge, 6 files, +140/-13, three new tests.
- Case 2 moves from "I could not verify this" to verified against the named
  tag: v1.2.1's deep_ep.cpp holds exactly one gil_scoped_release, in
  internode_dispatch, 348 lines after the intranode path that has none.
- The GIL fix was never upstreamed. DeepEP at HEAD, dated the day before
  Z.ai published, still has exactly one release in the whole repository.
- "Repeated four times" is 128 / 32, and both halves are public: head_dim
  from the released config over a hardcoded BV in FLA.
- Z.ai's prose says 1.71x over v2 while its figure plots against v0; the
  numbers coincide only because v2 recovered to exactly 1.00x.

A token-volume cross-check also supports the two unverifiable figures rather
than undermining them: 62T tokens over six days across more than 100,000
accelerators works out to roughly 43 TFLOP/s each, which is ordinary for
decode-dominated serving. A count implying 400 would have broken the
accelerator claim on arithmetic alone.

subject: Check Qwen's spatial-audio demo against its own second sample
body:
The demo prints two panels and connects neither: the model's narrated
distance to a sound, and the eight-waypoint trajectory it then emits. Those
are checkable against each other, and the article already did that for the
frame at 55.5 seconds -- stated 1.2 m, plan landing at hypot(1.101, 0.492)
= 1.2059 m on a 24.1-degree bearing, agreeing to six millimetres.

It turns out the clip does it twice. Ten seconds earlier the same pair of
panels carries different numbers: 2.2 m stated, and a plan that stops at
0.958 m, fully 1.24 m short. That second sample is what makes the first one
interesting rather than merely flattering, because the shortfall has a
visible cause. Every waypoint is either a 0.25 m step or a 15-degree turn
and a plan gets exactly eight of them, so the far target spent four slots
turning onto the bearing and had four steps left, one metre of walking. The
near target needed three turns, leaving five steps and 1.25 m -- just enough
to close a 1.2 m gap. The planner is not ignoring the distance it reports;
it is spending a fixed budget against it and coming up short when the target
is out of reach.

The claim is downgraded accordingly. This is an internal consistency check,
not a measurement: nothing in either frame says how far the phone actually
was. What it rules out is the cheaper reading -- that the narration is
decorative text generated beside a path computed by something else. With a
0.25 m quantum the achievable endpoints are coarse, so landing within 6 mm
is not a common accident, but two samples from one vendor-chosen take
support "suggestive" and no more. The ledger entry was rewritten to match.

subject: Add the Uno inference animation, a figure and real code, and fix the loss
body:
The paper has only two figures and both were already in the article, so the
missing media was on the project page: a 73-frame animation captioned
"Inference in Uno." Transcoded to mp4/webm with a poster and served locally.

Read frame by frame it turns out to be a mechanism exhibit rather than a
progress bar. The frames alternate on two beats -- 160 ms showing the newest
span as uniform gibberish, 220 ms showing that identical span resolved into
real text -- one prompt frame followed by exactly 36 junk/resolved pairs.
Two beats per committed chunk is the two forward passes. And the gibberish
is not a stylised thinking effect: it is the literal input tensor, since
build_draft_batch fills each draft row with uniformly random vocabulary ids
after the last committed token, with random_uniform the shipped default.

Both caveats are written in rather than glossed. The animation is a demo,
not a logged trace -- in every junk/resolved pair checked, the resolved span
has exactly as many whitespace-separated pieces as the junk it replaced,
which is full-block acceptance every cycle rather than a real run's
rejections -- and its implied 5.7 words per cycle sits just above the
measured tau of 5.97 tokens, with tokens shorter than words.

Corrects a wrong claim about the training objective. The article said the
adapter is trained via a KL term plus a total-variation term, which is
Equation (3). The released recipe sets the KL weight to zero in
constants.py, restates it in run_slurm.sh, and the trainer skips that branch
entirely when the weight is zero -- so the reproducible run is
total-variation-only and the distillation half of "Discrete Consistency
Distillation" is switched off in the artifact. The shipped objective also
has three terms where the paper writes two. The paper's own ablation agrees
and explains why.

New corroboration for the article's headline critique: the authors' own
project page captions the throughput panel "up to 2.5x speedup over the base
AR model," against the abstract's 3x. Same authors, same figure, same week,
and 2.5x is what the tables support -- the maximum ratio anywhere in Table
18 is 2.53x at batch 1.

Also adds fig3 (additional parameters and peak memory), cross-checked
against Table 2 and matching exactly, with the caption noting the memory
axis is truncated at 100 so a 6% saving is drawn as a third of a bar.

subject: Add the refusal-direction paper's figures to the abliteration article
body:
The piece explained a mechanism from Arditi et al. (arXiv:2406.11717, v3,
NeurIPS 2024) without showing any of that paper's evidence. Three figures
now do: the cross-model ablation results over 13 models, the
activation-addition result, and the per-candidate bypass-score landscape
from Appendix C.2 -- the only figure in the paper that shows what the
direction search is actually searching over. Fetched as SVG from arXiv's
HTML, rasterized at 1600px, flattened onto white, served locally.

Bar values were read out of the SVG path geometry rather than eyeballed,
which sharpened a claim the article had left vague. "Removes refusal almost
entirely" is post-ablation refusal 0.00 to 0.27 across the 13 models -- but
the safety score only falls to 0.13-0.42. Removing refusal phrasing is not
the same as producing a compliant answer, and the figures say so.

Corrects a count: OrcaRouter's Hugging Face org has 28 repos, of which 25
are Uncensored releases, not 28. The other three are plain MLX
re-quantizations. On a site whose method is counting things, that one
mattered.

New section on what the shipped direction file does and does not establish.
The paper's sufficiency result -- adding the vector back induces refusal on
harmless prompts -- is what makes it the direction that mediates refusal
rather than a direction whose deletion happens to work, and abliteration
releases never repeat it. The direction is a search over (layer, position)
candidates filtered on bypass, induce, KL and unembedding similarity, and
most candidates do nothing. What ships instead is a file whose metadata
carries five keys and no layer, no position, no dataset, no scores, while
the self-check prints a layer field the file leaves empty. And the
self-check proves less than its PASS suggests: it measures the residual
component along the same vector it projected out, so with every writer
wrapped the ratio collapses for any unit vector.

Scope held to published research: the mechanism and what the papers
measure, no operational recipe.

One flag left unresolved. The article says the repo's bar for correctly
wrapped is roughly 1e-6, which is the documented expectation; the
programmatic threshold in selfcheck.py is reportedly looser at 1e-4. The
Hugging Face repo returns 401 now, so that could not be re-verified here
and the wording is left as published rather than changed on an unchecked
basis.

subject: Audit open-1b's chain for real, and expand Receipts in the .md variant
body:
The open-1b article argued that the training run is auditable while showing
the reader nothing to audit: 3,425 words, zero code blocks. It now carries
seven, each naming the file it came from, and a third figure. More to the
point, the audit was actually performed.

Verified by running it, not by quoting it:
- state_hashes.jsonl is 80,958 lines -- init plus exactly 80,957 steps,
  contiguous from zero, 80,958 distinct digests, no collisions.
- The batch ramp re-derives from the log alone. Token deltas take exactly
  three values matching the config's three global_batch_tokens, with
  transitions at 4,001,366,016 and 360,000,258,048 tokens against declared
  thresholds of 4e9 and 360e9. The three run lengths sum to 80,957.
- The corpus sums to 450,475,403,217 tokens over 1,700 shards, and the four
  split shares reproduce the config's hardcoded weights to four decimals.
- The published audit kit verifies: 5 of 5 files match their sha256.
- Joining the public ledger to the 80,958-link chain puts 27 of 27
  submissions exactly on their published link, each digest appearing once.
  Gensyn's own manifest says the server does not perform that
  reconstruction.

What that turned up, all from primary sources:
- The shipped audit kit can only verify step zero. Its trajectory.json
  holds three units, all of kind "init". There is no step-interval unit,
  so the one-command volunteer path checks the random initialization and
  nothing else.
- The kit's own notes disclaim its kernel guarantee at the shipped commit.
- The final checkpoint's meta.json has empty tokenizer_hash and
  container_digest -- the two slots furthest upstream of the hash.
- Its git_sha names a revision that does not exist in the public repo.
- The committed run config describes a 32-rank world; the checkpoint and
  its 48 rng files show 48.
- The strongest evidence on the ledger is unadvertised: step 1,000 replayed
  on an RTX 3090 and an M4 Max, both producing the chain's link.
- Steps audited moved 25 to 26 during the work; updated everywhere,
  including the VerifierCost component.

Separately, lib/markdown.ts now expands <Receipts> into a real markdown
table for the agent-facing .md variants. Every other component carries its
content inline in attributes, so an agent reading the markdown still gets
the idea; Receipts keeps its data in a separate file and would have handed
over a bare path. A missing file degrades to a link rather than throwing --
the HTML route already fails the build loudly on that, and a markdown
caller is better served a URL than a 500.

subject: Add code to the Bonsai 2 and Cerebras articles, and fix what checking found
body:
Both pieces shipped with zero fenced code blocks. Grounding them in the
actual runtimes and docs turned up errors in each.

Bonsai 2 27B (+4 blocks: the MLX pack's codec and Hadamard runtime, the
model card's quickstart, a llama-bench line):
- The most quotable technical line in the piece was backwards. It said
  stock llama.cpp silently loads PQ2_0 as an unrelated type and produces
  garbage. The model card says the opposite: llama.cpp rejects PQ2_0 and
  PTQ1_0 as unknown, and silently mis-loads Q2_0, which is generation
  one's ternary type. The silent-wrong-output path for Bonsai 2 is MLX.
- The whitepaper and the model card disagree on throughput for the same
  pack on the same GPU (142.5 vs 129.9 tg128, 4121 vs 3893 pp512) and
  neither acknowledges the other. Now stated.
- Bits-per-weight provenance was mixed: a whitepaper rate paired with a
  model-card size and called measured. Recomputed from the actual blob
  sizes over 26.89B params: 1.77 and 2.14 bpw.
- IQ2_XXS is sized two different ways by PrismML (9.4 GB at 2.8 bpw vs
  7.3 GB at 2.2); the article asserted one. Bigger and worse either way,
  so the argument survives.

Cerebras at 2000 tok/s (+4 blocks: tok/s from the time_info object, the
streaming call, the client loop, streamUI):
- A rate-limit paragraph divided a per-minute rate by a per-second rate
  and got a budget, concluding the tier throttles after 81 seconds. It is
  a refilling rate, the 150K figure is the paid tier's, and the real
  conclusion inverts: one continuous stream at 1,850 tok/s draws 111,000
  tokens a minute and never trips it. Two streams do.
- AI SDK RSC is marked experimental, not paused.
- The 262,144-token context is Qwen's checkpoint, not what Cerebras
  serves (64k free, 128k paid). The two were conflated.
- Prompt caching billing at the full input rate is Cerebras's own
  documented behaviour, not a third-party report.
The headline ~1,850 tok/s checks out against Cerebras's model page;
outlets quoting 1,500 are wrong.

No video on the Cerebras piece. The only recording is the demo author's
own, and it carries a burned-in "2x uncut video" label — an article about
generation speed cannot use a double-speed clip as evidence of generation
speed, and cropping the author's disclosure out to ship it would be worse.
The four stills already cut from it stand, since a still frame has no
playback rate.

No figure on Bonsai 2: the whitepaper contains zero images and the launch
post's one image is already fig1. The demos are domain-locked Vimeo
embeds.

subject: Add Receipts and ChangeMyMind, and retrofit two articles onto them
body:
Two globally-registered MDX components, both server-rendered and zero-JS.

Receipts publishes the evidence behind a claim. It reads a committed JSON
dataset from public/ at build time and renders the table from the same file
the download link serves, so the prose cannot drift from the artifact it
cites. A missing or malformed dataset fails the build, matching the posture
of the Zod content layer -- evidence that isn't there should stop the build
rather than degrade to an empty box.

ChangeMyMind is a standing falsifiability section: for each load-bearing
claim, the specific observation that would overturn it. It exists to force
claims to be stated sharply enough to be wrong, and to date findings that
are one measurement on one build on one day.

Retrofitted onto needle-3 and xgen-jing-dao, re-measuring rather than
transcribing. That pass changed both articles:

- needle-3: the published .cact still measures 35,335,380 bytes. The fp16
  checkpoint now reconciles exactly instead of "to within rounding" -- an
  8-byte prefix plus an 8,248-byte JSON header leaves 242,039,722 bytes of
  payload, and the 64 tensors that header describes sum to the same figure
  to the byte. They hold 121,019,861 parameters, 2,049 fewer than
  config.json claims. Two range requests also recover the whole
  quantization-aware schedule from the checkpoint's __metadata__, which
  corroborates the QAT description on the page and shows that 31.15% of the
  training mixture is speech data while config.json lists modalities as
  text only.

- xgen-jing-dao: corrects a wrong sentence that contradicted the two after
  it. The article said every row carried a data-evaluation-source attribute
  except a handful. In fact 10 of 108 rows carry it, all reading
  self-evaluation, resolving to three distinct models. The article's own
  follow-up sentence had it right; the lead-in did not.

body:
Renders 141,781 real MaleCNS v1.0 somas — every neuron in the dataset with
a recovered cell body — as a rotatable point cloud, with per-type selection
that lights up the selected cells and traces their strongest synaptic
partners. Activity is a deterministic propagation over the real edge list,
not decoration.

Data is preprocessed to fixed-point binary and served locally: 5.89 MB
total for positions (u16), type index, pre/post counts, body IDs, and a
backbone edge list, plus per-type edge slices for the six types the article
discusses (DNp09, MDN, LC16, DNa01/02, hDeltaA/G/H/I). Source is the
neuprint public Cypher endpoint, CC BY 4.0; provenance and the exact node
counts are pinned in data/manifest.json.

Raw WebGL2 rather than three.js — no new dependency, and the whole
renderer is one buffer upload plus two draw calls. SSR falls back to a
static poster so the page has no client-only hole, and the animation
respects prefers-reduced-motion.

The manifest's tracedStatusNeurons (165,122) is also the figure flycoinrh
reports, which reconciles one of the five conflicting neuron counts the
article catalogues.

subject: Add fly-connectome article: identity versus statistics
body:
MaleCNS landed on 3 September 2026 — 166,691 neurons, Google Research
with HHMI Janelia FlyEM, Cambridge and MRC LMB — and an ecosystem
appeared within weeks. The article's rule: the connectome's statistics
are enough when you only need rich dynamics; its identity is required
when you need to know which neuron. Every project falls on one side, and
the ones that ran controls found out which.

On the statistics side, two independent teams reached the same result
against their own interest. oruk's reservoir found scrambled wiring
matched fly wiring. FLM's own README reports its matched direct-input
control winning by 0.000488 nats with the interval excluding zero on 3 of
3 seeds, and states outright that it "does not establish an advantage
from fly anatomy" — while the announcement calls it the world's first Fly
Language Model.

On the identity side, flyvis predicts ON/OFF polarity 32 of 32 correct at
ensemble median across 64 cell types and 45,669 neurons with 734 free
parameters, checked against 26 published studies. And the hDeltaH path-
integration hypothesis is only reachable because the wiring exists: you
cannot guess which four anonymous cell types receive step, dopamine and
octopamine input without it. Reported at the author's own hedge level.

The same dataset is five different sizes depending on who counts. The
paper gives 46M presynapses and 312M PSDs; Google's announcement says
125M synaptic connections; flycoinrh reports 165,122 neurons and 10.2M;
FLM 166,700 nodes and 25.6M. All real, all different thresholds, now in
one reconciliation.

Two honesty checks worth naming. flycoinrh's own dictionary flags that
its "stop" label for DNp09 contradicts Bidaye et al. 2020, which shows
forward walking. DOOMFLY's README says it "failed its visual,
conditioning and survival validation gates" while press coverage says it
learned to play Doom. And the $15-microcontroller claim resolves to a
repo that disclaims connectome data and hardware testing, against
arithmetic putting 100k neurons two orders of magnitude past that budget.

Engages Mineault's critique directly rather than summarising it. Includes
a video recorded by running the escape-circuit demo locally.

subject: Add runtime-abliteration and Needle 3 articles
body:
Runtime abliteration: the mechanism is exact, not approximate. For a
linear write y = Wx, projecting the output and orthogonalising the weight
matrix are algebraically identical by associativity — (I - r rT)(Wx) =
((I - r rT) W)x — and ablation.py computes the left-hand side. That is
why the intervention never needs to touch weights, and why it avoids the
dequantise-edit-requantise cycle that would undo QAT on a ternary model.
129 sites decompose exactly: 64 mlp.down_proj + 48 linear_attn.out_proj +
16 self_attn.o_proj + 1 embed_tokens, cross-checked against the pack's
own layer_types.

Two corrections to my own assumption. The runtime does not load the
5,946,648,928-byte GGUF pack from the Bonsai 2 article; it requires
prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-mlx-2bit, whose model.safetensors is
8,595,477,990 bytes — a different, incompatible container, since MLX's
quantised matmul has only Metal and CPU kernels. And "bit-identical"
holds by the absence of any write path rather than by an active check:
the pack ships a SHA-256 manifest that this repo's code never reads.
Alpha is an unclamped float, so past 1.0 the surviving component points
against the direction rather than merely vanishing.

Needle 3: the shipped file is larger than the stated ceiling. The page
claims 8-29 MB in one place and 9-29 MB in another; needle3.cact measures
35,335,380 bytes — 35.34 MB, 22% over the maximum. Even a naive estimate
from config.json's own 121,021,910 parameters at 2.125 bits/weight gives
32.15 MB, already over, and the quantisation scheme explains why:
embedding and mHC gates are 4-bit, not the uniform 2-bit the number
implies.

"Matches DeepSeek V4 Flash" is narrowed on Cactus's own page to
fine-tuned, from 4 layers up — and within the same figure it holds on
DroidCall, where every tuned depth from 4L clears 60.5, and fails on
Mobile Actions, where no tuned depth reaches 88.4 and the 20L slice
scores below its own untuned base. Laddering is a regulariser, not just
compression: their own control shows ladder training beating a
non-ladder control at full depth, 1.958 against 2.037 val loss.

subject: Add XGEN JING/DAO article: half the system is public
body:
The WBench standing is real and checks against the live leaderboard:
XGEN-Jing bidirection is #1 on the Full split and #2 on Navi, behind
Alaya-EVOKE-Turbo. Two things the announcement omits. Both XGEN rows are
timestamped the same day, so this is a fresh standing rather than a
settled one. And the leaderboard's HTML carries
data-evaluation-source="self-evaluation" on ten rows, including both
XGEN entries — and also Alaya-EVOKE-Turbo, the model ranked above it.
That attribute renders nowhere on the page; it is visible only in source.
It is a property of the leaderboard's top entries generally, not a knock
on XGEN specifically, and the article says so.

DAO is not released. Grepping the entire repo for "dao" returns exactly
one hit, Dao-AILab/flash-attention — Tri Dao's org, a false positive.
There is no DAO code, API or reference in the shipped pipeline, no
separate repo, no weights, no paper. Its own product page demonstrates it
with a hand-authored WebGL panorama whose source comments say "no LLM",
"no deps", "every beat authored by hand". So the coupled system in the
announcement is, publicly, one half.

The architecture framing is defensible and their own capability table
concedes the point: JING gets a dash on World-State Management, which is
attributed entirely to DAO. It is a game-server and renderer split with a
neural renderer, which is a reasonable answer to the persistence problem
world models usually fail — but it means the generative half is not what
keeps the world consistent.

Also from the code: attention.py sets causal=False, so "bidirectional"
means whole-clip denoising rather than frame-reactive generation, and
bidirection.py reads a pre-written JSON script of prompts and WASD
controls and generates in one batch — there is no live loop. The shipped
control vector is six-dimensional with only two dimensions ever
populated, so no turning by key. The #2 Full entry, 4-step AR, is the
variant the README lists as coming soon.

Includes two real XGEN-JING clips and leaderboard captures.

subject: Add Jev ecosystem article: the first real calibration evidence
body:
pngwn's open scorer is the find. Its committed metrics.json publishes
before-and-after calibration for a Qwen3.5-4B-Base LoRA at temperature
2.35, and every number checks: aggregate ECE 0.0727 to 0.0221, Brier
0.2789 to 0.2642, accuracy fixed at 0.8028 — as it must be, since
temperature scaling cannot move an argmax. That is the first checkable
calibration evidence anywhere in this story, and the parallel-constrained
-decoding article predicted it would be the missing piece.

The catch is better than the headline. Under the same global temperature
the severity category gets worse, ECE 0.0375 to 0.1263, and escalate
drifts too. One scalar improves the aggregate threefold while making a
slice of traffic three times worse — which matters because the whole
point of a calibrated score is routing on it per request.

Fourteen repos read at source rather than from READMEs. Of those, four
report real measured benchmarks, four a single anecdote or timing, and
six ship real code with no numbers at all; jevlogs and HA-Jev disclose
"not yet measured" themselves. vlad-terin/jev-browser 404s on every
access path and is flagged unverified rather than written up from
mirrors. An open unanswered issue on jevlike shows its shuffled-context
control leaking the true target 39.4% of the time, which complicates its
reported 26-vs-8 gap.

The taxonomy is the argument: route, select, rank, classify, verify. The
ecosystem converges almost entirely on one shape — a cheap classifier in
front of something slower or riskier — which is a real and useful thing
and is narrower than frontier decision intelligence. jev-search is the
outlier, doing retrieval reranking with, in its own words, no generated
answers. The trading bot defaults to a mock heuristic and dry run, and
claims no profitability anywhere; it is reported as an experiment.

Access via Vercel AI Gateway as typesafe-ai/jev is real, no waitlist,
$0.042/M input.

subject: Add generated-web article: real speed, and nothing to be wrong against
body:
The speed is real and the round number is generous. Cerebras publishes
~1,850 tok/s for Qwen3.8-27B on the shared tier at batch 1. Frames pulled
from the demo recording show three different figures at once: a 1,520
tok/s OS readout, a fixed 1,950 badge in the browser titlebar, and a live
per-request counter reading 758, 1,830, 722, 843 and 1,042 across five
page loads in one clip. "2,000" is the most generous read of any of them.

The architecture is why it works: 44 GB of on-die SRAM at 21 PB/s against
a GPU's ~200 MB of on-chip memory, so the weights never leave the wafer.
No H100 comparison is given here, deliberately — every Cerebras-vs-H100
table found benchmarks Llama-3.1-70B, not this model. Same-model
consumer baselines are used instead: 65 tok/s on the author's own 4090,
~120 on a tuned 3090, ~14 on a Mac Studio.

The sharpest finding is in the demo itself. YouTube was registered in
February 2005, six years after the "1999" tab the model renders — and the
model's own 2026 Google-search page, captured in the same recording,
correctly states the February 2005 launch. It knows. Nothing in the loop
ever asks it. That is the boundary: this is generation where hallucination
is the feature, and the moment a real page with real data is wanted the
speed buys nothing and retrieval comes back. Vercel pausing AI SDK RSC in
favour of model-driven fixed components with real tool-call data is
independent corroboration of the same line.

Websim and Solipnet already did the hallucinated web page by page. The
contribution here is latency, not the concept.

At published rates a 4,000-token page costs about $0.006 against roughly
$0.0000014 to serve the same bytes from a CDN — about 4,600x. Zero
gigabytes on disk trades storage for inference.

subject: Add Grouped Value Attention article: the circulating number is not in the paper
body:
The figure doing the rounds is 44.18 against GQA's 44.36, a loss of 0.18.
Fetching arXiv 2609.13285 raw, both v1 and v2, 44.18 appears zero times.
The paper's own number is 44.35, and v2's abstract states the gap
outright: "a gap of 0.01 points, within seed variation". The 44.18 traces
to a paperswithcode.co scrape, not the primary source. So the headline
check is not "is a 0.18 loss inside the noise" but "is a 0.01 gap
meaningful at all".

On variance the paper is better than most and still short of the claim.
It does average three seeds per configuration and its own limitations
section warns against reading small differences as significant without
assessing seed variability — but it publishes no per-seed values and no
standard deviation, so "within seed variation" is asserted rather than
shown. Two paper-sourced spreads give the sense of scale: its own seven
GVA-family variants, differing only in init and normalization, span 0.64
points, and GQA against MLA — two genuinely different architectures — sit
0.48 apart in the same table. Both dwarf 0.01.

The cache claim checks out and understates itself. Backing G x d_h out of
the two reported percentages reproduces 45-47% exactly, and at real
production widths such as Llama-3-8B's 8x128 KV config the saving is
nearer 49%. MLA still saves about 72% at DeepSeek-V2's width, so GVA
lands between GQA and MLA on bytes rather than past MLA. Reconstruction
cost is fixed per query token, independent of context length, so it
should not eat the bandwidth win — though the paper reports no wall-clock
measurements at all.

What exists today: no kernel repo linked anywhere. The one downloadable
checkpoint, Lumma-0.6B-Base, implements the shared-KV ablation the
paper's own Figure 3 shows failing to match GQA, and which the paper
states is "not a proposed system". The open transformers PR adds that
same shared-KV architecture, not decoupled-RoPE GVA.

subject: Add CUDA Rust article: which aliasing, and which races
body:
The compile-time safety claim holds, narrowly, and the scope is the whole
story. cuda-oxide's DisjointSlice and launch-contract machinery genuinely
catches pointer aliasing between kernel arguments in global memory — a
real error[E0502], at zero runtime cost. It does not check shared-memory
races between threads in a block. That is Tier 2 in the project's own
safety model, it needs unsafe, and its own docs concede thread
divergence, warp convergence and memory-space awareness are all
unenforced, with the blunt note that "if you're writing a vecadd, a GEMM,
or a reduction, you will rarely leave Tier 2".

cutile-rs makes the stronger claim by deleting the problem rather than
checking it: a tile is one logical thread, per-thread indexing does not
appear in the source, so the race concept never arises. Different move,
worth naming as such.

"On stable Rust" is true — 1.89+, no nightly, no custom LLVM — but the
mechanism is Span::source_text capturing the AST for a hand-written front
end, not a real rustc backend, and the DSL validator confirms the cost:
no closures, no user structs, only tensor references and scalars.
cuda-oxide's nightly buys full Rust through real MIR instead.

Worth noting against the safety pitch: the accompanying paper says
Rust-CUDA, rust-gpu and cuda-oxide alike "treat the kernels being
compiled as unsafe code".

The blog publishes no benchmarks at all — it points at the paper. Figures
here come from arXiv 2606.15991, "Fearless Concurrency on the GPU", and
are attributed to it rather than to the blog. Those numbers put safe Rust
within 0.3% of raw Tile IR at 2.07 PFlop/s on B200, which is a real
result and is also cutile-rs's own paper. cuda-oxide has no equivalent
numbers.

subject: Add Dream-RSI article: the compute ledger runs the right way, and is incomplete
body:
Provenance checks out. 14 of 17 authors are Google or Google DeepMind,
both corresponding authors are @google.com, and the paper carries a
Google copyright line. arXiv 2609.14858 resolves and matches. The repo
being under a personal handle is normal pre-org-sync housekeeping. What
is stale is release maturity: the README's arXiv badge still says "coming
soon", CITATION.cff carries a literal arXiv:XXXX.XXXXX placeholder, and
the repo ships no code at all — its own release table marks the codebase
and reproduction scripts as still being prepared.

Nothing learns. The only versioned artifact is roughly 150 lines of
Python scheduling a frozen discovery agent, with weights and prompt both
fixed, against a frozen evaluator. The agent that rewrites that code is
itself another frozen LLM. There are zero gradient steps anywhere, and
"dreaming" is free replay against a cached discovery-tree history rather
than a learned world model. So this is iterative refinement of a fixed
pipeline's control code — the AlphaEvolve family, one level up — and the
article says so without pretending that is not worth doing.

The matched-compute check comes out the other way from the usual. The
Recursive Fixed Exploration baseline holds agent, evaluator, init and
round-1 budget fixed and varies only the policy; across nine reported
comparisons Dream-RSI wins eight, several at lower compute — Lasso at 317
calls against 550 and 1.22x faster. The ninth is a real loss, on
Autocorrelation Inequalities, 1.456375 against 1.456001. The gap in the
ledger is that "discovery-agent calls" structurally excludes the
policy-development agent's own LLM calls, whose count is never reported,
and the three math tasks report no compute column at all.

Only the ConvDiv ablation publishes a per-round curve: nine rounds,
0.427 to 1.898, no plateau. The headline Lasso and math results publish
round counts but no matching curves, so saturation past nine rounds is
unanswered. Figure 3b's Lasso curve is also non-monotonic — flat or
slightly worse through rounds 2 to 4 before jumping at round 5 — which
only the figure shows.

subject: Add GLM inference-infra article: one checkable artifact in the whole post
body:
"Throughput tripled" is measured against their own first working run, not
against a rival engine. Figure 1's twelve labelled points run from a
W8A8 baseline at 1.00x to linear attention at 3.22x over thirteen days,
and it is the only quantitative figure in the post. There is no
comparison against vLLM or SGLang — both of which GLM-5.3-Flash's own
launch lists as day-one serving paths — no absolute throughput unit, and
no named hardware beyond "a cluster of over 100,000 Chinese-made
accelerators".

Read as deltas rather than as a smooth line, that curve is not monotonic:
T+2 to T+3 is a small decrease, 1.42x to 1.41x, and T+7 through T+9 sits
flat at 2.67x across three separately named kernel changes.

Of the three case studies, exactly one is independently checkable. The
numerical-precision fix links a real PR, and diffing the actual commits in
fla-org/flash-linear-attention confirms the description and adds a nuance
the summary omits: the tf32x3 path is opt-in, off by default, not a change
to default kernel behaviour. The GIL case has no linked artifact. The
decode-kernel case is self-consistent, including an honest v0-to-v1
regression before the net win.

The methodology is the part worth keeping, and it converges with what
this site found independently in the GeoGuessr and Soup pieces: build the
cheap local feedback loop first, because the cost of one experiment sets
how many hypotheses a fixed window can test. A post arguing for dense
measurement that publishes no scripts, logs or benchmarks is worth noting
on its own terms.

subject: Add Uno article: the draft model was already inside the target model
body:
"Lossless" here is the precise speculative-decoding sense, not a
euphemism. The verifier in nano_vllm_uno/engine/two_pass_decoding.py
implements the Leviathan et al. rejection rule exactly — accept if
uniform < min(1, p/q), residual resample from clamp(p-q, 0) — over a
gated-LoRA drafter riding the same backbone. Corroborating: the paper
tested a rival method that claims losslessness in theory and found its
released sampler breaks it, so the authors treat the property as
falsifiable.

The pitch's "2.2x" is the honest number and the paper's own abstract is
the generous one. 2.2x is Table 7's measured batch-1 result, 383 against
176 tok/s on a single H200. The abstract's "up to 3x" traces to nothing in
the body — the largest figure anywhere is 2.5x, and the largest-batch
results are 1.5-1.6x, not the claimed 2x.

The paper does not dodge the real incumbent. Table 2 compares against
EAGLE-3 and DFlash directly and Uno dominates both at every batch size,
1.07-1.5x, with fewer added parameters and a shared KV cache. That is a
narrower and more interesting win than the framing against other
diffusion LLMs, which is what the announcement leads with.

Three inconsistencies. The base repo is named K2-Horizon-7B, the paper's
Table 1 calls it 8B, and safetensors.total reports 8,999,178,240 — 9.00B,
confirmed by 17,998,356,480 bytes at bf16. SWE-bench Verified for one
checkpoint appears as 58 in Figure 1, 68.4 in Table 1 and 70.1 on the HF
card. Tables 1 and 7 disagree on Uno's own throughput, 405 against 383.
Figure 1's "Tau2 Banking" bars match Table 1's Telecom row.

Also: short outputs are slower, provably — the two-pass cycle makes it
0.5x at one token regardless of predictability, converging to tau/2 only
as outputs lengthen. And the adapter ships in float32, doubling its
download for no accuracy benefit.

subject: Add GOAT article: one-sided transport, and a sink that moves rather than dies
body:
GOAT does not use two-sided Sinkhorn optimal transport. Its Appendix A is
titled "Proof of Attention as One-Sided Entropic Optimal Transport", and
the words "two-sided" and "column marginal" appear nowhere in the paper.
There is a row constraint only, no column budget, and no Sinkhorn
iterations at any point. What the paper proves is that plain softmax
already is a one-sided EOT solution with an implicit uniform prior; the
contribution is generalising that prior to a learned one, giving
softmax(score/tau + log pi). In the released code the prior is a Fourier
relative term plus a key-only bias from a small MLP, both additive logit
biases folded into extra Q/K dimensions so it rides inside one ordinary
scaled_dot_product_attention call.

It also does not eliminate the sink. Its own Theorem 5.1 proves a sink is
the optimal response to a low-signal query. GOAT moves the sink out of an
entangled high-norm content key and into a disentangled bias term, and
argues that is more stable as context grows.

Length generalisation gives three different answers depending on the eval.
Perplexity at 125M: GOAT 30.95 against ALiBi 32.49 and RoPE 33.24
in-distribution, but on the extrapolation curve ALiBi stays flat while
GOAT drifts to the 55-65 range by 32,768 — worse than ALiBi at the longest
length tested. Passkey retrieval is the opposite: GOAT holds near 0.90-1.00
while ALiBi falls to ~0.49 over the same range, so flat perplexity does not
mean flat retrieval.

No Sinkhorn means no iteration cost; the only timing numbers in the paper
are from the DNA task, 1.2% slower than RoPE at 36% less peak memory. The
flagship C4 experiment reports no throughput at all. Scale is one
operating point per modality. There are no quantisation or KV-eviction
experiments, which is where sinks actually hurt. The pos_rank knob has
three different values across the README, the code factory and Appendix G.

subject: Add open-1b article: what "you don't have to trust" actually removes
body:
Gensyn's open-1b is a chained bit-exact hash over every training step —
not proof-of-learning, which the paper names and rejects for its
exploitable acceptance tolerance, and not a succinct proof. There is no
SNARK: checking a step costs that step's compute, redone. That is a real
and useful property, and it is a different one from the headline.

The live audit API confirms the scale of what has been checked. As of
2026-09-18, three days after launch: 25 of 80,957 steps audited (0.031%),
0 of 810 segments confirmed, 11 contributors, 7 active claims. Low
coverage three days in is expected and the article says so. The structural
points matter more. The manifest's own artifactCheck is "loss-checked" —
the server compares loss and z-loss and a file digest, not an independent
hash recomputation; the bit-exact check runs on the volunteer's machine
and is self-reported. Per-step replay ranges from ~25 min on an H100 to
~19.2 h on an M4 Pro, and even the fastest logged H100 rate sustained
across all steps comes to ~3.8 GPU-years against the original run's ~3.65.
Full verification is not cheaper than training; it is relocated onto
volunteers.

The hash covers weights, optimizer moments, gradients and batch digest.
It does not cover RNG position, data-stream cursor, spike-skip state or
descriptor flags, per the repo's own audit-replay doc. And the chain
covers the base run only: the midtrained and SFT checkpoints — the
instruct model most people will actually run — start their own chain,
and the audit site's manifest, coverage, ledger and the GCS logs prefix
contain exactly one hash log.

On benchmarks Gensyn discloses its own 10x token-budget gap and
reproduces OLMo 2's MMLU before comparing. Credited as such.

subject: Add jina-ocr-v1 article: the active count assumes a tied embedding
body:
Total checks out to the parameter: safetensors.total is 3,372,238,080,
and summing the shard header shapes by component — vision encoder 401.4M,
decoder 2,934.7M, FastMTP block 36.1M — reproduces it exactly. "570M
active" does not. Computing per-token active compute from the real tensor
shapes (one dense layer, eleven MoE layers at 6-of-64 routed experts, plus
embedding and output head) gives 739.6M. The gap is one embedding matrix:
config.json sets tie_word_embeddings false, and vocab 129,280 x hidden
1,280 makes each of embed_tokens and lm_head 165,478,400 parameters.
Subtract one and you get 574.1M. The paper's arithmetic assumes a tied
embedding this checkpoint does not have, and its "under 1B whole-model
active" bound only clears with the uncorrected figure — at 739.6M it is
1.14B.

The vision encoder is real and counted in the 3.4B, but it runs once per
page at prefill, not per decode token, so the two costs are never paid on
the same forward pass.

Speculative decoding is FastMTP: one shared dense block reused
recursively for K steps, not a draft model, Medusa heads or n-gram.
On an L4 at batch 1 it is 1.95x at K=3 in eager mode with 57.6%
acceptance. Under CUDA graphs the non-speculative baseline itself gets
3.71x faster, so the fixed draft cost stops paying: K=1 is best at 1.17x
and K=3 — the deepest and most quoted setting — is the worst at 1.09x.
Those numbers were measured on vLLM 0.20.1 while the model's own README
requires vLLM 0.21 or newer.

Weakest category is degraded scans at 42.6 on olmOCR-Bench, not tables
(88.8) or multi-column (85.5). Licence is CC BY-NC 4.0.

subject: Add tiny browser models article: six models, five orders of magnitude
body:
gpu-lexer, gpu-time, gpu-query, neural-flexbox, gpu-cron and tinySarf all
shipped within about a week — task-specific models small enough to serve
as a static asset and run on the viewer's own GPU. All five public repos
were cloned and read, so the numbers come from their model cards rather
than their homepages.

Which matters, because the two disagree. gpu-time's model card says 38,745
parameters while the project homepage's explainer video still says 24,761.
gpu-lexer's own card flags that an earlier public 88.02% figure used a
different label taxonomy, and its per-language table shows under 50%
agreement on jinja, liquid, razor, vala and vb. neural-flexbox trained in
177.53 seconds — a number only in packages/training/active/report.json —
and its own out-of-distribution split drops from 94.4% to 74.4% with a
76.67px max error. tinySarf agrees with its teacher on 87% of fields but
gets the full analysis right 12.52% of the time, and its evaluation is
teacher agreement rather than human gold, as its card repeatedly says.

gpu-cron has no public repo, so it was tested live in a headless browser.
Asked for "every 90 minutes" it correctly refuses, which is cron's
representational limit and not a model error. Fed pure gibberish it
returns a biweekly schedule at 95.8% confidence. That is the shape of the
ceiling: these models do not know when a question is not theirs.

The economics hold up anyway. A CDN-delivered model has no per-call cost,
no round trip and no rate limit, and the article works that against
current API pricing. Cross-links parallel-constrained-decoding — both are
attacks on the same idea, that most decisions in software do not need a
frontier model.

subject: Add Bend 2 and Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash articles
body:
Bend 2's shipped runtime does not use interaction nets, and its own paper
says so: "Readers of the author's earlier runtimes may expect interaction
nets here; there are none" (bend2/docs/BendRT/main.typ:142). Affine
ownership replaced the graph machinery — losing optimal reduction of
shared redexes, gaining native-speed sequential code and a readable cost
model. The article explains interaction nets anyway, as the HVM lineage
worth understanding, but does not attribute them to this runtime.

The proof checking is real. bend.ts is a 3,734-line kernel; bend.lean is
20,981 lines with zero `sorry`, verified by grep. On defs_12800 the
checker runs 0.295s against Lean 4's 36.177s and Rocq's 5.985s. Two
caveats the project states itself: the Lean mechanization does not yet
match the shipped checker ("we are resyncing the two"), and comp.ts —
6,251 lines sitting between a checked proof and the binary — is described
in its own README as 99% AI-written and not fully audited. The
Navier-Stokes comparison is an analogy about method; Bend had no
involvement in it.

Past the paper's 12-benchmark table, the fuller 16-benchmark pin has an
outlier it omits: hashmap runs 4.4x slower than its C twin at one thread,
well outside the claimed 0.8-1.5x band.

For Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, the widely shared "51.8% fewer tokens" does not
appear in the source. Qwen's own figure is 45.7% (145,736 to 79,117 on
OmniVideoBench), and accuracy rises with it, 63.4 to 67.8 — a Pareto win
rather than a tradeoff. The blog says "close to Gemini 3.8 Flash" on
audio-visual and "exceeds" on audio; the second is carried almost
entirely by multi-speaker diarization, while Gemini leads all four
ordinary single-speaker audio benchmarks. The "89% cheaper video" is a
flat-rate pricing collapse, $1.40 to $0.15 per 1M, not a demonstrated
tokenizer change. Qwen-Live-Harness was announced as open-sourced; the
repo 404s while the npm package ships compiled dist only.

subject: Add two Jev articles: the claim, and the mechanism
body:
parallel-constrained-decoding covers how it works. Prefill once, broadcast
the KV cache across fields, score every field in one batched pass, gather
only the candidate rows and softmax over those. The clever part is
os.path.commonprefix: the shared prefix of the enum choices is hoisted
into the suffix text, so only the first token of each remainder has to be
distinct, and an empty remainder falls back to the closing-quote token.

That trick has a failure mode, and it fires on the repo's own presets.
Verified against Qwen2.5's real tokenizer: the pretokenizer isolates
\p{N}, so numbers split per digit — "000" and "001" are not vocab tokens,
"0" and "1" are. The high_cardinality_255 preset's customs codes run
CAT_000 to CAT_254, so after the CAT_ prefix all 255 choices reduce to
first digits 0, 1 or 2: three distinguishable values, in the preset the
README benchmarks at 89ms and "100% validity". In fintech_fraud,
SANCTIONED_ZONE kills the common prefix of counterparty_jurisdiction_risk,
so TIER_1_LOW, TIER_2_MODERATE and TIER_3_HIGH all resolve to first token
"T" — "TIER" is not in the vocab. Three of four choices collide.

The engines then diverge. engine_mlx.py branches on has_collisions and
falls back to a bounded greedy decode. engine_torch.py unpacks
has_collisions and prefixes and never reads them again, so the CUDA and
ZeroGPU path breaks ties toward the first-listed choice, silently. The
two paths also report confidence as different quantities under one name:
a subset softmax on one, a clamped product of greedy token probabilities
on the other.

jev-system-one-models covers the product claims. openjev, holding model
and hardware fixed, measures the isolated architectural win at 5.21x
(1.023s vs 5.332s), against headline figures of 40-200x. TypeSafe's own
docs decline public benchmarks and state plainly that calibration "does
not guarantee that an individual answer is correct". No ECE, Brier or
reliability numbers appear anywhere in ~19k lines of their docs. Free
output tokens are close to a definitional consequence of never generating
text. "Two years in stealth" is fair for a trained calibrated model and
not for the architecture, which the tracker reproduced in days.

subject: Add Bonsai 2 27B article: 98.2% of which aggregate?
body:
The size claims check out to the byte. Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf is
5,946,648,928 bytes against an F16 sibling of 53,808,408,928 — 5.95 GB,
53.8 GB, a ratio of 9.05x. The word doing the work is "language": the
vision mmproj is a separate 0.63-0.93 GB file, so a real multimodal
download is about 6.58 GB, not 5.95.

"98.2% of FP16" is real and computed two different ways in Prism ML's own
documents. The whitepaper and launch post use a 20-benchmark suite (83.9
vs 85.4); the model card uses a different 14-benchmark suite (84.78 vs
86.32), dropping four vision benchmarks plus tau2-Bench, AA-LCR and
BigCodeBench in favour of MuSR and MMMU-Pro. Both round to 98.2%, and the
FP16 baseline differs between the two. Per-benchmark the losses are
uneven: OCR Bench v2 -6.7%, BigCodeBench -5.6%, GPQA Diamond -5.2%. The
two benchmarks run specifically to test the agentic-coding claim,
Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench Verified, retain about 75% — and neither
appears in either aggregate.

"55 tok/s with WebGPU on M5 Max" could not be found in the launch post,
the whitepaper, either README, or the linked WebGPU Space. The only
verifiable M5 Max figure is 46.8-47.0 tok/s on native Metal llama-bench
at batch 1, tg128, vision tower excluded.

Ternary is not free: activations stay high precision, the rotated
Hadamard basis needs a runtime transform on the critical path at batch 1,
and stock llama.cpp produces garbage on these files rather than refusing
them. On Prism ML's own intelligence-density metric their older 1-bit
Bonsai 27B scores 0.530/GB against Bonsai 2's 0.444/GB.
