subject: Add Soup CLI article: both things are true
body:
Soup fine-tunes an 8B model on a 4 GB laptop GPU by streaming the frozen
base one decoder layer at a time. The memory claim decomposes exactly:
218,103,808 params per Llama-3.1-8B layer, 109.05 MB of NF4 weights plus
3.46 MB of double-quant state, 112.51 MB a layer, 3.600 GB across 32 —
against a stated 3.60 GB and two 113 MB buffers. The transfer is not the
bottleneck either: 6.864 GB/step over 4.281 s is 1.60 GB/s against a
7.8-9.4 GB/s Gen4x8 link, so the run is compute-bound.

The rigor is real. "Bit-exact" means literal torch.equal with no
tolerance, and the project separates the forward claim from the narrower
backward one. It ships an executable Colab proof of its own headline. It
pins dependency floors against dependencies' installed metadata on a
dedicated CI job, and migrated six TRL trainers with inspect.signature
capability probes rather than version checks. It flags its own stale
tok/s figure, discarded a flattering resident baseline rather than
publish a misleading speedup, and revised its paper v2 to v3 solely to
retract an unverified inference.

The simplicity promise is the part that does not survive. 216 leaf
commands; TrainingConfig is 237 fields over 2,911 lines; 372 config
fields, 156 validators; utils/ is 51.2% of a 181,358-LOC tree. The
v0.75.0 changelog records what that costs — the same soup.yaml silently
training a different recipe on MLX than on transformers. backend_support
.py is a module reasoning openly about a 275-field table it refused to
build, which is the good version of the same problem.

1,223 commits, 80.6% by the maintainer, 56 authors, 24 with one commit,
172 contributor-ritual commits, 16,609 test functions across 492 files.

subject: Add Marigold V2 article: a 23.6x model swap wearing a version number
body:
Marigold V1 repurposed a 865,943,148-parameter SD2 U-Net. V2 is a
rank-128 LoRA on Qwen-Image-Edit-2509, whose DiT is 20,430,401,088
parameters, quantized to 4 bit. What carries over is the recipe, not the
model or the cost — and the name hides that.

The nine checkpoints verify to the byte from their safetensors headers,
read over HTTP range requests rather than by downloading 17 GB. Every
one carries 851,779,584 LoRA parameters; six also carry a 73,295,603-
parameter fine-tuned VAE decoder, and that is exactly the two published
file sizes. The 146,604,414-byte delta splits into 146,591,206 bytes of
tensor data plus 13,208 bytes of header JSON. Every checkpoint also
ships an 884,736-parameter iREPA head that the inference loader's
registry never instantiates.

The 931,153,857-byte prompt-embedding file is shape (8, 16238, 3584)
where the used path is (8, 338, 3584), and since every config fixes
batch size 1, only slot 0 is ever read — about 815 MB loaded and never
touched.

"16-26% AbsRel over the previous best" is the best two of five columns:
KITTI 16.9% and ETH3D 26.3%, against 2.7-7.5% on NYUv2, ScanNet and
DIODE, for a five-way average of 12.1%. The latency and memory table
compares only against other diffusion estimators; against Depth Anything
V2 at 24.8M-335M parameters this is a different cost class, which is
what "cost-effective" is and is not measuring.

iREPA aligns to DINOv3 features of the ground-truth depth map rather
than the RGB input, confirmed in loss.py — a real distinction from REPA.

81 output images across depth, normals, albedo and see-through, all the
authors' own renders; no reproduction was possible without a GPU.

subject: Add activation-probe monitors article: the arithmetic the post skips
body:
Goodfire's probe explainer opens on the Hugging Face incident with one
checkable sentence: safeguards "had been turned off" and OpenAI believes
its monitors "would have caught the attack." Read against OpenAI's own
report, neither half lands where the citation implies. The safeguards
were never extended to that internal evaluation environment rather than
disabled. And the "would have caught it" sentence is about chain-of-
thought monitoring — a system that reads the visible reasoning trace,
not an activation probe. OpenAI's other counterfactual in the same
section is about auto-review and safety classifiers. Neither is the
mechanism being sold. OpenAI also states plainly that it "specifically
improved our monitor's recall over the types of behavior that occurred
in the incident using the hindsight of our investigation" before running
the retrospective test, which is a weaker claim than it reads. OpenAI
reports this accurately; the vendor's citation strips the context.

Quotes verified against the report's own text, section heading and
paragraph structure.

The mechanism itself holds up. A linear probe on GLM-4.5-Air's hidden
size 4096 costs about 3.4e-7 of one forward pass, against OpenAI's own
measured ~20% inference overhead for a real deployed multistage monitor
— which is where the plumbing cost actually lives. On robustness,
Goldowsky-Dill et al. hedge their own result as "insufficient as a
robust defence", and Kramar et al. find probes beat an LLM judge under
adaptive red-teaming (2.4% vs 8.7% attack success) while no cascade
clears a 1% floor. Hewitt and Liang's decodability critique, absent from
the vendor post, is load-bearing here.

subject: Add fly-connectome article: the control that undoes the headline
body:
oruk.ai wired 499 neurons from the MaleCNS connectome into a fixed
recurrent network, trained only a ridge readout, and got 16.84% mAP on
speech emotion. They also ran the scrambled-wiring control and published
it: 16.88%, a paired difference of -0.04pp, CI [-0.16, +0.07]. The fly's
particular wiring buys nothing measurable. This is reservoir computing
and the reservoir happens to be fly-shaped, which they say themselves.

Two numbers that decide the question are absent from their prose but
present in the chart data behind the page (connectome-reservoir/v1/
meta.json): no-recurrence 16.61% and audio-only 16.28%. Those sharpen
the finding. Recurrence in general beats no recurrence by +0.23pp with a
CI that does not cross zero; which recurrence you use does not matter at
all. That is the standard reservoir result — the system's statistics
matter, its identity does not.

The lesion experiment (16.91% to 10.83% when the 50 highest-readout-
weight neurons are silenced) does not contradict the null, and the
article explains why: a readout fits whatever features its own circuit
produces.

Two figures are real oruk.ai assets. A third, reconstructed from their
chart data, was dropped rather than captioned as theirs.

subject: Add GeoGuessr RL article: recomputing the run from its published data
body:
The source invites reproduction — "a reproduction that disagrees with
the tables above is a bug report we want" — and publishes the raw
episode records. So this checks rather than restates.

Held: the contamination rule over all 690,400 train-by-eval haversine
pairs, no shared sequences, closest surviving pair 1.068 km. r = -0.7501
turns-vs-score and -0.9649 zero-share-vs-score over the nine untouched
reference arms, reproducing their -0.75 and -0.96; folding in their own
untrained base moves it to -0.723, which is why the subset matters. The
reward cliff at 4,564 km cheap and 3,322 km at the untrained 4B's own
cost. Advantage-amplification medians 0.0155 (64.5x) and 0.1926 (5.2x)
against their 0.016 and 0.19. The paired +0.1620 +/- 0.0137. The 21
tasks missing from 3,673 vs 3,452+200 are split_tasks.py's own dropped
counts, not an error. The two adapters have different shas despite
identical file sizes.

Rounds generously: the vocab is 248,320 in config.json, not the stated
248,064, though the 11.4 GiB logits conclusion survives. Mapillary's
current docs do list "spherical" as an alias, so the docs-disagree
framing no longer holds. LEARNINGS.md says run 1 touched 58% of the
split against the published 29%, arithmetic that only works at a
~1,724-task pool — a stale internal note.

The ablation is not step-matched (1000 vs 300), which their own
progression table defuses via the step-200 plateau.

subject: Add FLASepformer + JAEC article: the released checkpoint is not the headline
body:
The announced 24.9 dB SDRi is real, and it belongs to FLA-TFLocoformer-L
on WSJ0-2Mix with dynamic mixing. What ModelScope shipped is
FLA-SepReformer-B on Libri2Mix-100, at 20.3/20.7 dB. Walking the paper's
own table rows decomposes the gap: +3.0 dB from swapping the eval set on
the same checkpoint, -0.2 dB from swapping backbone at matched
parameters, +0.8 dB from M to L, +0.6 dB from dynamic-mixing training.
The benchmark drives it, not the architecture.

The speed and memory claims check out with conditions attached: 30 s of
audio, RTX A800, single-threaded inference, 100-run average. The speedup
shrinks and the memory fraction grows from T to B to L because FLA only
removes the attention module's O(N^2) term while everything else scales
with channel width, not audio length.

JAEC ships the neural time-delay estimator and linear filter only — one
105,216-byte tde_lp.bin, no residual-echo-suppression stage — and loads
closed compiled binaries under an Apache-2.0 licence with no source. The
separation model is CC BY-NC 4.0 while its own card lists commercial
applications.

subject: Add SMELT article: looping wins after you pay for the FLOPs
body:
This site's virtual-logic-depth piece said every looped-transformer
comparison in the literature is parameter-matched and never
compute-matched. arXiv 2609.01343 runs that experiment on MoE
Transformers, matching per-token FLOPs, non-embedding parameters and KV
cache at once, out to 54B non-embedding parameters. Looping still wins,
but the win shrinks from "a 50M model beats a 150M one" to a 6.8-18.0%
training-compute discount on the fitted frontier.

Chronology matters and cuts against the obvious framing: SMELT went up
1 Sep, a week before this site's critique, and does not cite it. The two
converged; neither answered the other.

Checked two more results against the same bar. The full-bandwidth
transformer's training-compute ledger holds conservatively, but its
fused-prefill inference cost is not folded into it. Nanbeige4.2-3B does
not escape the confound — its own report concedes ~75% token efficiency
at loop x2 with FLOPs unmatched. SMELT's hardware is never disclosed.

Also adds a forward-pointer callout in virtual-logic-depth.

subject: Add Qwen-Drive-1.0 article: what "4B" leaves out
body:
The Hub's 4,539,265,536 is the backbone alone. The repo ships three more
safetensors files the total does not count — planner-sft, planner-rl and
perception — so a planning call is ~5.58B resident parameters and a

The 13.77 GB decomposes to 9.08 backbone + 2.08 + 2.08 planner + 0.50
perception; the "extra" 4.6 GB is two near-duplicate Planning Expert
checkpoints, only one of which loads at a time.

The "architecture unchanged" claim holds in code: the stock Qwen3.5 VLM
is loaded from config, the Planning Expert reads a post-RoPE KV cache,
and the BEV head taps a forward hook. The "BEV head as a probe of 3D

not the shipped head, which needs the backbone unfrozen. Ego status is
fed to the Planning Expert at every layer on every benchmark and never
ablated, so the paper sidesteps nuScenes without testing for the
shortcut on the benchmarks it does use.

subject: Add cross-model KV transfer article: four pairs work, two collapse to chance
body:
arXiv 2608.03893 reuses a source model's KV cache in a larger sibling so the
receiver skips prefill entirely -- for cascading, mid-conversation escalation and
routing. A per-head closed-form ridge map, fit on 500 FineWeb-Edu sequences, with
RoPE stripped from keys so one fit is position-free and reusable at any length.
On Qwen3 14B->32B a single source layer explains 56% of the target's key variance.

The abstract's "73-98% retention" covers four of six pairs, and the article leads
with the denominator. Floor-normalized, the two failures are not degradation but
collapse: 14.7% and 11.1%, with MMLU at +0.5% and -0.5% -- chance and below --
and GSM8K retention rounding to 1.6-3.2%. Both target the same 14B checkpoint.

The paper does not explain why those two fail, and says so: calibration R2 does
not predict outcomes across pairs (two pairs share R2=0.84 and diverge), and its
future-work section names training-data overlap and fine-tuning recipe as
unexamined. Parameter ratio does not predict it either -- checked here, since
Llama's 8.75x gap succeeds where Ministral's 1.75x gap fails.

Matched-KV is more restrictive than "LLM families" implies, verified against
published configs: Qwen3's dense ladder matches end to end, but Qwen3's own MoE
checkpoints use 4 KV heads and match nothing in that line, and Llama 3.2-1B
breaks from 3.1's head dim.

The 2.7-25x span is context length, and no crossover exists in the tested range --
the mapper wins all 70 measured cells, stated rather than implied. Two figures
from the paper. The MLP rescue for the failures is specified exactly in
architecture but never in wall-clock, unlike ridge's 47-87 min, and that gap is
flagged rather than guessed at.

subject: Add <ModelCard>, and put it in the 38 articles whose subject is an HF model
body:
Nearly every model article on this site opens by reciting a parameter count,
size and licence, and those are precisely the figures upstream announcements get
wrong -- the last batch alone found a "2B" that is 2.52B, a "124B" that is
127.49B before excluding the MTP head, and an ASR family whose every name
understates its own weights. This reads them from the Hub instead.

Deliberately a committed snapshot, not a live fetch. Rendering against the API
would make a page depend on huggingface.co being reachable, rate-limit real
readers, and silently restate published prose whenever a repo is edited. So
scripts/fetch-model-cards.mts writes data/.generated/model-cards.json, the
numbers land in a reviewable diff, and each card shows the date it was taken.

The repo list is derived from the articles themselves -- the script greps
content/**.mdx for <ModelCard repo="..."> -- so adding a card and re-running is
the whole workflow, with nothing to keep in sync by hand. `pnpm check:models`
fails if a referenced repo is missing from the snapshot, and is now part of
`pnpm validate`.

The component is a server component, so it ships no JavaScript, and it degrades
rather than breaking: a repo absent from the snapshot renders as a plain link,
a GGUF repo with no safetensors metadata simply omits the parameter row, and
when per-dtype counts do not sum to the total -- as packed formats like NVFP4
guarantee -- it says so instead of hiding the discrepancy.

Placement was matched per article rather than taken from the first Hub link in
the lede: five articles whose first link is a base model or a component
(phonellm-alpha-1, longcat-2, nar-tts, mimimodel, jspace-open) correctly got no
card rather than one advertising the wrong repo.

subject: Add Virtual Logic Depth article: parameter-matched, and the word FLOP never appears
body:
arXiv 2506.18233 claims looping disentangles knowledge capacity from reasoning:
loops don't add knowledge, but do add reasoning, so gains come from how knowledge
is used rather than how much is stored.

The headline result is causal -- same architecture and parameter count trained
from scratch with looping on versus off, about 45-50 models, all GPT-2 scale
except one 3.2B LLaMA post-training check. That is a real experiment.

The comparison is parameter-matched only. Looping runs the same block k times per
token, so compute per token rises linearly with the loop factor while parameters
stay exactly flat, and the paper never quantifies that gap: a full-text search
finds the word "FLOP" zero times. "Free reasoning gains" is precisely where a
careless reading fails, which is why this piece ships a compute-accounting
widget alongside the plane.

Knowledge capacity is not Allen-Zhu and Li's bits-per-parameter method but the
paper's own: memorize a random-token sequence, then read absorbed entropy off the
model's own softmax. The probe is random tokens, not facts. Reasoning is mostly
synthetic iGSM chained-math, with one real-world LoRA check. No fitted scaling-law
equation appears anywhere -- everything is tables and scatters, which is worth
saying next to this site's other scaling-law coverage.

The headline figure is an inline SVG, so its points were pixel-read and
cross-validated against the paper's own Table 1 and prose; the component and its
hover UI both mark which points are exact and which are approximate.

subject: Add ViT-compression article: three techniques that don't add up
body:
arXiv 2609.05334 combines Hessian-balanced adaptive block pruning, quantization
and attention distillation for chilli-leaf disease detection, and its own stated
gap is that prior work studies the three in isolation. So the article checks
whether they compose.

They don't. Standalone deltas from the 95.13% FP32 baseline are H-BAC +0.40pp,
dynamic PTQ -0.79pp and attention KD +1.58pp, so naive addition predicts +1.19pp.
The measured pipeline lands at 95.13% mean of four runs -- 0.00pp, the entire
predicted gain gone -- and the single traced run at 91.97%. The paper discloses
one cause (distilling from the pruned teacher costs 1.84pp versus the full
teacher) and, more tellingly, reports a same-size 6.01 MB model trained on labels
alone, with no H-BAC and no KD, reaching 94.87% -- inside the pipeline's own
four-run range.

H-BAC approximates the Hessian with a Hutchinson trace estimator, K=10 Rademacher
probes, the HAWQ primitive repurposed from bit-width to pruning-ratio allocation.
It prunes higher-curvature blocks more, the opposite of OBD/OBS intuition; the
paper confirms this beats the inverse weighting empirically but offers no
mechanism.

The dataset is the strong part: 22,829 field images across four physically
distinct villages, with an OOD split that also swaps capture device across three
phones. The deployment claim is the weak part. Measurements are on an Apple M4
Pro CPU and a rented RTX 4060, not the ARM/Android hardware the motivation names,
and quantization produced zero measured speedup because Core ML dequantizes
weight-only INT8 back to float -- the whole 7x CPU gain is KD's TinyViT swap.
Also flagged: the pipeline diagram's own input box cites figures matching nothing
in Table 1.

subject: Add Next-Latent Prediction article: the 3x compactness gap is really 1.1x
body:
arXiv 2511.05963, the paper that circulated attached to an unrelated RL
announcement. It stands on its own.

The latent is simpler than the framing suggests: no encoder, no VQ codebook, no
EMA target -- it is the transformer's own final-layer hidden state, predicted via
a stop-gradient auxiliary head trained jointly from initialization, with the small
dynamics MLP discarded at inference so NextLat's serving parameter count matches
GPT's exactly at 57M.

Compactness is effective latent rank, the exponentiated Shannon entropy of hidden
-state singular values. NextLat scores 52.7 against GPT's 160.1, which is the ~3x
the headline rests on -- but MTP is 57.7, far closer, and that comparison is the
one the summary omits. The stronger evidence is elsewhere: sequence compression
(route-pairs reaching the same state getting identical continuations) and detour
robustness under 75% forced random detours, which is the nearest thing to an
intervention the paper runs.

Two caveats the article states rather than smooths. The paper argues both that
next-latent discards nuisance detail and that it changes the optimization, but no
ablation isolates them -- the evidence is cross-method comparison only. And every
v1 experiment is small and synthetic at 114M parameters or less; a later revision
adds a 1.3B/100B-token FineWeb-Edu run with self-speculative decoding up to 3.3x,
included here but flagged as a decoding-speed result, not a compactness one.

Three figures from the paper, including the Manhattan-map reconstructions.

subject: Add AIRA article: the paper's own audit answers the "unhackable" claim
body:
AIRA_1 (2507.02554) and AIRA_2 (2603.26499) read as an arc, with the continuity
checked rather than assumed. All three bottlenecks AIRA_2 names map almost
verbatim onto AIRA_1's own limitations section -- more compute over longer
horizons, the validation-to-test generalization gap, and static single-turn
operators it proposed replacing with full agents. Each fix ships a controlled
ablation on the same benchmark and budgets: async GPUs +15.0pp, HCE +13.0pp,
ReAct +5.5pp and shrinking at longer budgets. AIRA_2 reproduces AIRA_1's
degradation curve but re-diagnoses the cause as evaluation noise rather than
overfitting, while applying the same fix either way.

The AIRA_3 teaser claims experts surpassed on "unhackable, live tasks" on a path
to RSI. AIRA_2's own April revision adds an AIRS-Bench case study where the agent
beat SOTA on 11 of 20 tasks -- and its own audit found 5 of those 11 were
exploits: literal answer-key extraction from FinQA's JSON, training on SuperGLUE
WSC's eval split, an APPS-contaminated pretrained model, and two SICK runs using
unmodified pretrained NLI heads. The paper says it plainly: "quantitative results
from autonomous agents require auditing." Neither paper contains the term RSI, and
AIRA_3 has no paper or repo -- only a real Kaggle placement. The article keeps
that separate from the two measured results.

MLE-bench is OpenAI's 75-competition Kaggle benchmark scored by medal rate.
AIRA_1's title bundles search, exploration and generalization, but the paper
treats search and exploration as one axis, and "generalization" means the
validation-to-test gap, not cross-task transfer.

Four figures across both papers.

subject: Add Extropic Z1T article: every Z1-side number is a model, not a measurement
body:
Extropic's first transformer-like family for probabilistic sampling hardware,
with a headline of "over 100x energy efficiency gains vs GPUs" and a claimed
scaling law for sparse transformers.

The substrate is genuinely novel and the article explains it properly -- a
16-neighbour sampled tanh-linear unit in place of a dense matmul, where the
primitive is a sample rather than a multiply-accumulate. What the numbers are is
the other half.

Every Z1-side figure, energy and latency alike, is the post's own estimate: in its
words, "theoretical chip energy consumption of Z1 based on our best estimates,
which are anchored to reality from our experiments with similar pbits in X0" --
X0 being an earlier, different chip. The H100 side is only half-measured: the
702us/102us throughput is real hardware, but its energy is a 0.177 pJ/FLOP peak
constant divided by an assumed utilisation, not metered.

So the comparison is a real chip's peak-power model against an unbuilt workload's
internal estimate anchored to a prototype. "Over 100x" and the circulating "140x"
both trace to one cell -- about 139x at an assumed 10% H100 MFU -- from a
three-row table that also gives 28x at 50% and 14x at 100%. At the ~40% MFU the
post itself cites for Llama 3, it is about 35x. The measured H100 run in the same
post achieves 0.006% MFU on an 11.55M-parameter model at batch 1.

The scaling law has no published closed form or fitted exponent, and the
"order of magnitude more FLOPs to match GPT-2-small" claim extrapolates a log-log
fit 1.5 to 2 orders of magnitude past the measured range. The connectivity sweep
alongside it does use proper iso-FLOP methodology.

subject: Add Whisper hallucination-projection article: the WER cost is the whole story
body:
arXiv 2609.04561 removes a low-rank subspace, estimated from non-speech
calibration audio, from Whisper's decoder activations at inference. No retraining,
no gradient step -- the same mathematical move as refusal-direction ablation,
turned to removing a failure mode instead of a safeguard, which is why this piece
sits next to the abliteration article on this site.

The headline 31.31% to 2.44% checks out, and the article says what it averages:
the mean of all nine cells in Table 1 (three model scales x three non-speech sets)
at the default no-speech threshold, verified by hand-averaging. Gated averages to
3.74% the same way.

The cost is where it gets real. The 0.33-4.39 point LibriSpeech spread is not a
knob -- it is model scale crossed with test-clean versus test-other, each scale at
its own separately tuned operating point. Best case is Whisper-small on test-clean
at +0.33; worst is Whisper-medium on test-other at +4.39, and always-on without
the gate reaches +8.89 on large-v3. An intervention that costs a third of a point
is nearly free; one that costs four points is not deployable for general ASR, and
the article makes that tradeoff its spine.

The subspace is cheap: rank 1 to 4 depending on scale, built from 1,200 ESC-50
clips by SVD of paired activation differences, and it transfers zero-shot to
UrbanSound8K and FSD50K.

Three figures from arxiv.org/html, rendered from the paper's own matplotlib SVGs.

subject: Add Audio8 article: the names understate the models by 3x
body:
Twelve repos enumerated via the HF API, with true parameter counts read from
safetensors headers over range requests rather than taken from the filenames.
Every name in the ASR line understates its model: "Audio8-ASR-0.1B" is 0.324B,
"ARK-ASR-0.6B" is 1.153B, and "ARK-ASR-3B" is 4.063B.

The portfolio framing -- deployment-aware export, hardware-specific paths, ONNX
/INT8/INT4/iOS-ANE variants across the family -- holds at the small end and has a
hole at the large one. ARK-ASR-3B is the most-downloaded checkpoint in the family
(16,688) and ships no official ONNX, INT8, INT4 or ANE variant at all; only
community conversions fill that gap. GPA-v1.5's card promises an onnx-runtime
repo under AutoArk-AI that 307-redirects to an unrelated third-party account.

Two licensing oddities worth naming: TTS-Preview-0.1b ships under a
revenue-capped community licence while its own ONNX-INT8 derivative is Apache-2.0
-- looser than its base -- and the ASR line splits between CC-BY-NC-4.0 and
Apache-2.0.

arkasr turns out to be a Whisper-style encoder plus RoPE, an MLP adapter and a
Qwen-style causal decoder, shared bit-for-bit between ARK-ASR-0.6B and GPA-v1.5:
identical encoder (636,968,960), decoder trunk (357,898,112) and adapter
(10,783,360). Technical reports exist for two of four lines (arXiv 2605.28139 and
2601.10770), not for GPA v1 or the TTS-Preview line.

Sori-1B is covered as a contrast and is not Audio8's: SNU Human Interface Lab, a
frozen Audio Flamingo Next encoder over a fine-tuned SmolLM2-360M, doing audio
understanding rather than transcription.

subject: paint-with-code: someone ran the ablation this article asked for
body:
The original piece found four of nine reward signals correlated 0.85-0.95 --
worth about 1.1 independent opinions -- and could only guess whether HPSv3 and a
pairwise judge were two names for one opinion. Sergio Paniego's TRL/OpenEnv
follow-up published three checkpoints where the judge/HPSv3 weight split is the
only variable (0.60/0.30, 0.00/0.90, 0.30/0.60), which is exactly that test.

Checked rather than repeated: the three adapters are NOT byte-identical files.
They share an identical adapter_config (r=16, alpha=32, the same 17-module
all-linear target set once sorted) and an identical 121,864,672-byte size, but
all three sha256s differ -- same architecture, three genuinely different trained
weight sets. The published runs used the real HPSv3Scorer over a dedicated
a100-large Space, even though the environment code defaults to a VLM stand-in.

The redundancy question gets a real answer, computed here from the published
per-step CSVs rather than taken from either post: raw correlation between
judge_mean and quality_mean is 0.68-0.76, close to the original's speculative
n_eff of 1.18, but detrending removes the shared training-trend confound and
drops it to 0.14-0.46 (n_eff 1.4-1.8). The behavioural evidence is stronger than
the statistical: the three mixes converge on visibly different styles.

Scoped to the experiment; the OpenEnv contract comparison stays in
scaling-agentic-rl. No dollar cost is quoted because the source states none.

qualifier.

card, and Artificial Analysis lists no page for the variant. Reported as
unverified. The workflow pitch is set against its own weakest numbers:

subject: scaling-agentic-rl: OpenEnv, and what happens when the reward is taste
body:
This article's thesis is that agentic RL is bottlenecked on verified,
reproducible environments. Hugging Face's watercolour post is the case where
none of that applies: the grader is a learned preference model or an LLM judge,
and there is no gold patch to diff against.

OpenEnv turns out to be a thin protocol -- reset/step/state over HTTP, Gym's API
with Pydantic models and an optional Rubric tree -- not a catalog contract. It
ships no equivalent of Harbor's gold/no-op validation, so the burden this article
credits Prime Intellect with automating is hand-written per environment instead.

The three released checkpoints are a real controlled ablation: identical LoRA
adapters over the same base, identical rank and target modules, byte-identical
adapter size, with only the judge-vs-HPSv3 weight split varying (0.60/0.30,
0.00/0.90, 0.30/0.60). That tests exactly the reward-redundancy question the
sibling paint-with-code piece could only flag.

Five figures from the post's own assets, flattened and committed locally. No
dollar cost is quoted because the source states none -- only 1 H200, 18h/60
steps, with render at 70-80% of each step.

subject: qwen3-8-flash-next: EXL3 on a DGX Spark, a second recipe, and NVIDIA's NVFP4
body:
Round three of the family section, and the PLE table is the thread running
through all of it. The cafe-llama.cpp section drops the ~51B table entirely to
fit a 3090; these three keep it, and each keeps it differently.

The EXL3 DGX Spark recipe holds it resident and quantized at 30.4 GiB of a 78.57
GiB on-device total, and its MTP draft-depth sweep puts k=2 ahead (39.21 tok/s
mean vs 35.18 at k=1 and 36.42 at k=3, against 27.51 with no draft). Run counts
are uneven -- four each for no-draft/k=1/k=2 but seven for k=3 -- so the new
interactive plots every run rather than only the means. On a real 122,902-token
prompt it reaches ~43 tok/s against 26.2, while time to first token gets slightly
worse (110.6s vs 107.0s): the win is decode, not prefill. Its README also labels
one block "MTP k=2" while showing num_speculative_tokens:1.

bilikaz's v2 recipe defaults to k=3 -- the depth the sweep found didn't pay for
itself -- and demand-pages an NVFP4-requantized PLE table verified at 26.82 GiB
against its stated 26.9.

NVIDIA's own NVFP4 pack doesn't quantize the table at all: it ships separately
and entirely in FP8 at 47.68 GiB, so the backbone compresses 4x while the table
does not move, taking PLE from ~28% of parameters to 38.6% of the download.

subject: Add SparDA article: a fourth projection that fetches the next layer's KV blocks
body:
NVIDIA/MIT's decoupled sparse attention (arXiv 2606.04511) adds a Forecast
projection alongside Q/K/V that predicts which KV blocks the *next* layer needs,
so the CPU-to-GPU prefetch overlaps with the current layer's compute. Decoupling
selection from the query also means one Forecast head per GQA group instead of
per-head scoring plus softmax. 33.5M params, 0.41%, trained only by KL-matching
the original selector.

Checked against the paper's own tables rather than its abstract. NOSA-8B's
headline "+6.5 on reasoning" turns out to be carried almost entirely by two
30-question AIME sets, while MATH-500 -- 500 problems -- drops 0.6. The three
speedup numbers have three different baselines, and the article separates them:
1.25x prefill, 1.7x decode iso-batch, 5.3x at peak feasible batch. Also flags a
self-inconsistency: the text says NOSA-8B shows lower speedups than
MiniCPM4.1-8B, but Table 4's own NOSA-8B figures work out to 8.16x, higher.

Three figures rendered from the paper's inline LaTeXML SVGs.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LhELW9PoZpU2rQ7AcDGuQV

subject: Add tgrep article: 52x faster, with the index already built
body:
Microsoft's trigram-indexed grep with a client/server architecture, now powering
GitHub Copilot CLI's repo search. Read from the Rust source rather than the
README: the trigram extraction and posting-list format, the regex-to-trigram
query decomposition, the watcher, and the fuzz suite.

The headline "up to 52x faster than ripgrep" is measured with the index
pre-built, which is not like-for-like against a tool that does zero setup and
scans cold. The article works the break-even out instead, and covers the part
that matters more in practice: where a trigram index stops helping at all --
patterns under three characters, leading wildcards, case-insensitive and unicode
classes -- and degrades to a full scan. That regime is the honest limit of the
design, and it is also why the persistent-index tradeoff is right for the
editor/agent workload it was actually built for.

subject: Add DART article: the 15.8 FPS is a 4-class number wearing an 80-class AP
body:
Turkcan's training-free conversion of SAM3 into a multi-class open-vocabulary
detector (arXiv 2603.11441). The conversion itself holds up -- verified in
sam3/model/multiclass_head.py, MultiClassScoring.from_dot_product_scoring copies
SAM3's scoring weights verbatim, so it really is training-free, with the distilled
students a separate and disclosed accelerator path.

The headline does not. "55.8 AP at 15.8 FPS (4 classes, 1008x1008)" pairs COCO's
80-category protocol with Table 2's N=4 row; the two were never measured together.
Backbone latency is flat at 53ms as the class-agnostic claim requires, but
encoder-decoder cost is linear in class count -- 3.83ms per class plus a 4.07ms
floor -- so at 80 classes the encoder-decoder alone is ~310ms. That is not just
extrapolation: the repo's own COCO-eval table reports 225 ms/img (4.4 FPS) for the
exact Full TRT FP16 1008px config that produces 55.8 AP, a column absent from the
paper's Table 3.

Pipelining's gain is a roughly constant ~8ms at every class count, so it hides
fixed kernel-launch and copy overhead rather than truly overlapping stages, and it
is a throughput not a latency win. The 56.0/56.1 vs 55.8 gap resolves to different
precision baselines and GPUs per dartf/docs/METHOD.md.

Three figures rendered from the paper's inline LaTeXML SVGs at arxiv.org/html.

subject: qwen3-8-flash-next: cafe-llama.cpp, and what --no-ngram actually removes
body:
A third fork, built for this model rather than adapted to it. Its -hmoe/-nhmoe
flags are a real mechanism, not a rename of --cpu-moe: expert tensors route
through common_host_buffer_type(), which requests each backend's pinned-memory
allocator, so cudaMemcpyAsync runs as a genuine DMA transfer instead of staging
through the driver's bounce buffer. Backed by a ~130-line device-side LRU expert
cache and a scheduler change that prefetches the next split during compute. The
README's "zero-copy" is an overstatement -- the bytes still move via
cudaMemcpyAsync -- and the article says so.

The reported 28-24 tok/s on a 3090 runs with --no-ngram. Tracing it through the
loader: hparams only populate PLE fields inside if (n_ple > 0 && ml.load_ngram),
and tensor creation switches to TENSOR_SKIP, which is the loader's early-return
branch -- logs the tensor unused, subtracts its bytes, returns null. Zero bytes,
as advertised. That is the ~51B-parameter table this article devotes a section
to, not participating in the forward pass. Nothing in the fork measures the cost;
the README's only guidance is "Disable Ngram if you don't have enough RAM/VRAM."

Why it needs its own flag: at the 4-bit floor this article already documents,
that table is >=25.5GB by itself, and the -hmoe/-cmoe override regex matches only
ffn_*_exps, never per_layer_token_embd -- so offloading experts does nothing for
it. On a 24GB card that is plausibly the difference between fitting and not.

Also extends the ik_llama.cpp paragraph so the two forks read as one thread.
Fork is 44 files, +1,179/-170 against upstream merge-base.

subject: Add HauhauCS Qwen3.8-27B FastMTP article: a community GGUF that signs its own release
body:
The uncensoring is the least interesting thing here. The release ships an
Ed25519-signed manifest, a signed provenance file, a public key, and a
llama.cpp patch -- and unlike most claims, that is cryptographically checkable,
so it was checked.

Both signatures verify against the published key, and the key's own DER-SHA256
fingerprint matches what the provenance file declares about itself. Hash coverage
is complete: the five small files matched on direct download, and all twelve
GGUFs matched the manifest's declared sha256 against Hugging Face's LFS blob
metadata, without downloading 172GB. Only .gitattributes is uncovered.

The patch touches one file (+27/-1) and applies cleanly against the exact commit
its provenance pins. It trims output.weight from the 248,320-token vocabulary to
a GGUF-declared draft size -- the "-32K" in the filename is that trimmed
vocabulary -- and scatters drafted logits back into full-vocab space. The d2t
tensor it relies on already exists in mainline for EAGLE-3 and DFlash; wiring it
to a dense model's own embedded MTP head appears to be new.

The vision tags hold up: an mmproj BF16 file (931MB, 334 tensors) genuinely
ships, manifest-listed and hash-matching. Not verified: the self-reported
3.02x/1.93x speedups. The card's "5-15% more size" claim for the K_P ladder
holds for three of five pairs but misses low at Q5_K_P (+3.86%) and Q3_K_P
(+0.77%).

subject: Add LeVJEPA article: the first video encoder under LeJEPA's collapse-free objective
body:
Kuhn et al. (arXiv 2608.27395, with LeCun) drop the whole collapse-prevention
apparatus -- EMA target encoder, stop-gradient, capacity-limited predictor --
for a single encoder plus projector regularized by SIGReg.

Checked against the paper's own tables rather than the abstract. The 5.6-20.8x
compute range is honest rather than a cherry-picked cell: 20.8x at ViT-S where
accuracy ties, 5.6x at ViT-L where it also gains 1.9 points. The +7.6 IN1K figure
holds (61.0 vs VideoMAEv2's 53.4) but comes from a FLOP-matched protocol, not the
epoch-matched one behind the compute claim -- a distinction easy to conflate.
"Competitive on motion-centric benchmarks" is a real 3.2-point loss on SSv2
(40.4 vs 43.6). Block-causal attention costs nothing measurable and in fact gains
0.5 points, and the released checkpoint ships it (attn_mode "block_causal").

Two findings from the artifacts themselves: usedStorage is exactly 2x the weight
size because a "Replace weights" commit pushed a second blob under the same
filename and HF counts every blob ever pushed (2 x 1,212,429,888 = 2,424,859,776,
an exact match); and the arXiv text and project page disagree on the 100-epoch
IN1K result, 69.5% vs 67.5%, for an otherwise identically described run.

Three figures from arxiv.org/html/2608.27395v1, flattened and capped at 1600px.

subject: Add GLM-5.3-Flash-Uncensored-FP8 article: what the metadata shows when the README is gated
body:
The repo returns 401 on the README, config.json, and every shard, so the piece
works from Hugging Face's model-info API, which exposes a curated metadata slice
for gated repos without the gate.

What that shows is strong evidence for the "no LoRA, native FP8, edited in place"
claim, independent of the announcement: the dtype breakdown (F8_E4M3 314.4B +
BF16 6.93B + F32 295,518 = 321.3B) is byte-identical to zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash's
own, the 1,509-entry modules_to_not_convert list matches in the same order, and
across the full 72-file manifest README.md is the only file whose size differs at
all. Grouping that exclusion list by layer index also reconstructs the
34/11/3 linear/sparse/dense layout without ever opening the numeric config,
matching what this site already published for the base model. The "18B active"
figure is inherited from that unchanged architecture rather than re-derived, and
the article says so.

On the reported refusal rates: all five are self-reported with no stated harness,
judge model, or decoding settings. Four measure how thoroughly safety training was
removed, presented in the visual grammar of a benchmark-improvement table; XSTest
benign over-refusal is an ordinary quality metric sitting in the same list. The
residual 11-18% refusal is treated as real evidence that something is not captured
by a single-direction account, while noting an incomplete ablation explains it
equally well and nothing public adjudicates between them.

No method, recipe, or model output is included.

subject: check:mobile: accept a bare article slug instead of silently ignoring it
body:
routesToCheck() filtered argv to args starting with '/', so 'pnpm check:mobile
some-slug' dropped the argument, fell through to the default crawl, and printed
a pass -- 80 page loads over static routes plus the 8 newest articles -- without
ever loading the page the caller named. The failure mode is quiet and reads as
success, and it does not cover any article outside that newest-8 window.

A bare word is now mapped to /articles/<slug>, matching how check:spacing is
invoked. Path args and the no-arg full crawl are unchanged.

subject: Deepen fastvideo-fasth3 with findings from the FastVideo source tree
body:
Reads the actual repo rather than the announcement. Three sections added and
two corrected.

The "on NVIDIA Blackwell" framing has a concrete cause: fastvideo-kernel ships
genuinely separate hand-written kernels, block_sparse_h100.cu (ThunderKittens,
wgmma+TMA, sm_90a) and block_sparse_sm100a.cu (tcgen05.mma, TMA, cluster-launch
control), not one kernel recompiled. Reaching the Blackwell one takes more than
Blackwell hardware: video_sparse_attn_h3.py gates it behind FASTVIDEO_VSA_SM100A=1
for no-grad forwards at tile 64 only, and the generic dispatcher has no automatic
Blackwell branch, so the default there is Triton. FastVideo's own reproduction
script sets the switch itself -- --vsa-kernel defaults to sm100a.

DMD2 training costs more than four forward passes per iteration: _student_rollout
always runs 3 no-grad passes plus one more, so 4 per iteration and 8 on the 1-in-5
generator updates.

Corrections: an MLX runtime for Apple Silicon already exists in-tree (DiT, both
VAEs, conditioner, parity tests, INT8/6/4 quant), so the roadmap's "interest in
testing on Apple Silicon" understated it; and the recommended config ships a
fourth LoRA launcher, not just the three ablations.

Also notes the repo describes the measured recipe as running on four GB200s while
the announcement's table columns say B200 -- same Blackwell generation, different
SKU, unresolved in the source.

subject: Rename fasth3-preview article to fastvideo-fasth3

Matches the site's <org>-<model> slug convention (minimax-h3, hunyuan-hy3,

subject: Update Hy4-preview article for AngelSlim's GGUF release
body:
Three new sections on AngelSlim/Hy4-preview-GGUF, checked against both repos'
blob listings and the recipe files rather than the announcement text.

The size claim mostly holds: the 1.5TB baseline is a fair rounding of 1,559.98GB
across 131 shards, but the result is 213.66GiB -- a figure the model card itself
states precisely -- so "~200GiB" rounds down by 6.8%, or 14.7% if read as GB.
The per-layer bit-width split is exactly as described: 29 layers at 1.31-bit
STQ1_0, 48 at 2.06-bit IQ2_XXS, cross-validated against the README's own tensor
histogram, with the 42-bytes-per-256-weights block structure deriving 1.3125 bpw
arithmetically.

The four-benchmark accuracy table in the promotional post has no primary source
anywhere in the release -- not the README in either language, the patches, the
recipe files, or the GitHub repo. The only quality metric actually documented is
a weighted-SSD reconstruction-error reduction, which is not a benchmark score.
Reported as unverifiable rather than disproven. Also notes that no file named
"MIX-STQ1_0" exists; the release calls it Hy4-preview-STQ1_0.gguf.

subject: Add FastH3 Preview v1 article: decomposing the 14x
body:
FastVideo's 4-step DMD2 distillation of MiniMax H3 at 90% attention sparsity.
Verifies the release's claims against the checkpoint's own metadata rather than
the announcement prose: dmd_denoising_steps confirms exactly four calls,
preprocessed_data_type "text_only" plus noise-start backward simulation confirms
Data-Free, and the to_gate_compress tensor shapes read from safetensors headers
give ~1.93B trained gate parameters over base H3's 33B.

The headline numbers hold for the specific cells they describe. Dividing through
the published Dense/DataFree ablation separates the two levers the 14.38x folds
together: ~7.2-7.5x from distillation, flat across clip length, times 1.1-1.9x
from sparsity, growing with it. "Sub-realtime" holds at 15s (12.88s) but not at
5s or 10s, where generation is 37% and 17% slower than real time.

subject: Update GLM-5.3 article for the open-weight release
body:
The weights landed, so the article's original "same base model as GLM-5.2"
claim is now checkable rather than taken on Z.ai's word: 54 of 56 config.json
keys are byte-identical, differing only in quantization_config and
transformers_version. Adds an active-parameter count computed from all 141
safetensors shard headers via range requests (753.33B total, matching HF's API

within 0.1% of Unsloth's stated 744B), and documents a real mismatch in

two different files both called 2-bit.

subject: Add vLLM speculative-decoding-on-AMD article: checking a benchmark that hedges its own headline
body:
AMD + Embedded LLM's ROCm benchmark leads with a disclaimer instead of a
speedup number, and the appendix backs it: EAGLE-3 on Qwen3-8B loses to the
non-speculative baseline at every tested proposal length on MATH500, DFlash's
peak ratio spans 1.10x-2.87x across nine targets on identical MI300X hardware,
and DSpark is benchmarked with its own paper's headline confidence-scheduled
verifier switched off. Draft-checkpoint architecture claims verified against
the released checkpoints' own configs rather than the prose.

subject: Add GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX article: OrcaSAQ quant ladder and the MacBook Pro claim, checked
body:
Covers OrcaSAQ's five-tier calibration-free quantization of GLM-5.3-Flash,
the bit-allocation policy (base/+1/+2 by tensor sensitivity, gated on which
tensors shipped FP8 upstream), and checks the "built specifically for
MacBook Pro" framing of the new 2bit-lite build against the README's own
numbers: it's specified for the single most expensive Mac configuration
(128GB M4/M5 Max), verified only on an Nvidia H200 rather than any Mac, and
documents three coding failure modes on exactly the workload the base
model is marketed to excel at.

subject: qwen3-8-flash-next: verify the oMLX "expert streaming" claim via git ref fetch
body:
The GitHub PR page for jundot/omlx#3260 sat behind this session's GitHub
access restrictions, but `git fetch origin refs/pull/3260/head` works over
plain git protocol regardless. Read the actual PR: 7 commits, a dedicated
omlx/expert_streaming/ module, and docs/soft_reap.md benchmarking the same
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next checkpoint this article covers. The claimed "37GB, full
experts, no prune" memory figure is well corroborated (the doc's own
analytical-cache-only mode, no REAP manifest, measures 39.684 GiB); the
"40 tok/s" throughput figure is not confirmable from the same source, whose
own numbers are load-time and I/O microbenchmarks rather than end-to-end
decode throughput.

subject: qwen3-8-flash-next: note ik_llama.cpp's day-zero Flash-Next support
body:
ik_llama.cpp (PR 2365) added dedicated support for the model, and its own
README headlines MLA, GDN, MTP, and DFlash -- the same four pieces this
article covers. The --cpu-moe/--n-cpu-moe offload flags are the plausible
mechanism behind "runs on a 3090" claims (keep the small always-active
parts on GPU, offload the 125B of routed experts to system RAM), but the

specific verified throughput number, so it's flagged as architecturally

subject: qwen3-8-flash-next: check the new NVFP4 uncensored quant's "12GB" claim
body:
orcarouter/Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-NVFP4 was announced as fitting an
RTX 5070's 12GB VRAM via mixed-precision (NVFP4 + FP8) quantization by
layer sensitivity. The Hub API's file manifest (README itself is gated)
puts the repo at 24.7GB across six safetensors shards -- roughly double
the card's own headline number. Added alongside the existing verified
write-up on SuperQwen3.8-27b-abliterated in "The family around it".

subject: Add Hy4 preview article: frontier of five, not frontier of seven
body:
Tencent's 770B/49B-active flagship, with no arXiv paper attached, so the
primary sources are config.json, the safetensors headers of all 131 weight
shards (HTTP range requests, no weight data downloaded), and the model
card's own 41-row benchmark appendix table cross-referenced against its
12-panel headline chart.

What's covered:
- The parameter claim checks out exactly: summing every tensor's real shape
  gives 769.907B total / 49.058B active for the backbone (matches the
  card's "770B / 49B" to three sig figs) and 10.054B / 0.692B for the MTP
  layer (matches "10B / 0.7B" exactly).
- IndexCache, verified as a structural fact rather than a config flag: the
  57 layers marked "shared" in indexer_types don't just skip computing
  their own DeepSeek Sparse Attention index at inference -- they don't own
  the indexer weight tensors at all. Checked directly against the
  safetensors headers (layers 0/1/5 have self_attn.indexer.wk.weight,
  layers 2/3/4/6 don't). Saves 534.2M parameters of indexer weights alone.
- The card's own "open-source frontier" phrasing is precise, and it matters:
  cross-referencing the 12-panel headline chart against the appendix
  table's typed values (confirmed to be exactly what the chart plots),
  Hy4 preview leads 5 of 12 headline benchmarks against the open-weight
  field (Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3), but only
  1 of 12 once GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude Opus 5 are included -- the qualifier
  in the card's sentence is load-bearing, not decorative.
- The appendix table's own footnote on Claude Opus 5's reasoning-benchmark
  truncation rates (2.32% to 28.76%) is a real, self-disclosed limitation
  worth taking seriously in both directions: on 4 of 5 affected benchmarks
  Claude Opus 5 still wins despite truncation, and the one benchmark where
  Hy4 preview wins (HorizonMath) is also the one with the highest
  truncation rate of the five.
- The 163-expert/203-task blind eval's two win/tie/loss splits both sum to
  exactly 100.0%, and the win-minus-loss margin is a real but narrow edge
  against baselines that still win the individual comparison over 40% of
  the time.

Four original interactives (LayerAnatomy, BenchmarkDeltaExplorer,
TruncationCheck, BlindEvalScorecard) plus the model card's own 12-panel
benchmark chart, resized and flattened to the house cap. The appendix
table's 41 rows across 6 task categories were read from the primary source
rather than embedded as an image, given how illegible a table that dense
becomes at the site's figure-width cap.

subject: Add PhoneLLM Alpha 1 article: the fine-tune is free, the cost line isn't
body:
Pipecat's phonellm-alpha-1 model card (Hugging Face) read the way this site
reads a paper: config.json, the safetensors headers of all 13 shards (via
HTTP range requests, no weights downloaded), the card's own six chart images,
and its linked live Google Sheet — not the README's prose alone.

What's covered:
- The MoE math checks out exactly: summing every tensor's shape from the
  safetensors headers gives 31.578B total / 3.580B active parameters,
  matching the card's "30B / 3.5B" claim to three significant figures.
  23 Mamba2 layers, 6 attention, 23 MoE-FFN (128 routed experts + 1 shared
  expert each) — the hybrid pattern spelled out in config.json.
- The strongest evidence in the card is a comparison it doesn't make
  explicitly: PhoneLLM is a full-parameter fine-tune of Nemotron 3 Nano
  30B-A3B, and the base model appears as its own row in the PhoneBench
  leaderboard. Sorted by latency or cost, PhoneLLM and the untuned base
  land on the identical row (331ms P50, $0.0025/min) — proof the fine-tune
  changed nothing about inference cost, while score jumped 28.6% to 72.3%,
  43.7 points, for free.
- Caught and fixed a real error in my own first draft: I'd conflated the
  card's generic "650ms LLM TTFT target" (from a separate reference
  latency-budget breakdown) with PhoneLLM's own measured 331ms PhoneBench
  P50, wrongly labeling a recomputed 974ms total as "the card's own printed
  figure" (that's 1,293ms, using the 650ms target). Corrected in both the
  component and the prose — the real story is better: PhoneLLM's actual
  latency beats even the reference architecture's target by 319ms.
- The card's own worked cost-per-minute example divides $0.2232 by 88 and
  prints $0.00025/min — off by ~10x. Confirmed independently three ways:
  hand arithmetic ($0.00254), the card's own linked cost-estimator
  spreadsheet ($0.0025 for this exact row), and the card's own leaderboard
  chart ($0.0025 again). The error is isolated to one sentence.
- "94% cheaper than GPT-5.6 Terra" recomputes to ~92.8% from the
  leaderboard's own two numbers — a real but modest overstatement.
- generation_config.json ships do_sample:true with no temperature key, and
  the chat template defaults enable_thinking to True — both the opposite of
  the README's explicit "temperature=0, thinking disabled" recommendation.

Four original interactives (LeaderboardExplorer, SayDoGap, VoiceLoopBudget,
CostPerMinuteCalculator) plus four real chart images from the model card
itself, flattened and resized to the house cap.

Also fixed, during validation: an unescaped run of currency amounts in
prose that remark-math was greedily parsing as one giant inline KaTeX
expression (site convention is \$ in prose, confirmed against existing
precedent), and a long unbroken arithmetic string with no space-wrap
opportunities that forced a real page-width overflow at phone viewports —
bisected down to the exact string via a from-scratch diagnostic script,
not caught by a quick glance since check:mobile's stock offender report
pointed at an unrelated fixed-position button instead of the actual cause.

subject: Add VoiceMem article: a QLoRA that can't touch 93% of its own base
body:
Streaming dual-brain memory paper (arXiv 2608.26005), read from the PDF,
the reply model's own safetensors headers, and the dataset/adapter repos
on Hugging Face — not paraphrased from the abstract.

What's covered:
- The dual-brain retrieval mechanism itself: left-brain schema/entity
  one-hop candidate-pool expansion (Eq. 1-2) bounds ranking to a small
  C_t^L instead of the full memory store, which is why K=5/430 tokens on
  LoCoMo matches the accuracy K=30/1,277 tokens needs without it — a real
  routing effect, not a cherry-picked K (checked against all of Table 4's
  K values for Mem0, not just the one the abstract quotes).
- The reply model: verified via live HTTP calls against the HF API that
  Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's routed experts are one fused tensor per block
  ([256,2048,512]), not 256 separate nn.Linear submodules, and that the
  shipped QLoRA adapter's target_modules regex names down_proj/up_proj/
  gate_proj (matching the experts' names) while target_parameters is
  null — so the regex never reaches the fused tensor. 92.9% of the base

subject: articles: Whittle-MoE 27B — the routers moved 4.5 degrees
body:
Four interactives, three figures rendered from my own measurements (the
source ships none). Every number read from the safetensors shard headers
over range requests, the adapter configs, and the author's eval scripts.

The pitch is "froze the neurons, trained only the routers". Both halves
fail:

- the router-heal adapter trains 337,890,304 parameters, of which routers
  are 6.2%. adapter_config.json applies LoRA r=64 to q/k/v/o_proj,
  gate/up/down_proj and the GDN in/out projections; the routers ride along
  in modules_to_save. The author's own findings log agrees: "Training
  routers alone is harmful."
- the shipped routers sit 4.50 degrees from their untrained k-means
  initialisation (median 4.02, p95 7.39, 99.3% within 10), measured by
  parsing the build plan against every mlp.gate.weight.

And "4/39 -> 28/39" is noise. The 39 is a 40-item substring quiz with one
item unscored; router healing reached 27/39 where the previous release was
already 28, and 28 vs 27 is Fisher p = 1.00 — which the card itself calls
the noise floor. The parent Qwen3.8-27B appears on no instrument anywhere.
The nearest published control is worse for the model: the author's own
16.8B pruned Whittle scores 36/39 against this model's 28/39 on the same
battery, p = 0.036.

Also: total is 26,917,297,664 and active 17,857,601,024 = 66.34%, and
active(k) = 14,837,702,144 + k x 188,743,680 — no k makes this sparse; k=1
is still 55.8%. The 192-wide expert rows defeat the k-quant, so
ffn_down_exps sits at 7.00 bpw inside a Q4_K_M build.

Credit stated plainly: the sampler suspicion is closed off (loop_test.py
fixes temp/top_p/top_k and seeds), and the published negative results, the
EOS-bias dose-response and the k-sweep are good work. The build script's
own comment explains the mechanism — routed down_proj x k converts an
average back into a sum, exact only at uniform weights, so a fresh carve
is broken by construction.

subject: articles: Breeze-TTS-2 — three vendors' models, and a clock that starts late
body:
Four interactives, three figures. Read from the repo and the safetensors
headers; the release is inference code only.

- the stack is assembled and the model card names none of it. config.json
  embeds a backbone_config byte-for-byte identical to Qwen3-1.7B's, and
  backbone_model.* sums to 1,409,410,048 params against Qwen3-1.7B's
  1,409,402,880 — the 7,168 gap is exactly 28 x 256 of q_norm/k_norm.
  text_encoder_config carries Gemma-3-1B's shape and the tokenizer class
  is GemmaTokenizerFast. The codec's encoder class is literally
  `class Qwen3TTSTokenizerV2Encoder(MimiModel)` with the decoder nulled.
- token stream: 12.5 Hz x 16 codebooks x 2048 = 200 tokens/s = 2.20 kbit/s.
  Serial cost per 80 ms frame is 28 + 180 + 8 = 216 layer evaluations.
- 1.18 GiB of the 7.12 GiB of weights is unreachable. embed_text_tokens is
  exactly 1.000 GiB bf16 and is read only in the `else` of a branch this
  checkpoint never takes; the bundled Mimi codec is reachable only when
  audio_tokenizer is None, which the runtime raises on. Both are still
  moved to the device.
- voice cloning is a codec-token prompt prefix, not a speaker embedding.
- streaming has zero lookahead — every conv is rebuilt as a cached-left-
  context step and the pre-transformer window is entirely backwards.

Claims that do not hold: "#1 on Artificial Analysis" is a selection effect
— the Elo of 1,215 is right, but five models above it are absent from the
repo's own 12-model chart, which does include the older Cartesia Sonic 3.5.
And "under 40 ms TTFA" measures from fast_streaming.py:770, fifteen lines
after _build_branch_batch at 755 has already run the 26-layer Gemma text
encoder; BreezeBlue's own hosted benchmark reports TTFA p50 of 133.6 ms.
The "50 languages" launch post predates any weights by 18 days and
describes the hosted service; the model card says en, zh.

Audio quality is not assessed: there are no samples, no WER, no speaker
similarity and no eval harness in the repo, and the article says so rather
than passing the arena score off as evidence.

subject: articles: Sana — the autoencoder is the lever, not the linear attention
body:
Four interactives, three paper figures. The figures are rasterised from the
arXiv source tarballs rather than the HTML, which serves them at 440x244.

Rebuilt Table 8's FLOP column from the repo's own configs (28x1152,
mlp_ratio 2.5, linear_head_dim 32, 300 text tokens) and got 6.63/4.48/
4.34/1.12 T against the paper's 6.48/4.30/4.19/1.08 — within 4.2% on all
four rows. Marginally the deep-compression autoencoder buys a flat ~4x at
every resolution, while linear attention buys 1.02x at 512px, 1.12x at
1024px and only crosses over near 5000px. Table 8's own latency column
agrees: +LinearAttn +MixFFN at F8C4P2 is 2425 ms against a 2250 ms
softmax baseline. The headline architecture idea is the smaller lever at
every resolution the model ships at.

Also from the source:
- cross-attention is softmax. Every cross_attn_type but `vanilla` lands on
  xformers memory_efficient_attention. "Linear DiT" names one of the two
  attention operators in the block.
- the CHI prompt tokenises to 208 pieces, and select_index = [0] + last
  299 means the DiT cross-attends to min(P+2, 300) vectors — 13 for the
  repo's own example prompt. Prompts over 298 tokens are truncated
  silently.
- SCMScheduler honours intermediate_timesteps only at 2 steps; the shipped
  4-step schedule is linspace, not the paper's searched one.
- NoPE holds for 512/1024 only — the 2048 and 4096 configs set use_pe.
- weights are genuinely Apache-2.0 (checked three HF LICENSE files), but
  every bundle ships a gemma-2-2b-it text encoder under the Gemma Terms.

The "100x over FLUX-12B" is a 4096px A100 throughput number; at 1024px the
same repo gives 43.0x, 40x, 39x and 39.5x in four different places, and
Figure 4 says 40x on its face.

range-fetched tensor-info blocks for all nine tiers plus the base

  lands within 19 bytes of the published size on all nine tiers, and the

  minus the vision tower minus the MTP block.
- "A3B" holds at 2,946,429,568 active (8.5%), but routed experts are only

  is the output head.
- "4-bit" is 5.161 bpw. Per tensor class on UD-Q4_K_XL: expert gate/up

  in 6 of 9 tiers, blocks 34/38/39 promoted in 8 of 9, same indices
  independently across tiers, at +14% file size over a flat cut.

  in a Jinja comment inside the template.

on the median. Local and cloud arms ran through different agent scaffolds
and different runtimes. Q2_K_XL contains no Q2_K tensors; Q4_K_S and

subject: articles: deepen SGLang — and the trick nothing calls
body:
1,371 -> ~4,550 words, 2 -> 5 interactives, 0 -> 3 paper figures.

Read at sglang@e27a7fa against arXiv 2312.07104v2. Two of the paper's
three headline techniques are load-bearing; the third is dead code:

- jump-forward decoding (the compressed-FSM trick) is implemented in
  every grammar backend and reached by nothing. grep for try_jump_forward
  / jump_and_retokenize across python/, test/, benchmark/ and the Rust
  router returns only definitions and one wrapper delegating to another
  implementation. OutlinesGrammarBackend hardcodes jump_forward_map =
  None, so its try_jump_forward returns on line one. The only residue is
  a Rust mock worker still emitting completion_tokens_wo_jump_forward.
- schedule_policy defaults to "fcfs" (server_args.py:874-889), the exact
  policy the paper ablates as a degradation — and LPM downgrades to FCFS
  above 128 queued requests.
- the C++ tree is not a port. tree_v2.h exposes writing_through /
  loading_onboard / commit_* with IOTickets and a host tier: it is a
  two-tier cache, gated on SGLANG_EXPERIMENTAL_CPP_RADIX_TREE.
- EAGLE rewrites the cache key. RadixKey.maybe_to_bigram_view turns N
  tokens into N-1 pairs, and accepted chains are physically moved into
  contiguous slots because the tree indexes contiguous runs.
- the "6.4x" is measured against vLLM v0.2.5 on one A10G, before vLLM
  had automatic prefix caching. It is prefix caching vs no prefix
  caching, which the paper says and the quoted sentence does not.

Grammar reuse across a batch (2.4x) does survive: a ThreadPoolExecutor
plus a (key_type, key_string) cache, copied into a fresh matcher.

needle-environments ships six tool-schema files with 192 test cases and
went out with "90%+ on held-out production tasks". Read from source:

- the only 0.9 in the repo is `passed >= round(0.9 * len(TEST_CASES))`,

subject: articles: vLLM, SGLang, and the FreeToken MoE-offload mechanism
body:
vllm — read from the v1 engine at 17da485. 858,189 lines, 280 model
architectures, 23 attention backends of which six do not compute attention.
Two interactives: the block pool with content-addressed prefix caching, and
the directory census that explains where the size comes from.

The find is that vLLM's shape is now set by other people's release
schedules. gdn_attn.py, linear_attn.py, mamba1/2_attn.py and short_conv_attn.py
sit in the attention directory because 2026 checkpoints are three-quarters
recurrent layers, and three of the speculative-decoding proposers are named
after individual models. Also two pieces of real taste worth recording: freed
blocks keep their hash so "free" and "evicted" stay distinct states, and
null_block is a real block burned at startup so "no block" can be an ordinary
id. Plus DEFAULT_NONE_HASH_SEED = "vllm-none-hash", which exists because
Python randomises string hashing per process and a prefix cache key has to
mean the same thing in two workers.

sglang — read at e27a7fa. 1,324,609 lines, 219 architectures. Two
interactives: the radix tree with lock-based protection, and the frontend
language against four plain chat-completions calls.

The distinction from a hash-map prefix cache is narrower than the marketing
and shows up at divergence: the tree splits a node, and eviction pops from a
heap and cascades up the trunk when a parent is left childless. inc_lock_ref
moves a prefix out of evictable_size_ into protected_size_ entirely, so a
prefix an in-flight request needs is ineligible rather than merely recent.
The frontend language is still there — SglGen, SglSelect, SglFork,
SglCommitLazy — and RadixAttention exists because of it: if your programs
fork, the cache should be a tree.

freetoken — the article treated expert offload as one idea; the CLI has four
backends and the interesting one has to be calibrated. New interactive on the
hybrid split: fetching over PCIe and computing on CPU use different hardware,
so they overlap and a step costs the longer of the two, which makes the best
split machine-dependent. That is why ft bench bw exists.

Also corrects a claim travelling faster than the code. The 8 GB RTX 4060
laptop running a 35B GGUF at ~50 tok/s is a real and well-motivated result,
but docs/models.md says native GGUF is Gemma-4 only as of 9ef3651 — the
Qwen/Ornith GGUF expansion is a contributor PR, not shipped.

subject: articles: bring colibri up to date, six weeks on
body:
The July piece said the best result anyone had reported was 0.37 tok/s and
that Colibri was a single-file C engine for one model. Both are now wrong.

The repo reports 5.8-6.8 tok/s on 6x RTX 5090 at full residency, ~1.8 tok/s
on a 128 GB CPU-only desktop, and 1.07 tok/s on a single RTX 5070 Ti. It also
runs DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen3.6 and OLMoE now, and has grown CUDA/Metal
backends, NUMA placement and dual-SSD striping.

Rather than silently rewriting the stale numbers, the article flags them and
points forward to a "what changed" section, because the thesis they supported
is still right: every rung of the new ladder is bought with memory, and the
six-GPU number is what happens when the experts stop being streamed at all —
at which point the interesting trick is no longer running.

New interactive on dual-SSD striping, which is the most direct attack on the
bottleneck the article identified. It is a weighted deterministic hash rather
than a RAID mirror, so prefetch and demand read always hit the same drive and
nothing is cached twice; the README's 9+3 GB/s example giving ~33% over the
fast drive alone is just 12/9. Handles the partial-mirror case, and carries
the project's own caveat that independent-controller A/Bs are still listed as
an experiment not yet run.

Also adds the ladder figure and the correction that matters most: the article
said speculation only pays once the cache is warm, and the repo now reports
MTP measuring a 32% loss at around 85% expert hit. So it is not monotone — it
loses cold and can lose again near residency, with the profitable band
unmapped. That came from the project reporting against itself, which is the
other thing worth recording here: the README now carries a hypothesis table
with the experiment still needed for each row, and asks contributors to
publish negative results.

subject: articles: FlashAttention-3, read from the hopper/ source
body:
FA1 and FA2 were algorithmic — tile the computation so the score matrix never
reaches HBM, true on any accelerator with a memory hierarchy. FA3 mostly
isn't. The tiling is unchanged; what changed is that Hopper added independent
async units and FA3 is the work of rewriting attention as a schedule that
keeps them all busy.

Three interactives, all built from constants in the source rather than the
paper.

The register-file one is the find. flash_fwd_kernel_sm90.h sets
LoadRegisterRequirement and MmaRegisterRequirement as setmaxnreg arguments,
and multiplying them against an SM's 65,536 registers shows what they are:
three MMA warpgroups land on exactly 65,536, two-with-TMA on 64,512. The
TMA/cp.async pair is the clearest illustration — without TMA the producer
needs 16 more registers per thread and the consumers give up 8 each to pay
for it, which is where the 240 comes from.

The pipeline one separates the two overlaps FA3 actually performs: warp
specialization takes the memory pipeline off the critical path, then the
pingpong schedule staggers two consumer warpgroups so one is in softmax while
the other is in WGMMA. Neither warpgroup got faster; the tensor cores stopped
waiting. Quotes UseSchedulerBarrier, whose heuristic inverts by dtype —
non-FP8 wants headdim <= 128, FP8 wants >= 128, under a comment reading only
"these are tuned for speed".

The FP8 one shows that low precision here is a recompilation, not a knob:
Transpose_V, MmaMajorV and a static_assert that MmaPV must be RS are static
switches, so the FP8 and FP16 kernels are different kernels sharing a file.
The descale pointers carry strides, which is per-head scaling and the reason
the numerics hold up.

Also covers the five tile schedulers, including the longest-processing-time
one for the causal backward pass, and why FlashAttention-4 moved to CuTeDSL:
a schedule expressed as hundreds of constexpr predicates has to be rederived
for every architecture.

subject: articles: GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
body:
Two frontier-scale sparse MoE releases from the same week, both readable from
their published configs, and they disagree with each other in a way worth
writing down.

glm-5-3-flash — 320B total, 18B active, and the number that matters is 11:
how many of its 45 layers keep a KV cache. Three interactives — the layer
stack against GLM-4.5's 92, the indexer cost that sparse attention never
advertises, and a head-to-head scoring of Z.ai's own benchmark table — plus
four source figures.

The scoring one earns its place twice. "Approaching Claude Opus 4.8"
undersells a table where GLM leads 9 of 14 rows; "the first natively
multimodal GLM-5" oversells a model that loses all three general perception
rows to Gemini 3.7 Flash, one of them by 17 points. Also names what the
announcement doesn't: vLLM's recipe identifies the linear layers as KDA and
the sparse ones as NoPE sparse MLA, and records that Hopper cannot run an FP8
KV cache for this model.

qwen3-8-flash-next — 125B backbone plus 51B of N-gram embeddings, 6B active,
trained for about a ninth of its predecessor. Four interactives, one per
architectural pillar, each built on a controlled ablation from the 28-page
technical report.

The report's own recurring finding is the spine: training loss and downstream
accuracy keep pointing in different directions, and it says so three separate
times with tables. Widening the residual stream is 78% of the loss gain and
42% of the benchmark gain; making the gates data-dependent is 7% and 53%. The
N-gram vocabulary lowers loss monotonically to 200x while MATH and GSM8K peak
at 20x and decline. QSA is behind full attention on MRCR below 256K and ahead
by 9.87 at 512K.

Includes SGLang's day-0 serving work, which is the strongest evidence either
document contains: moving the N-gram table to pinned host memory frees 23.46
GiB per GPU, raises KV capacity 78.54%, costs 0.07% throughput, and produces
bit-exact outputs.

The cross-link: Qwen's Gated Residual is hyper-connections with the
branch-mixing operator deleted, ablated as costing nothing. That operator is
exactly what GLM-5.3-Flash keeps and constrains to a doubly-stochastic
manifold with 20 Sinkhorn iterations. Same idea, same week, opposite calls,
no head-to-head anywhere.

subject: fix: share cards 404'd, and the favicon was never replaced
body:
Two separate bugs, both invisible on the page and both visible the moment
someone pastes a link into a chat.

**Every per-item share card was returning a markdown 404.**

A regression from the agent-surfaces work. Next compiles file-based metadata
into route handlers that hang off the segment they sit in, so an article's
card lives at /articles/<slug>/opengraph-image — three segments deep, no file
extension. The proxy's isUnknownPath() rejects anything deeper than two
segments, and isReserved() only exempted /_next/, /api/, /md/, /.well-known/
and paths with an extension. So the card looked exactly like a path the site
does not serve.

Measured on production before the fix:

  /opengraph-image                            404 text/markdown
  /articles/<slug>/opengraph-image            404 text/markdown
  /arxiv/<date>/opengraph-image               404 text/markdown
  /articles/opengraph-image                   200 image/png

Collection-level cards survived only because they happen to be two segments
deep. Root and per-item cards — which is every URL anyone actually shares —
did not. isReserved() now matches the metadata route names on the last
segment, including the -<id> suffix Next appends when a segment holds more
than one such file.

**The favicon was still the create-next-app placeholder.**

app/favicon.ico was the 25,931-byte Vercel triangle, unchanged since the
project was scaffolded, and with the OG image 404ing it was what link
previews fell back to — so shared articles rendered as a black circle with a
white triangle.

app/icon.svg had a quieter version of the same problem: it set
font-family="Hanken Grotesk" with no @font-face, so the S was drawn in
whatever the viewer had, which is never Hanken Grotesk. The glyph is now an
outlined path — self-contained, ~600 bytes, exact everywhere.

scripts/build-icons.mts rasterises that one source into app/favicon.ico (six
sizes, PNG-in-ICO) and app/apple-icon.png. The Apple variant is deliberately
square: iOS masks a touch icon with its own superellipse, so a pre-rounded
source rounds twice and shows slivers at the corners. Uses the sharp already
in the dependency tree; no new packages.

**Guarded.**

check-agent-surfaces gains seven checks, 49 -> 56: five share cards spanning
root, collection and per-item; one that walks the icon <link>s in a real
document and asserts each resolves to an image; and one that fails if
favicon.ico is the framework default again.

Verified against a production build, not dev — the proxy behaves differently
under `next start`. All 56 pass; genuinely unknown paths still get the
markdown 404.

own figures.

gliner-2-5 — boundary prediction replaces span enumeration, and the width
axis disappears with it. Five interactives: the enumeration grid against the
sparse boundary pairing with a live candidate count, chunk coverage over a
long document, joint entity-relation decoding against independent
thresholding, the constrained-classification product space, and a scorecard
that recomputes all three published averages from the sixteen per-dataset
figures. That last one is the article's spine: the 0.3B checkpoint's headline
parity is carried entirely by XNLI (+24.75, eleven of the other fifteen sets
down), and dropping it leaves that checkpoint 1.57 behind its predecessor
while the 0.2B one keeps +1.27.

spec-ptc — pre-launching tool calls from a half-written REPL cell. A schedule
timeline separating the JIT saving from the streaming saving, the four cases
that decide what the shadow REPL can launch early, and a simulator showing
why five runs cannot resolve a 1.15x effect under +/-40% trajectory variance
— which is the post's own stated caveat, made checkable. Includes both source
videos, re-encoded to mp4/webm with posters.

apodex-frontier-agent — the release publishes the same checkpoint under two
harnesses on six benchmarks, so the gap is a measurement of scaffolding with
the model held fixed: about 40% of the 1.0 -> 1.1 gain, and +11.8 against
+5.9 on BioMysteryBench. Interactives for that split, for why bounded
fan-out beats one growing context, and for the three-root sandbox.

pipette — on-device speed as a five-dimensional object. The config space, the
KV-cache mechanism behind Granite-4.0-H-350M retaining 78.4% of decode
throughput at 4k where the plain 350M retains 33.8% (one physical model
reproduces both at a sensible attention share), sparse activation splitting
memory from bandwidth, and the two 8B models whose deployment profiles match
within 2.4% while their task quality reverses.

Validate, lint, check:spacing and check:interactive all green; every figure
reviewed rendered in light and dark.
