subject: articles: scaling laws in 2026, and a 3D loss-landscape render
body:
The standard retelling of scaling laws ends in 2022 with "twenty tokens
per parameter" and presents it as the industry blueprint. Models shipping
now run at 214 (Llama 3 70B), 60,000 (Qwen3-0.6B) and 79,096
(LFM2.5-350M, 28T tokens into 354M parameters). That is not drift. It is
a different objective, and the piece traces how it moved.

Structure: what loss actually is, before it becomes a dot on a log-log
plot -- then Kaplan's shallow exponents, the 6ND cost identity,
Chinchilla's reallocation, the emergence-versus-mirage fight, and the two
results that added a third axis to the budget (Sardana on serving cost,
Roberts on inference samples).

Corrections it makes to the popular version:
- The compute trend usually quoted mixes two Epoch series. Notable models
  grew 4-5x/year 2010-2024; frontier LLM training compute doubles every
  ~5.2 months since 2020, and cost every ~7-8.
- "20 tokens per parameter" is the answer for a fixed TRAINING budget.
  Inference-aware fits move it to 100-200, and test-time sampling moves
  it further.
- Links to the existing skaling-law piece for the deeper problem: the
  additive Chinchilla form gets the SIGN of the allocation trend wrong
  (+0.03 against empirical -0.14/-0.15).

Five interactives, four real source figures, and two turntable
animations rendered from scratch -- a chaotic landscape and a
well-conditioned bowl with momentum SGD spiralling in. No ffmpeg in the
toolchain, so they are animated WebP: full colour, unlike a 256-entry GIF
palette, which bands viridis badly. Renderer is numpy + PIL, painter's
algorithm over a quad mesh, with one turntable-wide camera fit so the
surface does not breathe as it rotates.

The loss-surface interactive draws to a canvas rather than SVG, so its
arithmetic does not need lib/dmath -- nothing it computes is serialised
into the DOM.

Verified: every token/parameter ratio recomputed from published counts;
GPT-3's 6ND lands at 3.15e23 against the published estimate.

subject: lint: clear the accumulated eslint debt (116 problems to zero)
body:
`pnpm lint` had been failing for a while: 81 errors and 35 warnings
across 107 files, most of it accumulated one article at a time. Nothing
here changes what any component looks like, and the two behaviours that
did shift are noted below.

Mechanical
- 39 unescaped entities in JSX prose, escaped in the house style
  (’, “/”) at the exact positions eslint reported.
- 35 unused declarations removed: dead colour constants, `cn` imports
  left behind when a component stopped needing it, an unused findBench.
- 16 internal `<a href="/articles/...">` links converted to next/link.
  Same markup, same classes, plus client-side navigation.

Needing a decision
- Two list components restored filter/sort/page from a mount effect,
  which is what the set-state-in-effect rule was flagging. They now read
  the query string during render through a new useUrlState hook built on
  useSyncExternalStore, with an empty server snapshot so the prerender
  and the first client render agree. The URL is the single source of
  truth, so there is no second copy in state to drift.
- Two mount flags (`useEffect(() => setMounted(true), [])`) became a
  useHydrated hook on the same primitive.
- The Kuramoto phase dials held their simulation in a ref written during
  render and forced a re-render each frame. The loop already allocated a
  fresh array per frame, so moving it to state costs the same and lets
  render read a value React knows about.
- Two components defined a child component inside their own render,
  remounting its whole subtree on every keystroke. Both hoisted; the MoE
  one takes `selected`/`setSelected` as props now.
- The terminal's search effect cleared `hits`/`searching` on every
  keystroke too short to search. Whether a query is searchable is decided
  during render instead, and the indicator goes up when the request
  actually starts rather than when the effect runs.
- nav-graph stopped its own walk with `setPlaying(false)` from an effect;
  `running = playing && step < last` says it in render.
- A field-offset accumulator mutated inside .map() became a prefix sum.

Two behaviour changes, both improvements
- Back now moves through filter and sort changes on /articles and
  /architectures. The old code read the URL once on mount, so it could
  not.
- The terminal's "searching pages…" indicator appears when the request
  fires rather than during the 140ms debounce.

One oddity worth recording: a JSX comment reading `{/* global state split
... */}` was being parsed as an eslint globals directive, which declared
each of its words as an unused variable. Reworded, with a note saying why.

Adds scripts/check-interactive-state.mts (`pnpm check:interactive`, 11
checks) because none of the above is visible to tsc or eslint: it drives
the real components and asserts the filters, deep links, animation and
click targets still work.

subject: agents: close the nine Is Agentic findings
body:
Every fix is asserted by a new check in scripts/check-agent-surfaces.mts,
which goes from 32 to 49 checks and passes against a production build.

Essential
- 404s: a nonexistent path answered a plain curl with 40 KB of app shell.
  The proxy now serves the markdown recovery map (sitemap, llms.txt, the
  API spec, section indexes) at a real 404 to any caller that did not
  explicitly ask for HTML. A browser still gets the styled page. Needed a
  catch-all matcher; the old one enumerated paths, so an unmatched path
  never reached negotiation at all.
- Markdown negotiation: the homepage had no markdown twin, so the one URL
  a probe checks first fell through to HTML. Adds a "home" page to the
  markdown layer -- an orientation document with when-to-use guidance --
  and makes Vary append to whatever Next sets rather than being clobbered
  by it.
- Heading structure: the homepage outline was h1 then five h2 and stopped.
  Item titles in each section are h3 now. Tailwind's preflight resets
  headings to inherit and these are flex items, so the rendering is
  unchanged; verified by screenshot.

Recommended
- OpenAPI errors: 4xx/5xx pointed at components/responses by $ref. Valid,
  and two hops from the operation -- a function-calling converter walking
  responses[code].content saw no typed error at all. Now inline on every
  operation: 61 error responses, each referencing Problem.
- MCP handshake: the endpoint returned 406 unless the client sent both
  application/json and text/event-stream. Spec-correct, and the reason a
  probe reported the server as broken. Any request that can accept JSON
  now gets the header the SDK wants. /api/mcp (the base path, not the
  endpoint) 308s to the transport instead of 404ing.
- Versioning: the policy existed only as an anchor on /developers. Adds
  /developers/versioning and /developers/versioning.json, an API-Version
  header on every /api/* response, and Link rel="deprecation". Nothing is
  deprecated, and saying so explicitly beats silence.
- when-to-use: added to the agent-skills index and ai-plugin.json, both
  naming the negative cases.
- Discoverability: names the developer surfaces in llms.txt, adds
  alternateName and hasPart to the WebAPI JSON-LD, and puts the new
  policy page in the sitemap.

Also makes the spec's 405 true rather than aspirational: Next answered an
unsupported method with a bare 405, so the proxy applies the problem+json
envelope the spec promises. POST /api/ask is unaffected.

One thing that does not work and is documented where someone will look:
Vary: Accept on the HTML half of a negotiated page. A next.config
headers() entry reaches routes-manifest.json and is then overwritten by
the page render -- confirmed by shipping a uniquely-named probe header
and watching it never arrive. It is set in vercel.json instead, applied
by the CDN after the function returns, and its check runs only against a
deployment.

subject: articles: deepen the Kimi K3 post-training section
body:
The nine-expert funnel and the tau-annealing were already covered. A
closer read of section 4 of the technical report turned up three
mechanisms the article skipped.

- MOPD writes distillation as a dense per-token REWARD, not a loss: the
  clipped stop-gradient log-ratio between the matching teacher and the
  student (Eq. 15). That is what lets it drop into the existing RL
  framework and inherit partial rollout. Moonshot also reports trying
  finer-grained top-k distillation objectives with no clear advantage.
- The Agentic Generative Reward Model's mandatory four-step protocol
  (read output, then write a rubric, then score against it, then record
  to a scorepad) plus the verbosity guillotine at sigma * l0.
- Kernel-task rewards: correctness as a gate, 0.5 at expert parity,
  toward 1 at the hardware roofline, and a hacking-detection system for
  CUDA graph replay, input caching and precision reduction.

Adds one interactive, reward-cliffs, drawing all three together. They
share a shape worth naming: each is a smooth score with a hard
discontinuity on the axis a policy would otherwise trade away. A smooth
penalty is an exchange rate; a cliff has no exchange rate.

The kernel curve marks its own assumption -- the report fixes 0.5 at
parity and ->1 at roofline and says nothing about the shape below.

subject: articles: RL on a reward you have to author yourself
body:
Covers Surya Narreddi and Cameron Franz's project training a language
model to paint by writing p5.brush code, judged by a model against a
hand-rated reference pool.

The article's own contribution is the arithmetic the post leaves
implicit: for k equally-weighted signals with common pairwise
correlation rho, n_eff = k / (1 + (k-1)rho). At k = 5 across the
reported 0.85-0.95 band, the five quality judges are worth 1.04 to 1.14
independent signals -- five judges, one opinion.

Five interactives:
- training-loop: the five stages, marking which two are hand-authored
- redundant-rubric: nine signals vs four, with the n_eff computation
- pairwise-vs-absolute: why a 3-level reward beats an 11-level one,
  since GRPO reads the within-group ranking and ties carry no direction
- pool-funnel: 1,664 rated -> 117 love -> 581 shipped, and why a pool
  made only of the best paintings would reintroduce the compression the
  pairwise switch was meant to fix
- allowlist-vs-reference: 400 lines of API docs vs an 8-method
  allowlist, drawn so the unmeasured span between them stays visible

Three figures from the project page, flattened onto white; fig3 is a
filmstrip built from the first run's progression, ending on the flat
five-petal flower the post describes.

Verified: 117 + 266 + 198 = 581; 1,664 - 383 = 1,281 (77% nope); the
second rubric's weights sum to 1.00.

subject: Add MimiModel article: a 45M LLM on a $5 chip, and 20 points in the decode loop
body:
memovai/mimimodel runs Cactus's Needle 2 on an ESP32-S3 from a single C99 file.
Two stories in one repository, and the second is the one that generalizes.

The port: 13.7 MB of weights that are never loaded into RAM. A CQ-quantized
matrix needs a Walsh-Hadamard transform to reconstruct, but H is symmetric and
orthogonal, so (unit·H)·x == unit·(H·x) — the transform moves onto the activation,
which is shared by every output row. Verified against needle.c: fwht() is a
textbook butterfly and the README's "896 adds" is exactly 128·log2(128). The
saving factor is precisely the row count, which the HadamardTrick interactive
makes visible by letting you drag it.

The result: the official Cactus dylib and this repo ship byte-identical weights —
same 13,737,807 bytes, same SHA-256 — so the former 20.4-point accuracy gap was
entirely engine-side. Paired ablations attribute it row by row: reasoning cap
90->256 (+44, because 139 of 961 rows had not opened <tool_call> by token 90),
protecting the prompt prefix (+63, one row loses its date-bearing system
instruction to the sliding window), one continuous byte grammar instead of
segmented teacher-forcing (+96). 469+44+63+96-3 = 669 = the published 69.6%, and
the arithmetic closes exactly.

Four interactives: AblationLadder (the ladder plus the cross-check run in the
other order, which shows the two fixes are not the same fix), HadamardTrick,
MemoryBudget (160 sink + 256 recent = 416 rows, the same allocation the old pure
ring used), SpeedLog (including the int16 PIE path that was numerically correct
to 5.5e-5 and three times slower, because PIE has no 2-bit unpack instruction).

Three source figures rendered from the README's own mermaid diagrams, served
locally. Also documents what is still broken: name accuracy 90.8% vs 98.1%, and
the report's own finding that the residual under-calls are now a retrieval
problem rather than a grammar one.

body:
Second pass on agent readiness, plus a dependency upgrade. The verification
script now runs 32 checks and passes against both dev and a production build.

Discovery surfaces added:

- RFC 8288 Link headers on every page and API response, advertising the
  api-catalog, service-desc, service-doc, describedby and search relations.
  lib/discovery.ts declares those URLs once and projects each format from them
  so five documents cannot drift apart.
- RFC 9727 API catalog at /.well-known/api-catalog, as an RFC 9264 linkset.
- MCP server card (SEP-1649) at /.well-known/mcp/server-card.json. Its tool list
  is now asserted against what the live server serves, so the card cannot make a
  promise the server does not keep.
- ARD capability manifest at /.well-known/ai-catalog.json, CORS-open, with 2-5
  representative queries per entry.
- Agent Skills index at /.well-known/agent-skills/index.json, listing the 16 real
  brand-crew skills with a sha256 of each SKILL.md — and serving those bytes at
  the URL the digest names, so the check verifies a digest end to end.
- Content-Signal directives in robots.txt (ai-train=yes, search=yes,
  ai-input=yes), which required replacing the metadata route with a text route.
  The permissive stance is deliberate and matches the CC BY licence.
- /auth.md stating plainly that there is no authentication.
- x-markdown-tokens on markdown responses so a caller can budget context.
- WebMCP: navigator.modelContext.provideContext() exposing search and ask,
  feature-detected and inert where the API is absent.

Deliberately NOT published: /.well-known/openid-configuration and
/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. There is no authorization server here,
and describing one would send agents chasing a token endpoint that does not
exist. /auth.md says so instead, and a check asserts all three stay absent.

Dependency upgrade:

- next 16.2.7 -> 16.3.2, react 19.2.8, and every other patch/minor.
- The Next upgrade deprecated the middleware file convention, so middleware.ts

subject: Make the site agent-ready: negotiation, problem+json, typed spec, dev portal
body:
Works through the Is Agentic audit (69/100). Every fix is verified by a new
scripts/check-agent-surfaces.mts, which probes a running server and asserts the
contract an agent depends on — 22 checks, all passing against both the dev
server and a production build.

Failures fixed:

- Markdown content negotiation. New middleware.ts routes Accept: text/markdown
  to the existing .md twins and sets Vary: Accept, Accept-Encoding. lib/accept.ts
  parses q-values properly so */* never counts as a request for markdown — a
  substring match there would have started serving .md files to every browser.
- JSON error responses. lib/api-error.ts implements RFC 9457 problem+json with a
  stable `code` field and a recovery `hint`; a new /api/[...unmatched] catch-all
  returns it for unknown API paths, which previously fell through to the HTML
  404 page. /api/search, /api/posts/[slug] and /api/ask now use it too.
- Agent-friendly 404s. /md/[...slug] returns a real markdown recovery document
  (sitemap, llms.txt, openapi, section index) instead of "not found". Required
  flipping dynamicParams to true so unknown slugs reach the handler at all.
- Rate-limit headers. RFC 9331 RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy on every /api/*
  response, not just 429s, via middleware over the existing limiter. tooMany()
  now returns problem+json.
- Typed error model, response schemas, operationIds, versioning. openapi.json
  rewritten: 20 operations, each with a unique operationId, a real description,
  typed parameters and a typed 200 schema, plus shared RFC 9457 error responses
  and documented rate-limit headers. Every endpoint is also mounted at /api/v1/*
  with a stated 180-day Deprecation/Sunset policy for future versions.
- Developer portal and discoverability. /developers documents all four surfaces,
  the error table, rate limits, versioning and MCP setup, with the product name
  in the title so name-based search can find it.
- MCP manifest. public/.well-known/mcp.json describes the server that already
  existed at /api/mcp/mcp but was undiscoverable.
- Agent when-to-use guidance. llms.txt and ai.txt now open with what this site
  is and is not the right tool for, rather than leaving an agent to infer it.

- Heading structure. The homepage section labels were bare links; they are now

  Organization gains description, address and contactPoint.

subject: Add nanoGPT speedrun frontier article: 153 runs, no new ideas
body:
Prime Intellect ran 18 frontier models autonomously on modded-nanogpt track 3,
each on an 8xH200 node with no internet, for up to eight days. The headline is
negative and the post says so: the best run closed 81.7% of the gap to the human
record, and none of the runs produced a fundamentally new method.

The metric checks out exactly — every published percentage reproduces from
(3290 - record) / 690, baseline to human record. So does the verification bar:
program.md derives 3.27859 as 3.28 - 0.004/sqrt(8), and at per-run sigma 0.0013
that is z = 3.07, one-sided p = 0.0011, matching the repo's "roughly one in a
thousand".

Three interactives. RecordLadder carries the 19-row table with a cost mode that
reorders it completely: Grok 4.5 bought steps at 0.27M tokens each, GPT-5.6 Sol
at 11.7M — a 43x spread orthogonal to rank, with Opus 5 the only model strong on
both axes. NoiseGame works out what one trial can actually tell you: a recipe
with no real gain clears the bar 14% of the time at n=1, while a genuinely better
recipe loses its head-to-head 29% of the time, which is the error that costs you
ideas and the one the weaker models kept making. HarnessDelta covers Kimi K3
appearing twice under two harnesses — 6.1x fewer tokens and a better record under
Prime Agent — with the serial-era confound stated inline.

The best thing in the source is a paragraph: they wrote a deliberately-inflated
noise estimate into the rulebook and counted who checked. 62 of ~100 runs measured
it themselves and those runs are the top of the table; 42 found undocumented
same-seed GPU nondeterminism and rebuilt their screening around it.

Also documents a tension the post does not: program.md already instructs a pruning
round every ~8 ideas and forbids concluding the baseline is optimal, so some share
of what is scored as research taste is rulebook compliance, and the design cannot
separate them. Plus the caveats — serial-era rows at ranks 2 and 3, records
reconstructed from traces, and a README/site discrepancy on Kimi K3's number.

subject: Add Qwen3.8 open-weights article: reading the collection out of the files
body:
Four repositories, two licenses, one architecture. There is no technical report,
so the article works from config.json, the weight index, the chat template, the
FP8 exclusion lists, both vLLM recipes and two GGUF publishers.

Reconstructing the 2.4T from config alone gives 2.446181T against the index's
2.446183T — the residual is layernorms. Three things fall out that no card says:
the 95B active figure only closes if you count the untied embeddings (the compute
path is 91.2B); q_proj is [32768, 8192] because attn_output_gate fuses the gate
into it, making attention twice as wide as num_heads x head_dim suggests; and the
MTP block is a complete extra layer with its own 512-expert MoE, 26.4B params.

The sharpest finding is three-way corroborated: the 2.4T FP8 checkpoint spares
every Gated DeltaNet projection, the 27B FP8 spares the DeltaNet gating path, and
an independent quantizer measured that lifting in_proj_z and out_proj by one step
cost 0.16 GB and removed 11% of remaining divergence. In a hybrid GDN/attention
model the linear-attention path is the precision-critical part. Routed experts are
97.97% of the 2.4T, so "quantize the experts, leave the rest" predicts 2.270 TiB
against vLLM's published 2.27 TiB.

Four interactives: ParamLedger (rebuild total/active/FP8 splits and check them
against the index), HybridStack (the 3:1 layer mix and the KV arithmetic — the
64 KB/token the 16 attention layers need against the 256 KB quoted, exactly 4x,
which is the hybrid interval), AgencySplit (the 27B wins all 13 agentic rows over
a larger previous-gen model and loses 5 of 7 recall rows), QuantLadder (half the
divergence at equal file size from tensor assignment alone). Source figure from
the AtomicChat GGUF card, served locally.

Also documented: reasoning_effort is two English sentences in a Jinja template
with medium setting nothing at all; preserve_thinking defaults on; the 2.4T
raises rather than allow thinking to be disabled; MTP-1 is negative at batch
(-23% at concurrency 256) while MTP-3 is worth 2.3x; and AtomicChat ships no
mmproj for a vision-language model, where unsloth's 0.93 GB file matches the
0.466B vision tower exactly.

subject: Add softmax bottleneck article: the output layer is a rank-d wall
body:
arXiv 1711.03953 (Yang, Dai, Salakhutdinov, Cohen — ICLR 2018 oral). A model's
logits are H W^T, so rank <= d no matter how good the network producing h_c is.
Softmax's row-shift invariance, the obvious escape hatch, is worth exactly one
rank (their Property 2), which makes the corollary airtight: below rank(A) - 1
no parameter setting in any function family matches the true distribution.

Three interactives: RankWall draws the factorization to scale with the two
"easy fixes" priced out (raising d to |V| costs a 23B-parameter output layer at
a modern vocabulary); MixtureLadder pairs the exact-bound measurement — Softmax
400, MoC 280, MoS 9,981 — with the K sweep where perplexity turns back up
precisely where rank saturates; BottleneckToday reads hidden_size and
vocab_size from published configs. Paper Figure 1 embedded locally.

The sharpest parts are the controls, not the perplexity table: MoC as a
matched-parameter near-miss that mixes in feature space and stays rank-bounded
(and the footnote classifying Shazeer et al.'s sparse MoE as MoC, which still
covers every MoE LLM shipping today), the 1B Word regularization control, and
the character-level inverse experiment that predicts and measures its own null
result at identical 1.49 BPC.

Cross-links to the full-bandwidth transformer article — the same "the interface,
not the network, is the limit" argument at the other end of the model.

subject: Add full-bandwidth transformer article: the feedback channel is one token wide
body:
arXiv 2608.08888. Between two decoding steps a transformer passes exactly one
sampled token — log2|V| = 16.6 bits for their 100,352 vocab — and discards the
1,536-dim top-layer state that produced it. Latent feedback fuses that state
with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit, leaving the
architecture, KV cache and objective intact.

Two interactives: BandwidthGap makes the channel-shape argument numeric (with
an explicit caveat that float width is an upper bound, not a measurement), and
ResultLedger grades six claims strong/qualified/limited with each one's catch.
Paper Figure 1 embedded locally.

The result worth building on is the quiet one: feedback passes double as a
training signal on hidden states, and the data-efficiency gain survives even
when latent feedback is not used at decoding. The result worth worrying about
is that the conciseness gain disappears after instruction tuning, because the
tuning traces were written by models that had no choice but to verbalize.

subject: Add nac article: an orchestrator that is not allowed to touch anything
body:
Arcee's open-source Rust harness, Apache 2.0, ~98k lines across three
crates. The design is one sentence taken literally: separate "the
temporary context needed to perform an action" from "the persistent state
needed to continue a workstream."

The orchestrator plans and dispatches and has exactly one action —
launching threads. It cannot run a command or edit a file. Workers get a
fresh process and context, work until the model returns a response with
no tool calls, and that response IS the episode; there is no separate
summarization pass. Then the worker's execution context is discarded and
never used as model context again.

Which is why nac has no compaction problem: it never lets a transcript
reach the orchestrator in the first place. A different answer to context
rot than compressing history — don't accumulate it.

Read the Rust where the prose was coarser. The blog says a cyclic batch
is "rejected"; crates/nac-core/src/agent/tool_exec.rs shows that on
DagError::Cycle or DuplicateName every thread dispatch gets an error
result while non-thread tool calls in the same turn still execute. That
matters if an orchestrator mixes a query with a dispatch.

Gave the honest seam its own place, because Arcee printed it rather than
hiding it: worker failures are not transactional, episodes persist only
on success but environment changes persist unconditionally and live
outside nac's state, so a worker that edits files and then dies leaves
the world ahead of the record.

Cross-linked to the DeepSeek Harness piece, which reaches a related
conclusion from the opposite direction — dsh makes the log the authority
and refuses requests it cannot reconstruct; nac keeps no shared log and
makes episodes the authority, refusing batches it cannot order. Both move
guarantees out of the transcript; they disagree on whether the transcript
should exist.

Flagged what is absent: no evaluation of any kind, no comparison against
a single-agent baseline, and no cost accounting for an architecture that
trades context length for context count. The repo is six commits old.

Two interactives: DispatchDag (valid batch, worker failure, cyclic
batch), ContextLifecycle. No source figure — the blog's architecture
diagrams are not in the served HTML and its only fetchable images are
decorative hero art and an unrelated logo.

subject: Add MAGI-2 Preview article: two sparsities, not one
body:
Sand AI's 114B unified audio-video model, Apache 2.0. Both halves of the
headline are checkable against the published weights.

The total is exact: the safetensors index reports total_size
228,107,858,176, which at bf16 is 114.05B. Reconstructing it from the
tensor shapes and config gives 113.88B — 0.15% apart, so the
decomposition is right rather than lucky.

The active figure is the finding. MoE routing is 256 experts x 12 heads
= 3,072 slots with top-6 per head, so 72 fire per token — and that alone
lands at 7.71B, not the stated 6B. The rest comes off a property the card
never spells out but the shapes give away: layer 0's linear_qkv is
[27648, 3072] where layer 2's is [9216, 3072], exactly 3x, with k_norm
[384] vs [128] to match. The model carries three sets of modality weights
and a token is video OR audio OR text. Apply both sparsities and it lands
at 5.96B against "just 6B parameters per token" — 1 active parameter in
19.1.

Also recovered from the tensor names a technique the README never
mentions: mhc_bias_res_attn is [4, 4] and mhc_norm.weight is [12288] =
4 x 3072, i.e. hyper-connections with four parallel residual streams. The
code confirms it — _hyper_connect_fwd_kernel in Triton, with the
connection matrices pushed through a Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization so no
stream can dominate. Plus attention sinks via FlashAttention-3 and
per-query-group gating (linear_g is [24, 3072] on MoE layers, [72, 3072]
on the 3x modality ones).

Noted the layout argument: mm_layers are [0, 1, 38, 39], so modality
mixing is treated as an entrance-and-exit problem — dense with private
weights per modality at both ends, one shared attention plus routed
experts through the middle. And the refiner is a different model, not a
smaller copy: 30 layers at hidden 4096, no MoE, local attention on all
thirty, for a job that is inherently local.

Reported what is absent: no evaluation of any kind — no VBench, no
comparison, no human study, no ablation — and no wall-clock figure for
the 100 + 5 undistilled denoising steps the release ships with. Also that
64 of the 307 GB is other people's models (Qwen3.5-27B text encoder,
Wan2.2 video VAE, stable-audio-open-1.0), which the repo names plainly.

No source figure: the technical blog sits behind a WAF that serves a
challenge page instead of content, and the repo's only images are I2V
input stills. Said so in the article rather than padding with a
decorative one.

Three interactives: ActiveBudget, LayerStack, CheckpointLedger.

The real page is the dots3-note Preview open-source launch:

  - TEMPO, the release's actual contribution: RL for tasks whose single
    rollout exceeds ten hours. The same agent switches from actor to

subject: Add dots3 article: a certified 42/42 at the IMO without a formal prover
body:
Xiaohongshu's dots team took an internal build of dots-note-3.0 to IMO
2026 as an invited entrant. The organizing committee's own graders
awarded 7/7 on all six problems — 42/42, a score seven of 666 contestants
from 117 countries matched.

The page is a Vue SPA served from rednotecdn with no server-rendered
content, so the material came out of the app bundle where the article
HTML is embedded as string literals.

Two things make it more than a headline. First, there is no formal
language anywhere: the model read the organizers' original LaTeX and
worked end to end in natural language plus Python, so nothing checked the
reasoning except itself and then a human panel. That is a weaker
guarantee going in and a stronger result coming out — what was certified
is a proof a mathematician accepted, not a term a type-checker accepted.

Second, the correctness burden lands entirely on a Proof-Verify-Refine
loop, and the dots team frames the whole result as a claim about
self-critique rather than about mathematics ("recursive self-improvement
begins with recursive self-critique"). The failure modes they name —
reasoning errors, logical leaps, insufficiently rigorous steps — are
exactly the three an answer-key cannot see.

The most informative published data is the proof lengths, since the six
scores are all the same number: 3, 10, 6, 5, 4, 3 pages, 31 total. That
distribution does not track the competition's usual difficulty ordering —
P6, traditionally the hardest slot, got one of the two shortest proofs
while P2 took ten pages.

Also surfaced the line near the bottom that reframes the announcement:
note is the LIGHTEST model in the dots3 family (note, jazz, aria), and
the entry was an internal version.

Listed what is absent, because the result invites over-reading: no
compute or time budget for a method built on "multiple rounds of parallel
reasoning" (humans get 4.5 hours per day for three problems), no
architecture or size, no possibility of independent reproduction, and six
problems is six data points.

Two interactives: MedalBoard, ProofLoop. No source figure — the page's
only image is a decorative title card and the proof PDFs are fetched at
runtime rather than linked in the bundle.

subject: Add Toast 1 article: the tokens were the cost of looking
body:
Mixedbread's specialised search agent takes the retrieval loop away from
a frontier model. The launch post's strongest evidence is not its
headline benchmark.

On Harvey's LAB firm-knowledge benchmark — one model, one task set, one
evaluator, only the retrieval stack changing — the number that matters is
the one that does not move:

  vanilla agent        80.6M tokens  21.7 turns  score 55
  + Mixedbread Search  47.0M         14.6        score 55
  + Toast 1 subagent   23.0M         11.2        score 55

The identical score is the finding. Because quality did not change, what
the experiment shows is that 57.6M of the vanilla agent's 80.6M tokens
were not contributing to the answer. Recomputed the deltas and all three
reproduce (-41.7% vs stated -42%, -51.1% vs -51%, 3.50x vs 3.5x).

Paired that with the two caveats it needs: this is a randomly selected
33-task subset (Mixedbread's own footnote), and a score landing on
exactly 55 three times is coarse enough that a small quality change would
not necessarily surface. The token reduction is measured far more
precisely than the quality preservation it is sold with.

On OfficeQA Pro V2, noted whose numbers are whose — the chart's own
footnote says Genie and harness points are Databricks' while the Codex +
Toast 1 points are Mixedbread's. The within-system comparison is the
informative one: the same GPT-5.6 Sol in the same Codex harness goes 33%
-> 70% when the search loop is delegated.

For the cost comparison, separated published figures from arithmetic:
both Toast 1 configurations have stated cost and latency, but the
frontier group has only a "7-11x cheaper" multiple, so that band is their
claim inverted rather than a measurement. The latency gap needs no such
inference — 8 seconds against 20 seconds to four minutes, quoted.

Figures are the post's own charts, rendered from the inline SVG in the
page rather than the decorative hero card.

subject: Add speech-to-speech article: an API boundary treated as an interface
body:
Hugging Face's voice-agent pipeline — VAD -> STT -> LLM -> TTS, each
stage a thread joined by queues, Apache 2.0.

The framing is the compatibility decision. The server implements the core
OpenAI Realtime GA event set at /v1/realtime over both WebSocket and
WebRTC, so the official client connects by changing a URL. What makes
that an engineering claim rather than a marketing one is that CI connects
pinned @openai/agents RealtimeSession instances through the SDK's own
stock transports — tested against the real client library, not a mock.
Quoted the repo's own scoping verbatim ("a tested core subset, not a
claim of full OpenAI Realtime API equivalence") rather than improving on
it.

Smart Turn v3.2 is the part worth the article. Silero decides that speech
stopped; Smart Turn decides whether the speaker was finished, from
content and prosody. The pipeline then speculates: complete turns start
STT and the LLM immediately with an 800 ms reopen window, incomplete
turns hold 600 ms and stay output-gated to 2 s, and resumed speech
reopens the turn as a new revision and discards the previous revision's
work before it reaches the user. That last rule is what makes the first
two safe — speculation is only free if the wrong guesses are inaudible.
All three defaults verified in src/speech_to_speech/VAD/vad_handler.py,
not just the README.

Also mapped the 90 backend combinations (6 STT x 3 LLM x 5 TTS, one VAD)
and pulled out why the "OpenAI-compatible API" LLM slot is not a
dependency: pointed at llama-server on localhost the whole pipeline is
local while the model stays behind a protocol boundary, which is what
keeps the slot swappable.

Flagged what is missing: for a project whose headline is "low-latency"
there is no published end-to-end figure — no time-to-first-audio, no
comparison against hosted Realtime, on any hardware. Also the CUDA wheel
matrix under `pip install`, and the components already moved to archive/
(Moonshine, MeloTTS, Parler).

Two interactives: SmartTurn, BackendMatrix. Two real figures — the repo's
endpoint-swap animation and its realtime-engine architecture diagram
rendered from the committed mermaid source.

subject: Add WorldClaw article: a 3D world generator that writes Blender programs
body:
Tencent Hunyuan's agentic open-world 3D system (arXiv 2608.05248). The
distinguishing feature is the output format — explicit instance-level
meshes on a continuous terrain, editable afterwards — and the way it gets
there, which is by generating programs rather than geometry. The middle
of the paper's own Figure 3 is source code.

Built the region-aware height field (eq. 6) as an interactive
cross-section, because the load-bearing detail is easy to miss: the
region masks are NORMALIZED, so neighbouring regions blend instead of
abutting and no stitching pass is needed. Toggling normalization off in
the diagram reproduces the artefact — elevations pile up wherever two
regions overlap. That is what lets a planning agent author regions
independently and still get one continuous world.

Also pulled out the placement solve, which is real geometry rather than
prompting: a per-object similarity transform with scale from the ratio of
depths and focal lengths, and a two-sided contact inequality that lets an
object sink slightly into a slope or stand proud while forbidding it from
floating.

Reported what the paper does not have: no quantitative evaluation at all.
Sections 3.2 and 3.3 are both "Qualitative"; all thirteen tables in the
HTML are display equations. No user study, no scores, no timing, no
numeric ablation. Defensible for a system paper whose claim is "worlds
built this way stay editable," but worth stating plainly.

The Limitations section is the most useful part and is unusually candid —
open-source LLMs "often struggled" to emit executable terrain programs,
open-source image models "frequently failed" on layout maps and pose
preservation, so validating the pipeline "still requires capable models
such as Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-Image-2, and Hunyuan3D." Decomposition made
the two stages whose output must be executable harder, not easier, since
neither degrades gracefully.

Two interactives: HeightField, ModelStack. Three real figures from the
paper.

subject: Add MiniMax Music 3 article: every card number checked against the bytes
body:
MiniMax's open-weight music model — an 8B global LLM over the first RVQ
codebook, a 646M local decoder for the other seven, flow matching to a
Flow-VAE, 32 kHz stereo out. The card names a parameter count for four
separate components, which is unusually specific and therefore checkable.

Pulled the safetensors headers by HTTP range request rather than dividing
file sizes, which mattered twice:

  - transformer/ is 9.73 GB over two shards. At bf16 that is 4.86B and
    the card's "2.4B" would be wrong by 2x. Every tensor is F32, so it is
    2,431.9M and the card is right.
  - The Global LLM is Qwen3ForCausalLM at Qwen3-8B's exact shape but with
    vocab_size 200,000 instead of 151,936. Qwen3-8B is 8.191B; widening
    the vocabulary adds (200,000-151,936) x 4096 x 2 = 393.7M for an
    untied embedding and head. Predicts 8.584B; the index says 8.584B.
    Both of the card's claims about this model are visible in that one
    number.
  - dav.pth is 491.8 MB = 123.0M at fp32 against a stated 123M.
  - rvq_depth_decoder is 646.0M BF16 against a stated 0.6B.

All five reconcile. The one component the card never mentions is a 25.2M
condition encoder (24 kHz in, 44.1 kHz out).

The repository is 57.35 GB for ~12B parameters because it ships the model
twice, once per runtime. The arithmetic that proves it: flowmatching_vae.
pth is 2,457.1M at fp32, and the diffusers transformer + condition_encoder
are 2,431.9M + 25.2M — the same total, not an approximation. The folder
named qwen_7B holds an AbabForCausalLM, MiniMax's own family, at the same
8.58B shape as the Qwen3 copy beside it, and nothing in
modular_model_index.json refers to it.

Derived the frame rate the card omits: "up to five minutes" and "limited
to 9,000 acoustic frames" only agree at 30 fps. That fixes the scale —
84 bits/frame across the 8 codebooks is 2.52 kbit/s, so a full song is
9,000 autoregressive steps over a representation ~406x smaller than the
32 kHz stereo PCM it decodes to.

Flagged what is absent: no listening tests, no comparison against any
other music model, no objective audio metrics. For a generative audio
release that is the entire evaluation.

Three interactives: ParamLedger, TwoLayouts, FrameBudget. One real figure
from the card.

subject: Add LFM2.5-VL-3B article: GUI grounding appearing from nothing
body:
Liquid AI's 3.1B edge VLM. The post lists four improvements over
LFM2-VL-3B and leads with the wrong one.

ScreenSpot-v2 on the previous release: 6.0, 7.6 and 2.5 across desktop,
mobile and web. Those are not weak scores, they are the scores of a model
that could not do the task. The new one is 78.7 / 81.2 / 82.2 — an
average of 5.4 to 80.7, a 15x move, filed under "significant improvements
in screen understanding."

Transcribed all 28 benchmark rows and recomputed every model's average;
each one reproduces the published Average row to within rounding, so the
table is internally consistent and the size-class claim rests on solid
ground. That claim is narrow and correctly stated: 69.4 is exactly level
with InternVL 3.5 4B and 0.7 behind Qwen3.5-4B, both 4.7B. "Competitive
against models twice its size" holds; "better than" would not, and the
post does not say it.

Row-by-row the tie is sharper than the average suggests: 14W-14L against
InternVL 3.5 4B and 14W-14L against Qwen3.5-4B, a dead heat against both
4.7B models from different labs. Where it loses is nameable — Qwen takes
the dense-OCR rows (DocVQA, InfographicVQA, OCRBench v2) and MMMU-Pro,
InternVL takes ChartQA, MMMU and all three GUI splits.

Two things the post does not mention that the table shows: CountBenchQA
drops 92.2 -> 87.3, the only meaningful regression against the previous
release, and POPE slips 89.2 -> 88.7.

Also separated the well-specified numbers from the rest. The GPU figures
carry their conditions (vLLM 0.26, BF16, 512x512 + 1,024 tokens, median
of 5, one H100 SXM5); the on-device ones — 228 tok/s on M5 Max, 116 on
Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 20 on a Galaxy S26 Ultra, ~3 GB — state no
quantization, prompt or batch size, and GGUF/MLX/ONNX all ship day one
and would each answer differently. Reported as claims.

subject: Add GLM-5.3 article: same base model, a month of post-training
body:
Z.ai shipped GLM-5.3 on the identical base model as GLM-5.2 — "Scaling
post-training is all we did" — which makes every number in the launch
post a post-training delta rather than a new-pretrain one. That is a
rarer thing to be able to say than it sounds, and it is the article's
spine.

Transcribed the full 16x8 comparison table from the launch bundle and
computed the tallies rather than repeating the post's framing:

  - 14 benchmarks score both GLM versions; 5.3 leads all 14. Terminal
    Bench 3.0 moves 4.6 -> 28.3 (6.2x), which is flagged as the weakest
    kind of evidence in the set: 5.2 was near the floor, so this is
    not-playing to playing, not a mid-range move.
  - Head-to-head: 16-0 vs GLM-5.2, 12-0 vs Qwen3.8-Max, 10-4 vs Kimi K3,
    7-2 vs DeepSeek-V4 Pro — but 6-9 vs Fable 5 and 4-9 vs GPT-5.6 Sol.
    "Most capable open-weights model for coding" survives checking;
    "open-weights" is the word carrying it.
  - Across the whole field GLM-5.3 tops 3 of 16 rows.
  - 13 of the 112 non-GLM-5.3 cells are blank, so several head-to-heads
    rest on fewer than 16 rows (DeepSeek-V4 Pro is nine).

The cyber section is where the two published claims pull apart. Both are
true — top CyberGym score at 84.5, and gains largest up the chain
measured against 5.2 (2.23x ExploitBench, 3.3x ExploitGym 6h). Read
together they suggest a model leading at exploitation; the same table has
it at 54.4 vs 78 and 76.5 on ExploitBench, and 130 vs 247 and 293 solved
on ExploitGym. The gap to closed models widens at the same rate the
capability is described as growing.

Also noted: the token-efficiency comparison puts GLM-5.3's High effort
against Opus 4.8's Max (29.5% at 120K is Opus's Max, not its High) —
legitimate as a frontier argument, not a like-for-like row. And Z.ai Code
Bench was run inside Claude Code 2.1.207, i.e. every model scored through
a competitor's harness, which is the right call and unusual to see
printed on the chart.

subject: Replace the dsh screenshots with the repo's own architecture diagrams
body:
The two figures were the Settings → Models page and the custom-provider
form. Both are just API-key inputs — they showed that the product exists
and nothing else, which is not what a figure is for.

The repo carries better ones it never renders to images: mermaid sources
under docs/, checked in CI by verify-mermaid. Rendered them with mermaid
11.16.0, the exact version the repo pins, and served the output locally:

  fig1  docs/tool-execution-pipeline.md — the guarded tool pipeline
  fig2  docs/agent-lifecycle.md — one turn across all nine participants

The pipeline diagram earned a new section, because it is the same
log-is-source argument in different clothes: tool/call is logged BEFORE
execution, and every failure path — guard denial, refused approval, a
throw in the tool body, a throw in a wrapper — converges through registry
normalization into one recorded tool/result. That is what lets the
agent-loop invariant hold for a turn where something went wrong, which is
the only kind of turn where reproducibility matters. Node text quoted in
the prose was checked verbatim against the mermaid source.

The lifecycle sequence sits beside TurnFlow rather than replacing it: it
adds who talks to whom and the two alt branches an ordered list cannot
show. Its labels needed the doc-site <code> wrappers stripped, since
mermaid escapes sequence message text instead of parsing it as HTML, and
sequence wrap enabled so the "claim pending next-step input plus one
queued prompt" note stopped being clipped mid-word.

Also corrected the pipeline alt text: approval resolves BEFORE the
monotonic guards, not after, per the doc's own ordering paragraph.

subject: Add DeepSeek Harness article: the log as the source of truth
body:
DeepSeek's dsh is an MIT-licensed agent harness on Cordis where every
part — the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, the agent
loop — is a plugin, across 219 workspace packages. The plugin count is
the advertised story and it is the less interesting one.

The finding is packages/core/agent-loop/src/invariant.ts, 63 lines that
run on every llm/stream the loop builds. It compares the outgoing
messages against session.deriveMessages() — a fresh replay of the durable
log made at dispatch time — byte for byte through JSON.stringify, and
throws if they differ. Sampling settings, system prompt and tool schemas
are checked against the folded request header the same way. It registers
with prepend so a short-circuiting replay listener cannot get ahead of
it. A plugin that slips an unlogged message into a request does not
degrade the session, it fails the request.

Measured rather than quoted, all at 47f9438:

  - bundle layering parsed out of the three committed patch files: base
    inserts 78 rows; web-app adds 51 and re-configures 27 of them;
    headless adds 3 and re-configures 3. Every override id resolves to a
    base row — checked, zero dangling.
  - 219 package dirs, 219 src/invariant.ts, zero unmatched either way.

That last one nearly shipped as "219 packages enforce runtime
invariants", which is wrong: only 35 ever call fail(). The other 184 are
empty installs — and scripts/package-invariants.ts requires an empty one
to carry a "No runtime invariant:" comment saying why, so the real figure
is 219 decisions, not 219 checks. Absence is recorded instead of assumed,
which is the better idea.

The surrounding discipline reads as a response to how the code got
written: 12,293 commits in 65 active days, first commit to npm in 61
days, 686 design notes in a proposed/implemented/rejected/archived
lifecycle, eleven repo skills, 27 verify-* scripts plus eleven generated
catalogs re-checked in CI, and more test code than source (222k vs 205k
lines).

Reported with the uncertainty intact: 209 of 984 merged PRs came off
codex/* branches, which is a floor on machine-authored work and not a
total — an earlier grep said 1,636 because it also matched
"Merge branch 'master' into codex/...". The note count is 686 English
files, not the 1,386 the raw .md count gives, since every note has a
.zh.md twin.

Four interactives: ProfileLayers, TurnFlow, LogInvariant (break the
invariant five ways and read the real error), RepoDiscipline. Two real
figures from the repo's own docs, flattened and served locally.

subject: Add a repo-wide space-drop check, and fix the three it found
body: JSX normalizes a text node by trimming every line, dropping blank ones, and joining the rest with single spaces. The familiar consequence is that whitespace between elements disappears when it spans a newline. The one that actually bit us is subtler: a *leading* space is trimmed too, as soon as its text node runs onto a further line, because that first line gets trimmed like any other. So C(m,2) pairwise judgments per iteration, and then prose that wraps onto a second line renders "C(m,2)pairwise". The identical markup with nothing after it on a second line is fine, which is why this survives review. Three real instances, all the same shape — an inline / whose following prose wraps: recursive-harness-self-improvement C(m,2)pairwise kimi-k3-in-c ~36 GBof arena inkling-small safetensors.totalfield scripts/check-space-drops.mts drives a headless browser and inspects the rendered DOM rather than the source, because a static regex over-reports by roughly 30:1 — sibling spans in a `flex gap-2` container are indistinguishable from the defect in source and are correct. It checks prose containers only, and skips three kinds of intentional abutment: KaTeX, sub/sup (wt), and a lone capital, which is the acronym-initial device — **M**oment**U**m **O**rthogonalized by **N**ewton-schulz is meant to fuse. It needs a dev server, so it stays out of `pnpm validate` and gets its own `pnpm check:spacing [slug...]`. Documented in CLAUDE.md alongside a note on lib/dmath, which had the same character: a rule that is invisible until it is written down. subject: Add Muse Glimmer article: an agentic model designed backwards from 24 GB
body:
Meta Superintelligence Labs' 30B open-weight agent model (Apache 2.0,
2026-08-09), covered from the announcement blog, the model card, and the
config/index/file-trees of all four shipped repositories.

The framing is that nearly every structural choice answers one question — how
do you fit an agent, its KV cache at 131K, a vision encoder and a speculative
drafter inside 24 GB at once — and that the answer is checkable.

Verified rather than quoted:
- The 24 GB claim closes. KV is 2*2*128*2 = 1024 bytes/token/layer; 13 global
  layers hold the full context and 39 are capped at a 2048 window, so at
  131,072 tokens the cache is 1.83 GB. With the measured GGUF sizes (16.76
  weights + 1.63 drafter + 1.40 vision) the total is 21.6 GB, 2.4 GB inside a
  24 GB card.
- The counterfactual is the finding: make all 52 layers global and KV becomes
  6.98 GB, total 26.8 GB, and the headline claim fails. The 3:1 sliding pattern
  is load-bearing, not a refinement. Without GQA the cache alone is 112 GB.
- The attention stack matches per layer. layer_types is LLLG thirteen times;
  layer_rope_theta is 500,000 on every local layer and exactly 0 on every
  global one, with zero mismatches across all 52 — so the global layers run
  NoPE, the same arrangement as Kimi K3 and Maple-Preview.
- All four promised artifacts exist, in three sibling repos the card doesn't
  link. The drafter's own config confirms the card exactly (5 layers,
  block_size 16, sliding 2048, 32Q/8KV).
- Config details the card omits: final_logit_softcapping 20.0, qk_scale_factor
  3.87, output_multiplier 0.19611613513818404 (= 16/sqrt(6656), matching to all
  17 digits), a post_norm_eps distinct from rms_norm_eps.
- Small correction: the card says "~29.6B" twice; the index says 29,776,626,688.

Reported honestly:
- Re-tallied Meta's own comparison: Muse Glimmer leads 12 of 22 scored rows,
  loses 8 to Qwen3.6-27B and 2 to Gemma4-31B, including OSWorld-Verified by 9.7
  and TerminalBench by 9.0. Publishing a table you lose a third of is the least
  common thing about the release.
- The chem/bio table inverts the usual reading — being less capable is the
  release argument, with Kimi K3 included as an uncontested upper bound.
- On safety Muse Glimmer loses both violation metrics to Gemma (26.4 vs 12.1
  contextual-integrity violations; 28.4 vs 25.6 attack success) and compensates
  on utility.
- Two of three preparedness designations are marked "inferred" from the
  distillation relationship rather than measured.
- The blog's chart carries error bars the card's table drops: on the 5090 the
  DFlash result spans ~132-340 tok/s, so speculation is worth 1.8x-4.5x and
  "3.1x" is a midpoint. Also noted that Meta truncates its speedup ratios
  (50.2/26.6 = 1.89 is published as 1.8x), so the component shows both.

Four original interactives (MemoryBudget, AttentionStack, SpecDecode,
BenchLedger) and two figures from the announcement, flattened onto white.
Verified in light and dark at 1000px: no clipping, no horizontal overflow, no
JSX space drops, zero console errors. `pnpm validate` green — 127 articles, 159
MDX files.

subject: Fix SSR/client hydration mismatch in every computed SVG diagram
body:
React reported "a tree hydrated but some attributes of the server rendered HTML
didn't match the client properties" on article pages carrying computed SVG
diagrams. The diff React printed named the culprit exactly:

  + y={56.51524933614009}       (client)
  - y="56.515249336140094"      (server)

Those are different doubles, not different formatting of the same one. The
ECMAScript spec does not require exp, log, pow, the trig family, hypot or atan2
to be correctly rounded — it asks only for an "implementation-dependent
approximation" — so Node and Chrome may disagree by one unit in the last place.
React stringifies numbers verbatim into SVG attributes, so a coordinate derived
from a softmax or a log scale serializes differently on the two sides and React
declares a mismatch it will not patch up.

The fix is to pin the value where the non-determinism enters, not where it is
used. Adds lib/dmath.ts, which wraps each non-correctly-rounded Math function
and rounds its result to 12 significant digits via toPrecision (which IS exactly
specified). Everything downstream — + - * / sqrt Math.round, comparisons — is
exact per IEEE-754 and identical on every engine, so pinning the source is
sufficient; there is no need to round ~1500 individual coordinate expressions,
and 12 digits is far more precision than rendered geometry needs.

Applied mechanically across components/: 302 call sites in 94 files, replacing
Math.<fn>( with the m<fn>( wrapper and adding the import. Math.min/max/abs/
floor/round/sqrt are left alone — those are exact and were never at risk.

Also audited the six `**` sites with non-literal exponents and left them: one is
inside a string literal, the rest are `2 ** <integer>`, whose result is exactly
representable in binary floating point and therefore engine-independent.

Verified: hydration warnings now 0 across attention-mechanisms, skaling-law,
ltc-gated-delta, maple-preview, kda-half-life, bm25, kimi-k3 and hunyuan-hy3
(previously present on the pages with transcendental-derived geometry). No other
console errors. `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm validate` green. eslint over
components/app/lib is byte-identical before and after — 101 problems, 79 errors,
22 warnings on both trees — so the sweep introduced no new lint findings.

subject: Add Skaling law article: Chinchilla's additive form assumes a zero cross-derivative
body:
arXiv 2608.07222 (Videau, Youbi-Idrissi, Lopez-Paz, Ahuja; FAIR at Meta,
2026-08-07) generalizes the Chinchilla scaling law with a single outer exponent:

  L(N, D) = (A/N^alpha + B/D^beta)^k + E

k = 1 recovers the additive Chinchilla law exactly, so Chinchilla is a special
case rather than a rival. The article's framing is that the additive form's plus
sign is a substantive, untested claim: a sum of a function of N and a function
of D has a cross-derivative of exactly zero as an algebraic identity, which
asserts that a training token's value does not depend on model size. The fitted
k on Farseer is 0.41 +/- 0.01.

Covered from the paper:
- The saddle-shaped residual the additive law leaves at grid corners (Fig. 1),
  and the paper's direct measurement of a non-zero cross-derivative.
- "Interpolation quality is not evidence" — Chinchilla reaches R^2 = 0.995 on
  the full Farseer grid and still extrapolates 3-4x worse than Skaling.
- The L-shaped sparse grid: Skaling fitted on low-compute edges at ~1/10th the
  FLOPs beats Chinchilla fitted on the full grid in every held-out regime
  (0.89 vs 1.48 ext-N, 1.35 vs 1.98 ext-D, 1.51 vs 2.46 far).
- The nine-parameter Farseer law being worse than three-parameter Chinchilla on
  several columns with large fold variance — more parameters bought instability.
- The consequential result: the compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter exponent.
  Two model-free surrogates give -0.14 and -0.15, Skaling gives -0.11, and the
  refit additive law gives +0.03 — the opposite sign.
- The paper's own caveat that E is not identified, since no run reaches
  saturation and the coupled term absorbs curvature the additive form can only
  express through a larger floor.

Self-correction section. The LTC/GDN article published four days ago used
Hoffmann 2022's coefficients to estimate that a compute-matched baseline would
have recovered ~0.061 nats of LTCAttention's 0.062-nat gain. Recomputing at the
same N and D: the same additive form refit on Farseer gives 0.031, and the
Skaling form on the same runs gives 0.026 — a 2.4x spread, with the published
figure the most pessimistic corner. Most of the movement is the coefficient
source rather than the coupling. Also notes that LTCAttention sits at D/N = 10,
inside the band the paper reports as Chinchilla's worst regime. The revised
reading: a compute-matched baseline probably recovers about half the gain, not
all of it; the wall-clock-matched experiment is still the missing one.

Four original interactives (CouplingKnob, AllocationDivergence, GridStrategy,
EstimateSpread) and two paper figures flattened onto white. Verified in light
and dark at 1000px: 35 KaTeX blocks render, no clipping, no horizontal overflow,
no JSX space drops. The one console warning (hydration attribute mismatch) also
reproduces on untouched pages, so it is pre-existing and site-wide rather than
introduced here. `pnpm validate` green — 126 articles, 158 MDX files.

subject: Add LTC + Gated Delta Networks article: two literatures, one recurrence
body:
A mechanism piece connecting Liquid Time-constant Networks (arXiv 2006.04439)
and Gated DeltaNet (arXiv 2412.06464), plus a close read of LTCAttention
(github.com/Rikka-Botan/LTCAttention), published today.

The central derivation is not in either paper. LTC's Algorithm 1 fused solver
step is

  x(t+dt) = [x(t) + dt*f*A] / [1 + dt*(1/tau + f)]

and since tau_sys = tau/(1 + tau*f) by definition, the denominator collapses to
1 + dt/tau_sys. So the update is x_{t+1} = a*x_t + write, with
a = 1/(1 + dt/tau_sys) — a gated linear recurrence whose retention factor is
input-dependent, i.e. exactly the object Mamba2/GDN/KDA call alpha. The only
difference is the discretization: LTC uses the [0/1] Pade approximant of the
exponential, gated linear attention uses the exponential itself, and in the
long-memory regime the two agree to a fraction of a percent. Ties together
tau, alpha and half-life as one number in three coordinate systems, extending
the framing from /articles/kda-half-life.

Also covers what each tradition knows that the other doesn't: LTC's Theorems 1
and 2 (bounded time constant, bounded state under arbitrary input) as the
under-cited ancestor of every gate bound in modern linear attention; and the
delta rule as the targeted-erasure mechanism the LTC formulation has no
counterpart for. Notes that KDA's Diag(alpha) is a per-channel vector where
GDN's alpha is a per-head scalar — a filter bank versus a single rate.

LTCAttention section, read off model.py and the checked-in results:
- Verified the query/key factorization algebraically. Decomposing q and k in
  the orthonormal modal basis, the centered factors multiply to exp(-(i-j)/tau)
  and the center cancels, so q'^T k' = q^T M_(i-j) k exactly as claimed, with
  SDPA remaining the only quadratic operation.
- The numerical hazard that trick creates, and the three things the code does
  about it: FP32/FP64 exponents under BF16, a fixed center at the middle of the
  context, and min_tau = max_positions/12 — which bounds the worst-case
  exponent at 6(T-1)/T ~ 6 independent of context length.
- The experiment: 3 seeds, paired, one epoch over 287.6M FineWeb-Edu tokens,
  4.07281 +/- 0.01777 vs 4.13471 +/- 0.02367, paired delta -0.06190 +/- 0.00646,
  negative in all three seeds.

Two confounds quantified from the repo's own reported numbers. The +1.20%
parameter increase is worth roughly 0.005 nats under a Chinchilla-form
sensitivity — an order of magnitude below the effect, so the gain is not
parameter count. But the comparison is token-matched, not wall-clock-matched,
and the author reports LTC running 12.40% slower; spending that on more tokens
for the baseline estimates to roughly 0.061 nats, essentially the whole
measured gain. Flagged as a rough estimate with its assumptions named, and as
the missing experiment rather than a refutation — the author disclosing the
throughput cost is what makes the check possible at all.

Four original interactives (LiquidTau, SolverBridge, GatedDeltaRule,
ModalMetric) and three real figures from the LTCAttention repository,
flattened onto white. Verified in light and dark at 1000px: 89 KaTeX blocks
render, no clipping, no horizontal overflow, no JSX space drops, no console
errors. `pnpm validate` green — 125 articles, 157 MDX files.

subject: Add Maple-Preview and TencentDB Agent Memory; date today's articles to 2026-08-06
body:
**content/articles/maple-preview.mdx** (new) — DeepGrove's 20B-A1.49B ternary MoE
reasoning model. The ternary claim is verified from the published bytes rather
than repeated: range-requesting single rows out of the safetensors shards shows
every row of every attention and expert projection holds exactly three distinct
values, {-s, 0, +s}, with a per-output-channel scale and 38-43% exact zeros.
A parameter census from the headers puts 19.58B of 20.21B (96.9%) in ternary
form, with embeddings, routers and norms left full precision.

Two findings that follow from the arithmetic:
- The 5.31 GB headline reconciles at 1.65 bits per ternary weight — just above
  the log2(3)=1.585 entropy floor, near five-trits-per-byte, well under naive
  2-bit. Independent corroboration that the checkpoint really is ternary.
- Once 97% of the model is under two bits, the un-quantized embedding tables
  become ~24% of the file. At this ratio the compression problem moves from the
  weights to the vocabulary.

Also stated plainly: the Hugging Face download is 40.43 GB of unpacked bf16, not
the 5.31 GB artifact; `"quantize": true` in config.json is never read by the
shipped code (MapleConfig doesn't declare it, MapleMLP.forward is a plain dense
matmul); and the activation clamps at ±7.0 are the QAT residue. Architecture
covered from the config: 24 layers, 3:1 sliding-512 to global with globals at
3/7/11/15/19/23, nope_on_global_attention, no shared expert. Benchmarks read
off the card's own table including the 10.7-point GPQA-D gap to Qwen3.5 35B-A3B,
and a note that the two models beating Maple on quality are absent from the
speed-frontier chart. New: TernaryProbe, BitBudget; both card figures.

**content/articles/tencentdb-agent-memory.mdx** (new) — Tencent Cloud's MIT
agent-memory system, read through ~148k lines of TypeScript rather than the
README. The thesis: the L0-L3 pyramid is sorted by volatility, not abstraction.
tdai-profile-memory-injector.ts injects L3 whole, L2 as a path index only, and
exposes L0/L1 as tools — the proxy README naming the reason as "avoiding
upstream KV-cache invalidation", and the install guide treating prompt-cache
misses as a documented multi-node failure mode.

Verified against source: RRF at k=60 over FTS5 BM25 plus vector similarity, with
graceful degradation when FTS5 is missing; a permission checker whose `private`
semantics are strict even against team admins, with a dated 2026-07 comment
explaining the change. Gaps found: the character budget the README advertises
ships disabled (maxCharsPerMemory and maxTotalRecallChars both default to 0 and
the budget function short-circuits), `restricted` ACLs are bypassed by team
admins, l1IdleTimeoutSeconds is documented as 30 and initialized to 600, the
injected memory-tools guide is hardcoded Chinese in an otherwise bilingual repo,
and MemoryCore's auto-recall hook contradicts the proxy's injection policy. One
benchmark (PersonaMem 48%->76%) appears only in the two READMEs. New:
InjectionPolicy, RecallCaps; two project figures.

**Dates** — pokee-isaac-28b and prime-agent were authored today but carried
2026-08-03; both now 2026-08-06. prime-agent's `updated` field is dropped as
redundant and its revision callout reframed from a dated update notice to a note
about the shallow-vs-full clone, which is what it actually describes.

Figures flattened onto white, served locally, capped at 1600px. Verified in
light and dark at 1000px across all four touched articles: no clipping, no
horizontal overflow, no JSX space drops, no console errors. `pnpm validate`
green — 124 articles, 156 MDX files.

subject: Add BTL-4 article: auditing a model card against its own weights
body:
BTL-4 (badtheorylabs/BTL-4) is a 35B agentic model posted 2026-08-05 with a
78.4% SWE-bench Verified claim, no technical report, no third-party evaluation
and zero all-time downloads. Rather than take or dismiss the card, the article
checks it against the artifact: config.json, the safetensors index, and HTTP
range requests into the shards. No model downloaded, no benchmark re-run.

What verifies:
- The `base_model: Ornith-1.0-35B` claim is exact. Ornith's config matches
  BTL-4's on every architectural field (40 layers, 2048 hidden, 256 experts
  top-8, 248320 vocab, 262144 context, every-4th-layer full attention, 27-layer
  vision tower), and both tensor maps hold the identical 31,666 names.
- Weights are real and complete: 21 shards, 70.21 GB, 35.11B bf16 params.
- Lineage lands next to existing coverage — Ornith is qwen3_5_moe, the same
  substrate as Intern-S2-Mobius, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's parameter count is the
  exact figure measured earlier for Macaron-V1-Tall's base.

What does not:
- The LiveCodeBench v6 table is arithmetically impossible. easy 99.1 / medium
  86.7 / hard 60.5 at the stated 45% hard pins the aggregate between 74.9% and
  81.7%; the card reports 66.1%. Reaching 66.1% needs 78.6% hard and zero easy,
  which would leave the easy row scoring an empty set. New LcbCheck interactive
  makes the bound draggable.
- The artifact says LoRA and the card does not. config.json carries
  `unsloth_version`, `transformers_version`, and a `model_name` of
  /vol/merged/btl4-pilot; the card says only "fine-tuned".
- SWE-bench Verified 78.4% is the largest claim with the least method: three
  words, no base comparison, no scaffold named, while BFCL and LiveCodeBench
  both get full protocol sentences and BFCL gets a proper paired comparison.

The weight diff, and a correction inside it:
Comparing dtype-matched tensors by range request shows every projection matrix
changed (expert gate/down_proj, shared expert, linear-attn in_proj_qkv,
full-attn q_proj) while routers, embeddings, lm_head, the whole vision tower,
and linear-attn A_log/dt_bias are byte-identical — a textbook LoRA target set.
The first pass wrongly flagged all norms as changed; they are F32 in BTL-4 and
BF16 in Ornith, so the comparison was across formats. The correction is
confirmed by arithmetic: the two checkpoints differ by exactly 603,136 bytes and
BTL-4 reports exactly 301,568 F32 params (301,568 x 2 = 603,136). The method
tab of the WeightProbe interactive documents this and the limits of a windowed
comparison.

A_log being untouched cross-links to /articles/kda-half-life: BTL-4's
forgetting timescales are Ornith's, unmodified.

The article also lifts out the genuinely good part of the card — the
reasoning_content accumulation warning for vLLM, which is correct, specific and
expensive to learn in production.

Two original interactives, no embedded figures (the repository ships none).
Verified in light and dark: no clipping, no horizontal overflow, no JSX space
drops, no console errors. `pnpm validate` green.

subject: Add Intern-S2-Mobius and RLM articles; expand and star Prime Agent
body:
Three articles, all dated 2026-08-06.

**New: Intern-S2-Mobius** (content/articles/intern-s2-mobius.mdx)
Shanghai AI Lab's 35B continual-pretrain of Qwen3.5-35B on the Mobius-v0
architecture. The central claim is verified against the released code rather
than paraphrased from the card: `block_idx = layer_idx % num_blocks` in
modeling_interns2_mobius.py means all 40 decoder layers share just four
physical MoE "memory bank" objects, each queried by ten layers spread across
depth. Also surfaced from the config, and stated nowhere in the README: the
memory-bank cycle and the attention-type cycle share a period of 4, so bank 3
is always the group's one full-attention layer.

Reported honestly against the card's own figures: Mobius loses to its base
model on UGD hard (73.02 vs 78.02) and HLE (19.11 vs 22.40); the 2.9-4.6x
throughput headline describes only the average panel, and on AIME 2026 and
HMMT 2026 the Transformer baseline is faster at three of five batch sizes;
the speedup tracks trace compression, so it shrinks wherever the model still
has to think at length. Two interactives (MemoryMap, TraceCompression) plus
three real card figures.

**New: Recursive Language Models** (content/articles/recursive-language-models.mdx)
The idea behind Prime Agent's interface, credited to its actual origin: Alex
L. Zhang (MIT CSAIL, October 2025), formalized with Tim Kraska and Omar
Khattab as arXiv 2512.24601. Draws the line between the paper's design, Prime
Intellect's RLMEnv reproduction, and Prime Agent's generalization of the same
two mechanisms to a whole coding agent. Quotes the abstract's exact
comparative numbers (26% over compaction, 130% over CodeAct with sub-calls,
13% over Claude Code, median across benchmarks) and the post-trained
RLM-Qwen3-8B result. Two interactives (RecursionTree, ContextInWindowVsVariable)
and both paper figures.

**Expanded: Prime Agent** (content/articles/prime-agent.mdx) — now featured
Rewritten from a full clone rather than the shallow one the first version had.
Four new sections and two new interactives:

- The typed host-request bridge. "One tool" is true of what the provider sees;
  behind the kernel are 21 typed handlers registered in
  _createKernelHostHandlers(), most of them conditionally. The schema did not
  disappear, it moved somewhere that costs zero prompt tokens per turn — and
  closing a gate removes the handler from the dispatch table entirely, which
  is capability gating in code rather than in a prompt. New HostBridge
  interactive.
- MCP without adding a tool: integrations are Python skills running the mcp
  SDK inside the kernel, with discovery moved into the turn.
- Two memories, one of which forgets: compaction summarizes the transcript
  while the kernel namespace is exempt, plus the 2000-char tool-result
  truncation and split-turn handling that the REPL design forces.
- What runs when nobody is attached: heartbeats, schedules, goals, autonomous
  mode with workspace-aware gate reruns, and the ACP _meta envelope.

Maturity section replaced outright. The previous one said the commit history
could not be audited; measured from a full clone it is 4,473 commits, 231
authors, 48 tags, first commit 2025-08-09. Mario Zechner authored 3,099 of
them (69%) through 2026-05-08; Prime Intellect's first commit is 2026-05-21,
and the Prime Agent era is 482 commits by 17 authors. New CommitHistory
interactive. Also corrects "hard fork" — the git history is pi-mono's own,
unbroken — and notes 0.7.0's collapse of the three agent-message delivery
modes into always-steering, which the docs still describe as three.

All figures flattened onto white, served locally, capped at 1600px. Verified
in light and dark at 1000px: no clipping, no horizontal overflow, no JSX
space drops, no console errors. `pnpm validate` green.

subject: Add Pokee-Isaac 28B and Prime Agent articles
body:
Pokee-Isaac 28B: a 28B "non-decoder-only" model claiming a 10M-token context on
a single B200 (137K tok/s prefill, 335 tok/s decode, RULER 93.3%), pitched at
regulated and on-device deployments where data cannot leave the boundary. That
deployment argument is real and underserved, and the article takes it seriously.

The central finding is what the report does not contain. "non-decoder-only" is
the headline architectural claim and appears exactly twice -- once in the
abstract, once in the introduction -- with no architecture section, no diagram,
no equation and no named mechanism anywhere in nineteen pages. Verified directly:
zero occurrences of state space, Mamba, SSM, recurrence, hybrid attention or
linear attention. The product page only repeats "purpose-built agentic
architecture". The one concrete clue is that "some weights in Pokee-Isaac are
fine-tuned from Qwen3.6-27B", a dense decoder model, against Isaac's 28B dense --
flagged as inference, not fact, since nothing in the report lets you check what
that gap is. Set against /articles/kimi-k3, whose report spends its page budget
writing down KDA's actual recurrence.

Also surfaced from the report's own tables: on MCP-Atlas, the benchmark built
against real production MCP servers, Isaac places 3rd of 6, behind two of the
cost-optimized cloud systems the abstract says it matches or exceeds; the report
calls Terminal-Bench "the one benchmark where a cloud baseline finishes ahead",
which does not square with that. On DTAP, Isaac ran under Pokee's own harness
while all five baselines ran the stock runner. And arXiv:submit/7908231 is a
submission-tracking number, not a public arXiv ID.

Prime Agent: an MIT-licensed coding and research agent whose interface to the
world is a persistent Python REPL rather than a tool-call schema, so context
becomes variables you can slice and subagents become function calls. The second
thread is /refine, a self-improving harness forbidden from touching its own base
prompt -- and the guard is code-enforced, not documentation: validateEdit()
returns "base system prompt is not editable" for any edit targeting it, with
snapshots for rollback.

The article states plainly that the repo publishes no agent-quality benchmark
numbers anywhere, so this is an architecture and a set of design decisions rather
than a measured result. Licence is MIT with dual copyright, Mario Zechner 2025
and Prime Intellect 2026 -- an acknowledged hard fork of Zechner's pi-mono. No
figures: the only images are a logo and TUI screenshots still carrying pre-rename
pi-mono branding, so using them would misrepresent the current product.

subject: Add kimi-k3-in-c: running a 2.78T model on one CPU in 8 GB
body:
A 4,779-line C99 engine (Apache-2.0, 176 KB binary) that runs Kimi K3 from a
1.56 TB checkpoint in 8.24 GB of RSS at 32.69 s/token, and claims byte-identical
output at every memory budget from 8 GB to 224 GB. Written from the source rather
than the README.

The three things worth the article:

MXFP4 inverts the usual intuition about quantisation. One expert is 132 MB as
fp32 and 17.55 MB packed; a token touches 1,472 of them. Because matrix-vector is
memory bound, reading 7.5x fewer bytes makes the packed kernel FASTER than
dequantise-then-multiply. Its own comment: "This is not an optimisation; it is
what makes streaming experts possible at all."

The determinism is engineered, not lucky. Four accumulators partitioned by i%4
and reduced as (a0+a1)+(a2+a3), written out explicitly to fix a summation order,
with the bf16 and both AVX2 paths reproducing the same tree so all three agree
bit for bit. It is equally clear about where it is NOT exact: the MXFP4 path
deliberately differs from dequantise-then-matmul, with every product exact in
double and the reassociation bounded near 1e-16 against a 1e-6 gate.

The cache is the point of the project, and the article keeps the unflattering
result: K3's Quantile Balancing keeps expert usage flat by design, which is
exactly what defeats an LRU cache, so below ~36 GB of arena the bytes read per
token do not move at all. A full-recompute trace predicted a 36% hit rate at 8
GB; steady-state decode measured 0%. The repo reported that rather than smoothing
it over.

Added three findings from my own pass through the source that the draft omitted,
each verified verbatim before quoting:

- The INFLIGHT slot state exists because of a real race the comment confesses to:
  the batch prefetch marked a slot EMPTY before reading into it, and pick_victim's
  fast path then handed the same slot to the next expert in the batch. It cost
  exactly one wrong token, 65 instead of 2494, and nothing in the fixtures because
  no fixture exercises the cache. One silently wrong token inside fluent output is
  the failure mode worth naming.
- Why the trunk stays bf16: a 31-tensor sensitivity study measures ~1% mean
  relative weight error at int8 against ~17% at int4, worst rows 45/56/65%. The
  missing bit-width knob is the decision being enforced. Noted the study's own
  limit, that it measures weight error and not output quality.
- O_DIRECT cold reads at 3.2 GB/s beat buffered on their hardware, which the repo
  flags as the opposite of the usual expectation and the reason the trunk is
  opened O_DIRECT.

subject: Confirm the KDA log-alpha inference from an independent C implementation
body:
The kda-half-life article inferred that gate_lower_bound: -5.0 is a floor on
log alpha, and flagged that as an assumption because neither the config nor the
report states the functional form. FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c computes it
exactly that way:

  const float gi = lb * sigmoidf_(u);   /* in (lb, 0]  -> log alpha */
  alpha[i] = expf(gi);                  /* in (e^lb, 1]             */

So the 0.14-token floor holds. Replaced the warning callout with the code and a
note that the inference is now confirmed.

The code also refines one claim: A_log is stored per HEAD, and the per-channel
variation comes from the z + dt_bias term inside the sigmoid, so a channel's
decay is a per-head base rate modulated per channel rather than a fully
independent per-channel parameter. Softened the body sentence accordingly rather
than leaving it to be walked back by the callout. The Diag(alpha_t) structure and
the spread of timescales are unaffected.
